d: Nothing — extensions inherit the original approval.
Resets the J&A posting clock.
Converts the bridge into a logical follow-on.
recall_advanced.x: Each repeat bridge escalates to higher approval — the system's way of making planning failures expensive. Extensions don't inherit the first approval; every one re-justifies against a bar that keeps rising.

recall_advanced.q: Why is apparent authority the trap in unauthorized commitment (UAC) cases?
recall_advanced.a: Because looking authorized isn't being authorized — the contractor can't rely on it, and neither can you.
d: Because apparent authority binds the Government retroactively.
Because it converts automatically to implied authority.
Because ratification cures it without any investigation.
recall_advanced.x: Apparent authority is the trap because it FEELS binding on the ground — a colonel said go — but binds nothing legally. The contractor can't rely on it and neither can you; only ratification by actual authority fixes what it breaks.

recall_advanced.q: Name the classic examples of source selection information.
recall_advanced.a: Proposed rankings, the source selection plan, evaluation results, competitive-range lists, the Government estimate.
d: The synopsis, the PWS, and the wage determination.
CPARS ratings and SAM registration data.
The clause matrix and Section K representations.
recall_advanced.x: The classics: proposed rankings, the source selection plan, evaluation results, competitive-range lists, the Government estimate. If it could hand an offeror an edge in THIS competition, treat it as SSI and control it.

recall_advanced.q: When must you spot an organizational conflict of interest (OCI) to have real options?
recall_advanced.a: Early — before solicitation; avoid, neutralize, and mitigate all work best pre-release.
d: At award — that's when the conflict legally attaches.
During discussions, once proposals are in.
At the debrief, when offerors raise it.
recall_advanced.x: OCI options exist before solicitation: you can still avoid (change the requirement), neutralize (restructure), or mitigate (firewall). After proposals arrive, most doors have closed and exclusion may be all that's left. Early is everything.

recall_advanced.q: Responsibility is decided as of when, on what evidence?
recall_advanced.a: At award, on the record before the CO — today's facts, documented.
d: At proposal receipt, on SAM status alone.
At solicitation release, on CPARS history.
Continuously — it's re-decided at each invoice.
recall_advanced.x: Responsibility is decided at award, on documented facts as they stand that day — not proposal-time snapshots, not continuous re-adjudication. A firm non-responsible today can be responsible next quarter; the determination is dated for a reason.

recall_advanced.q: Bundling rides on which research finding?
recall_advanced.a: Whether consolidating the requirement is necessary and justified — the research has to support it.
d: Whether the incumbent can absorb the added work.
Whether two NAICS codes share a size standard.
Whether GSA offers a comparable schedule.
recall_advanced.x: Bundling — consolidating requirements small businesses used to win separately — must be necessary and justified, and the market research is where that case lives or dies. It's a research finding, not a convenience call.

recall_advanced.q: What makes a source "mandatory" — and what doesn't unlock the open market?
recall_advanced.a: Being on the procurement list; price alone doesn't unlock the open market.
d: Agency preference; a D&F unlocks it.
A GSA listing; the ombudsman unlocks it.
Set-aside status; a J&A unlocks it.
recall_advanced.x: Mandatory means on the procurement list and meeting the need — and price alone doesn't unlock the open market. Fit and availability problems go through the program channels, documented; unilateral 'it's cheaper commercial' is the violation pattern.

recall_advanced.q: Which termination framework rides with commercial contracts?
recall_advanced.a: The commercial clause's cause/convenience framework — not Part 49's machinery.
d: Part 49 in full, like any other contract.
T4D with cure notices under 49.x.
No termination rights at all — that's the commercial trade.
recall_advanced.x: Commercial contracts terminate under the commercial clause's cause/convenience framework — Part 49's cure-notice machinery and reprocurement remedies don't apply as such. Boards love this seam; knowing which regime you're in is the answer.

recall_advanced.q: Simplified acquisition procedures (SAP) exists for what two purposes?
recall_advanced.a: Speed routine buys with less paperwork, and create small-business opportunity.
d: Avoid competition and reduce protest exposure.
Extend GPC limits and defer funding.
Test vendors before committing to IDIQ awards.
recall_advanced.x: SAP exists to speed routine buys with proportionate paperwork AND to create small-business opportunity — the micro-purchase threshold (MPT)-to-simplified acquisition threshold (SAT) reservation is baked into the band. It's not competition avoidance; it's competition right-sized.

recall_advanced.q: HUBZone brings what feature in full-and-open competition?
recall_advanced.a: A price evaluation preference.
d: An automatic 10% technical rating bonus.
Exemption from responsibility determinations.
First-refusal rights on the award.
recall_advanced.x: In full-and-open competition, HUBZone firms get a price evaluation preference — their offer is evaluated as if competing offers cost more. It's the one program benefit that operates INSIDE unrestricted competition rather than through a set-aside.

recall_advanced.q: "We've always used this vendor" is…?
recall_advanced.a: Not a reason — habit isn't an exception; the default is competition.
d: A logical follow-on rationale.
Exception (1) in embryo — document it and proceed.
Acceptable below $10M.
recall_advanced.x: Incumbency is a fact, not an exception. 'We've always used them' appears nowhere in RFO 6.103 — if the incumbent is genuinely the only capable source, prove THAT with research; the history alone justifies nothing.

recall_advanced.q: Cost/price and what else are mandatory evaluation factors?
recall_advanced.a: Quality AND past performance — three required factors in all, not two.
d: Past performance and small-business participation, always.
Schedule and data rights.
None — evaluation factors are fully discretionary.
recall_advanced.x: Three, not two. RFO 15.104(b) requires price or cost (b)(1), quality (b)(2), and past performance (b)(3) — “Past performance must be evaluated in every competitive source selection, unless the contracting officer documents the reason past performance is not an appropriate evaluation factor.” Quality is itself evaluated through one or more non-cost factors. ⚠ DoD-specific: 15.104(b)(1)(ii) lets the CO omit price or cost as an evaluation factor on an above-simplified acquisition threshold (SAT) multiple-award request for proposals (RFP) for same-or-similar services where award goes to every qualifying offeror — the carve-out a DoD panel is most likely to probe.

recall_advanced.topic: Certified Cost or Pricing Data & Proposal Analysis
recall_advanced.q: Who signs the Certificate of Current Cost or Pricing Data, and when?
recall_advanced.a: The contractor, at agreement on price — certifying the data current, accurate, and complete.
d: The CO, at award.
DCAA, after the post-agreement sweep.
The contractor's counsel, at proposal submission.
recall_advanced.x: The contractor signs the Certificate of Current Cost or Pricing Data at price agreement — certifying the data was current, accurate, and complete AS OF that agreement. That certificate is what makes defective pricing enforceable later.

recall_advanced.q: Why does cost-plus-incentive-fee (CPIF) need a "credible target"?
recall_advanced.a: The incentive only disciplines cost if the target means something — a fantasy target pays fee for noise.
d: Because DCAA audits the target annually.
It doesn't — CPIF works at any target.
Because fee is capped at 10% of target cost.
recall_advanced.x: CPIF's fee swing only disciplines cost if the target is credible — a fantasy target pays fee for noise, punishing or rewarding luck. No believable target, no incentive contract: that honesty check is the type-selection discipline.

recall_advanced.q: Fair opportunity means every holder gets what?
recall_advanced.a: A real chance to be considered for each order — genuine consideration, not rotation paperwork.
d: An equal share of orders over the vehicle's life.
A guaranteed minimum on each order.
A debrief on every order, at any value.
recall_advanced.x: Fair opportunity means each holder gets genuinely considered for each order — real evaluation, not rotation paperwork or 'considered but lost' templates. If your record couldn't convince the ombudsman the consideration was real, it wasn't.

recall_advanced.q: Options are evaluated when, and priced when?
recall_advanced.a: Both at award — that's exactly what makes later exercise unilateral.
d: Both at exercise.
Priced at award, evaluated at exercise.
Evaluated at award, repriced at exercise.
recall_advanced.x: Options are evaluated AND priced at award — that's what earns the Government the unilateral right to exercise later. An option that was never evaluated or priced can't simply be exercised; it's a new negotiation wearing an option's clothes.

recall_advanced.q: The assisted-acquisition agreement must define what, before funds move?
recall_advanced.a: Roles and responsibilities — who does what between the agencies.
d: The protest venue for future orders.
The servicing agency's fee cap.
A NAICS crosswalk between the agencies.
recall_advanced.x: Before a dollar moves in an assisted acquisition, the interagency agreement defines roles: who solicits, who awards, who administers, whose rules govern. Money without a role map is how interagency actions end up in the Government Accountability Office (GAO) reports.

recall_advanced.q: Non-severable effort funded incrementally "to stretch the money" — problem?
recall_advanced.a: Yes — non-severable work must be fully funded up front; incremental funding there is a fiscal violation.
d: No — increments are always authorized for services.
Only if the effort crosses fiscal years.
Only above the SAT.
recall_advanced.x: Non-severable work is a bona fide need of the award year and must be fully funded up front — incremental funding to 'stretch the money' violates Time and Amount at once. Severability isn't a style choice; it's a funding-law classification.

recall_advanced.q: Limited rights vs. restricted rights — which attaches to what?
recall_advanced.a: Limited → technical data; restricted → computer software (both born of private-expense development).
d: Limited → software; restricted → technical data.
Both attach only to mixed-funding items.
Limited → hardware; restricted → firmware.
recall_advanced.x: Limited rights attach to technical data, restricted rights to computer software — both born of private-expense development. Same concept, two vocabularies, and boards check whether you match the right label to the right subject matter.

recall_advanced.q: In-scope mods and the synopsis — what's the rule?
recall_advanced.a: In-scope mods aren't competed or synopsized; out-of-scope work is new work — compete it or justify it.
d: All mods over $150K are synopsized.
Synopsis is required only for cost growth over 25%.
Out-of-scope mods may proceed on bilateral signature alone.
recall_advanced.x: In-scope mods ride the original competition — no synopsis, no new competition. Out-of-scope work is a new procurement: compete it or justify it under Part 6. The synopsis question is answered entirely by the scope analysis.

recall_advanced.q: Furnishing Government-furnished property (GFP) changes the Government's posture how?
recall_advanced.a: The Government takes on performance obligations — late or faulty GFP is Government-caused delay.
d: It shifts all property risk to the contractor.
It has no schedule significance.
It converts the contract to cost-type.
recall_advanced.x: GFP puts the Government ON the performance path: late or defective property is Government-caused delay with equitable-adjustment exposure. You're not just lending equipment — you're accepting schedule obligations.

recall_advanced.q: Why do undefinitized contract actions (UCAs) weaken the Government's negotiating position?
recall_advanced.a: The contractor performs while the price is open — comfort without cost pressure; leverage decays monthly.
d: They don't — the NTE ceiling protects the position.
Because clearance happens at award.
Because fee is locked at the UCA stage.
recall_advanced.x: Undefinitized performance is cost-reimbursement comfort at negotiation leverage: every month without a definitized price, actuals accumulate and your position decays. The caps and the 180-day clock are the counterweights — enforce them.

recall_advanced.q: Clearance protects against what, fundamentally?
recall_advanced.a: Committing the Government before an independent set of eyes checks strategy, price, and compliance.
d: Contractor default after award.
ADA violations at obligation.
Debrief disputes before award.
recall_advanced.x: Clearance is the independent check between 'we negotiated it' and 'the Government is bound by it' — strategy, price support, and compliance verified by someone who doesn't own the deal. It exists because self-review is no review.

recall_advanced.q: The agency-protest venue's superpower?
recall_advanced.a: Speed and self-correction — fixing your own error fastest, without GAO.
d: An automatic stay stronger than GAO's.
Binding precedent for future buys.
Recovery of proposal costs.
recall_advanced.x: The agency protest is fastest and self-correcting — your own agency fixing its own error without the Government Accountability Office's (GAO) 100-day process. Its limits: no automatic-stay teeth like GAO, no binding judgment like the U.S. Court of Federal Claims (COFC). Speed is the trade.

recall_advanced.q: Interest on a claim runs from when?
recall_advanced.a: When the CO receives the certified claim.
d: The date performance costs were incurred.
The CO's final decision.
The notice of appeal.
recall_advanced.x: The Contract Disputes Act (CDA) interest runs from the contracting officer's (CO) RECEIPT of the certified claim — not from costs incurred, not from the final decision. That start date is why misclassifying a functional claim as a request for equitable adjustment (REA) is expensive: the meter was already running.

recall_advanced.q: Termination for convenience (T4C) exists because the Government reserves what?
recall_advanced.a: The right to end a contract in the Government's best interest — with the contractor made whole for work done.
d: The right to re-compete every contract annually.
A price-reduction remedy for market drops.
An offset against the contractor's future awards.
recall_advanced.x: T4C is the Government's reserved right to end a contract in its best interest — needs change, programs die — with the contractor made whole for work performed. It's the escape valve that makes long-term Government contracting possible at all.

recall_advanced.q: Other Transactions (OTs) trade away what, for agility?
recall_advanced.a: The mature protections framework of regulation-based contracting — spend that trade only when it buys something.
d: Intellectual-property rights entirely.
Access to nontraditional contractors.
Competition requirements — OTs are sole-source by design.
recall_advanced.x: OTs trade the mature protections framework — competition rules, cost principles, disputes machinery — for agility. That trade is worth making only when it buys something real: nontraditionals at the table, prototype-speed terms. Never as rule avoidance.

recall_advanced.q: Architect-engineer (A&E) selection runs on what basis?
recall_advanced.a: Qualifications-based selection, then fair-price negotiation with the most qualified firm.
d: Lowest price among technically acceptable designers.
A best-value tradeoff, like any service.
Rotation among registered local firms.
recall_advanced.x: A&E runs on qualifications-based selection: rank firms on qualifications, negotiate price with the most qualified. Design quality drives lifecycle cost far more than design fee — the statute does that math for you.

scenarios.scenario: Eight months before a satellite-imagery software sustainment need begins, the program manager (PM) tells you she's unhappy with the incumbent developer and "wants competition this time — put out a request for proposals (RFP) next month." The system was built on the incumbent's commercial platform; the development contract delivered binaries and user manuals; the Government "probably has rights to something, nobody's checked." Two integrators have expressed informal interest, "assuming they can get the code."

facts.why: Desire isn't feasibility. An RFP before the rights-and-deliverables inventory is a solicitation you may have to cancel — strategy first, paper second.
The competition's real constraint: without source, build environments, and interface data, "assuming they can get the code" is doing tectonic work. What we hold decides what we can compete.
The platform rides its commercial license — a competitor needs lawful access. That's a licensing workstream inside the strategy, not a footnote.
Real market signal — formalize it with a sources-sought shaped around what the Government can actually furnish, and let their responses size the feasible competition.

scenarios.board_answer: Eight months is enough if we spend it right: first the data-rights and deliverables inventory — what we hold decides what we can compete; then a sources-sought built on what we can actually furnish; then the strategy call. If the inventory says competition isn't feasible yet, the honest plan may be a shorter incumbent bridge while we buy the deliverables that make next cycle competitive — and that gets written down as the strategy.

coach.qtype: an acquisition-strategy question — RFO Part 7 planning built on RFO Part 10 market research: competitive posture, timing, and what the file must prove.
coach.smes: the program manager (PM)/requiring activity, Legal (JA), the Competition Advocate, and your pricing office.
coach.rule: Strategy precedes paper: no solicitation, bridge, or justification and approval (J&A) before the rights-deliverables-market inventory is done — and lack of advance planning never justifies skipping it (RFO Part 6).

scenarios.ask: The PM wants the RFP on the street next month. How do you advise her, and what's your plan for the next eight months?
scenarios.script: This is an acquisition-strategy question — RFO Part 7 planning riding on RFO Part 10 market research: competitive posture and timing. Before I answer the RFP request, I'd pull in Legal, my pricing office, and the program engineers on data rights. The default is competition under the Competition in Contracting Act (CICA) and RFO Part 6, and I want it too — but strategy precedes paper. First move is the inventory: what data rights, source code, interfaces, and tooling the Government actually holds, because what we hold decides what we can compete. Then a sources-sought built on what we can actually furnish. If the inventory says competition isn't feasible yet, the honest plan is a short, justified incumbent bridge while we buy the deliverables that make the next cycle competitive — written down as the strategy, with dates.

follow_ups.q: You said data rights decide what you can compete. Walk me through the rights levels for technical data.
follow_ups.h: Three levels, keyed to who paid for the development.
follow_ups.d: R-DFARS 227: development entirely with Government funds → unlimited rights — use, modify, disclose to anyone for any purpose. Mixed funding → Government Purpose Rights — internal use plus release for Government purposes (including competitive reprocurement under protections), converting to unlimited after the period. Entirely private expense → limited rights — internal use and emergency repair/overhaul only. The contractor asserts and proves restrictions through the assertion list; unasserted, unmarked data defaults toward the Government.

follow_ups.q: If you conclude only the incumbent can perform, what authority do you use — and who approves it?
follow_ups.h: One of the seven, plus a ladder that runs on dollars.
follow_ups.d: RFO 6.103-1, only one responsible source — a justification and approval (J&A) built on market research that would survive a competitor's lawyer. Approval rides the RFO 6.104 ladder: the contracting officer's (CO) certification to $900K, Competition Advocate to $20M, head of the procuring activity (HPA)/program executive officer (PEO) to $90M ($150M DoD), senior procurement executive (SPE) above. Post to SAM.gov within 14 days of award. For a sustainment effort of this size, expect the Competition Advocate or higher — and expect the market-research section to carry the whole document.

follow_ups.q: And if the follow-on can't award in time — what makes a bridge contract justifiable?
follow_ups.h: The cause has to be one the Government couldn't foresee.
follow_ups.d: A bridge stands on genuinely unforeseen causes — a protest, a directed strategy change, a regulatory shift — never lack of advance planning. It takes a rigorous justification: the need, the purpose and duration of the bridge, and the concrete steps that prevent the next one, in a decision memorandum. Repeat bridges escalate to higher approval each round, which is the system making planning failures progressively more expensive.

scenarios.scenario: During a staff visit you learn the fuels flight has been getting weekly analytics reports from a small software vendor since January. The squadron commander "approved it on a trial basis" after a vendor demo; the vendor now wants a PO for $95K covering the trial "as agreed." The commander points out he's a colonel with command authority, the unit genuinely uses the reports, and "there's end-of-year money to cover it." He asks you to just issue the purchase order this week.

facts.why: Rank and command authority are not contracting authority. Only a warranted CO binds the Government — this is apparent authority, which binds nothing.

facts.fact: The unit genuinely uses the reports
facts.why: Government benefit is real — that's one ratification element satisfied, and it's why ratification (not refusal) is the likely path.
The test is funds available when the commitment was made (January) and now — and the right color/year of money for what was actually received. "There's money lying around" isn't the test.

A PO now would paper over the violation. The path is a ratification package at the right level ($95K ≤ simplified acquisition threshold (SAT) → chief of the contracting office (COCO)), with the commander's signed statement in it.

scenarios.board_answer: That's an unauthorized commitment — command authority isn't contracting authority. I'd stop further performance, investigate, and build the RFO 1.405 ratification package: benefit's there, so it turns on fund availability in January and a fair-and-reasonable price; at $95K my COCO can ratify. And then I'd train that unit, because prevention is the real fix.

coach.qtype: an authority question — RFO 1.402 warrant authority and the RFO 1.405 ratification lane: who can bind the Government, and what happens when someone who can't, did.
coach.smes: Legal (JA) first, your chief of the contracting office (COCO)/flight chief, and financial management (FM) for the funds picture.
coach.rule: Only a warranted contracting officer (CO) binds the Government (RFO 1.402). Apparent authority binds nothing — an unauthorized commitment stays unratified until an official with actual authority runs all six RFO 1.405 elements.

scenarios.ask: The commander asks you to just issue the purchase order this week. What do you tell him, and what do you actually do?
scenarios.script: This is an authority question — an unauthorized commitment, RFO 1.405 territory. My phone-a-friends are Legal first, then financial management (FM) on the funds picture. The default rule: only a warranted contracting officer binds the Government — command authority isn't contracting authority, so the Government isn't bound yet. I'd stop further performance today, investigate, and build the RFO 1.405 ratification package: the work would've been proper if a CO had done it, the Government clearly benefited, so it turns on funds availability back in January and a fair-and-reasonable price. At $95K, ratification sits at my COCO's level. And then I'd train that unit — kickoff meetings and a who-can-direct letter — because prevention is the real fix.

follow_ups.q: Recite all six ratification elements for me.
follow_ups.h: Proper-if… benefit… authority… price… funds… and one more signature.
follow_ups.d: RFO 1.405: (1) the action would have been proper if a contracting officer had done it; (2) the Government accepted or benefited from the supplies or services; (3) the ratifying official has actual contractual authority; (4) the price is fair and reasonable; (5) funds were available at the time of the commitment AND remain available now; (6) Legal concurs. All six, every time — the one that most often fails is funds availability at the time of the commitment.

follow_ups.q: Who ratifies, and what sets the level?
follow_ups.h: Delegation sets the level — not the dollar value.
follow_ups.d: RFO 1.405(b)(2) sets no dollar tier: the head of the contracting activity may ratify an unauthorized commitment at any value, and agencies may delegate that authority — but never below the chief of the contracting office. So at $95K the level comes from my activity's delegation, not from the SAT. And note who never ratifies: the person who made the commitment, or anyone in their chain trying to paper their own problem — ratification is deliberately an independent decision.

follow_ups.q: Three types of authority — which ones bind the Government?
follow_ups.h: Two are real; one only looks real.
follow_ups.d: Express authority — written and explicit, the warrant (SF 1402) — binds. Implied authority — what reasonably flows from a position's express authority — is legally valid and binds. Apparent authority — someone acting as if authorized when they aren't — binds nothing, and a contractor cannot rely on it. The colonel's command authority is real authority over his unit and zero contracting authority; that seam is where every UAC is born.

scenarios.scenario: Your source selection evaluation board (SSEB) chair calls: a technical evaluator just accepted a job with one of the three offerors — starting next month. The evaluator "hasn't told the team anything," has already recused himself from this week's consensus meetings, and says his new employer "only knows the program exists, nothing else." The program manager (PM) wants to press on: "he recused himself, we're good — we can't slip the award for HR paperwork."

facts.fact: Evaluator accepting employment with an offeror
facts.why: Employment contacts between an offeror and a Government official with access to protected information are the PIA's second front. Self-recusal isn't self-clearing — this goes to Legal now, with a facts review of everything he touched and when the employment contact began.
His assurance isn't the standard. The question is what he had access to while employment discussions were live — that's established by record review, not by promise.
Recusal was right — but timing governs. Recusal after discussions began doesn't cure access that already happened.
Schedule pressure never outranks integrity of the selection. An award made on a tainted record invites protest and worse.

scenarios.board_answer: Recusal was step one, not the answer. I'd get Legal in immediately, establish when the employment contact started and what protected information he accessed after that, document it, and make the written determination whether the selection is compromised — and if it reached the offeror, that's the head of the contracting activity's (HCA) decision on how the procurement proceeds.

coach.qtype: a Procurement Integrity Act question — RFO 3.104: protected information and what its movement does to the competition.
coach.smes: Legal (JA) immediately; the head of the contracting activity (HCA) channel if the procurement is impacted.
coach.rule: RFO 3.104 protects two classes — source selection information and contractor bid/proposal data. Contain first, document everything; the written record closes the incident, not a reply email.

scenarios.ask: The evaluator has recused himself and says no harm was done. Is this handled? What do you do?
scenarios.script: This is a Procurement Integrity Act question — RFO 3.104. Recusal was step one, not the answer — my first calls are Legal, immediately, and then the HCA channel if the facts warrant. The rule: source selection information is protected, and the danger window opened when the employment contact started, not when he told us. I'd establish exactly when that contact began, what protected information he accessed after it, and whether anything could have reached the offeror. Everything gets documented — affidavits, a memorandum for record (MFR), and my written determination on whether the selection is compromised. If information reached an actual offeror, that's presumptive taint and the HCA decides how this procurement proceeds. The record closes this, not his reassurance.

follow_ups.q: What exactly does RFO 3.104 protect?
follow_ups.h: Two classes — one belongs to the Government, one to the offerors.
follow_ups.d: Source selection information — proposed rankings, evaluation results, the source selection plan, competitive-range lists, the Government estimate — and contractor bid and proposal information: an offeror's proprietary pricing, costs, and proposal contents. Disclosing either, or attempting to obtain it, is a violation. The procuring contracting officer (PCO) is the conduit and control point for all of it.

follow_ups.q: Walk me through your response steps on a suspected violation.
follow_ups.h: Legal first — then facts, containment, and a written determination.
follow_ups.d: Notify Legal immediately; gather the facts and documents; have any recipient delete all copies and confirm with signed affidavits and nondisclosure agreements (NDAs); notify affected parties; get an MFR from the person who disclosed; then write the determination of whether the disclosure impacts the procurement. No impact: the record goes forward for concurrence and the procurement proceeds. Impact: it goes to the HCA, who can proceed, investigate further, cancel, or disqualify an offeror.

follow_ups.q: Where do the post-Government-employment rules bite in this scenario?
follow_ups.h: The clock started at the employment contact, not the resignation.
follow_ups.d: The moment the evaluator began employment discussions with an offeror, disqualification duties attached — recusal from anything affecting that firm and prompt disclosure. His danger window isn't when he told the team; it's everything he touched after the contact began. That's why the investigation reconstructs the contact date first, then maps what protected information he accessed after it.

scenarios.scenario: Source selection for a logistics IT modernization is two weeks from final proposal revisions (FPRs). An offeror's capture manager, at an industry event, mentions to your chief of the contracting office (COCO) that a rival offeror "has our staffing rates — their teaming partner processes our subcontract invoices." The rival's proposal did come in with suspiciously well-aimed pricing. The source selection evaluation board (SSEB) chair suggests quietly normalizing the evaluated rates "so no one's advantaged," and notes that pausing now "looks bad for the program."

facts.fact: Teaming partner processes the competitor's invoices
facts.why: Classic unequal access to non-public information — a structural pipeline to a competitor's cost data. No intent needed; the imbalance is the conflict.
Evaluators can't launder an organizational conflict of interest (OCI) through the evaluation. The conflict is investigated and resolved on the record, not adjusted away.
An award over an unresolved, documented OCI allegation looks worse — that's a sustained protest with the remedy chosen by someone else.
Suggestive but not proof. It justifies the inquiry; the determination rests on what access actually existed.

scenarios.board_answer: That allegation is unequal access — I'd get Legal in, establish the facts of what data actually flowed, and make a written determination. If access is real, I need avoidance, neutralization, or an enforceable mitigation before this selection proceeds — and note that handling an OCI during source selection isn't 'discussions,' so I can work it without opening exchanges.

coach.qtype: an organizational-conflict-of-interest question — RFO 9.5: the type drives the remedy.
coach.smes: Legal (JA) and your reviewing chain; a waiver runs to the agency head or a designee and is never delegated below the head of the contracting activity (HCA) (RFO 9.503).
coach.rule: Identify the type first — unequal access, impaired objectivity, biased ground rules — then avoid, neutralize, or mitigate under RFO 9.5, in that order. A firewall can't fix ground rules already written. On a significant potential conflict the contracting officer (CO) analyses and recommends; the chief of the contracting office approves, modifies, or rejects the course of action in writing before the solicitation issues (RFO 9.506(b)-(c)).

scenarios.ask: FPRs are two weeks out. What do you do with this allegation, and does working it blow up your schedule?
scenarios.script: This is an organizational-conflict-of-interest question — RFO 9.5, unequal access to nonpublic information. Legal comes in now; the head of the contracting activity (HCA) owns any waiver if it comes to that. The rule: with unequal access, the imbalance itself is the conflict — I don't need proof anyone acted on it. So I'd establish the facts of what data actually flowed through that invoice-processing relationship and make a written determination. If access is real, I need avoidance, neutralization, or an enforceable mitigation plan before this selection proceeds — and the decision on that plan is mine as the procuring contracting officer (PCO). One more thing for the panel: handling an OCI during source selection isn't 'discussions,' so I can work this without opening exchanges or wrecking the FPR schedule.

follow_ups.q: Name the three OCI types — and which is hardest to mitigate.
follow_ups.h: Access, objectivity, and the one where the requirement itself is shaped.
follow_ups.d: RFO 9.5: unequal access to nonpublic information — the imbalance itself is the conflict, no bad act required; impaired objectivity — the contractor would evaluate its own work; and biased ground rules — the contractor shaped the requirement it now wants to compete on. Biased ground rules is hardest: no firewall un-writes a spec, so exclusion is the usual outcome. Impaired objectivity is the type most likely to be waived.

follow_ups.q: What are your three handling tools, in order of preference?
follow_ups.h: Kill it, structure it away, or manage it.
follow_ups.d: Avoid — exclude the source or remove the conflicted work from the requirement; neutralize — remove the contractor from the specific conflicted activity; mitigate — reduce the impact to an acceptable level through a formal, enforceable mitigation plan. In that order. If none works and the benefit still outweighs the conflict, the waiver lane exists — HCA approval, non-delegable.

follow_ups.q: Who has final say on the mitigation plan?
follow_ups.h: Panels advise. One signature decides.
follow_ups.d: The PCO. The review machinery — Legal review, the OCI panel with its recommendations — advises — but on a significant potential conflict the RFO puts the approval above me. I submit the written analysis and my recommended course of action to the chief of the contracting office before the solicitation issues, and that official approves, modifies, or rejects it in writing (RFO 9.506(b)-(c)); I then resolve the conflict consistent with that approval or the HCA's direction (9.506(d)(3), 9.504(c)). Say that plainly at the board: 'I own the analysis and the recommendation — the approval sits one level up.' It's exactly the kind of authority question panels probe to see if you know where your own signature sits.

scenarios.scenario: Award week on a grounds-maintenance indefinite-delivery/indefinite-quantity (IDIQ) set-aside. Your apparent awardee — a small business — was terminated for default by another base fourteen months ago; their proposal explains new ownership and a rebuilt crew. The program manager (PM) forwards a rumor from the old contract's contracting officer's representative (COR) that "these guys always bail mid-summer." Your specialist notes they're clean in SAM. The customer wants award Friday because the mowing season "won't wait for paperwork."

facts.fact: Prior termination for default (T4D) fourteen months ago
facts.why: A recent default squarely engages the performance-record standard. It's not automatically disqualifying — but it must be weighed on the record against the new-ownership facts.
Exactly the kind of countervailing fact the determination exists to evaluate. Verify it — org charts, key personnel, financing — don't just quote the proposal.
Hearsay isn't a finding. Chase it to documented performance history (CPARS, the T4D record) or drop it.
Necessary, not sufficient — exclusions and responsibility are different gates.
If the facts add to non-responsible, the Small Business Administration (SBA) referral happens regardless of the mowing season — and the CoC may still direct award.

scenarios.board_answer: I'd make the determination on documented facts — the default record versus verified evidence of new ownership and capacity. Clean SAM isn't the test, and rumors don't count. If I land on non-responsible, they're small, so it goes to SBA for the CoC decision — and Friday moves if it has to.

coach.qtype: a responsibility question — the seven RFO 9.104 standards, applied to today's facts.
coach.smes: your contracting chain, Legal, and the Small Business Administration (SBA) — a small-business referral is mandatory under RFO Part 19, and a CoC is conclusive.
coach.rule: Doubt cuts in the Government's favor — doubt means no. But the 'no' must stand on the RFO 9.104 standards and documented facts, never on undocumented distrust.

scenarios.ask: Award is scheduled Friday. Can you award to this contractor — and what do you do about the rumor?
scenarios.script: This is a responsibility question — the seven RFO 9.104 standards, applied to today's facts. My help: my chain, Legal, and the SBA, because this offeror is small. The default: doubt cuts in the Government's favor — but doubt has to stand on documented facts, not rumors. So I'd verify: is the new ownership real, is the rebuilt crew under contract, what does the default record actually show against the standards for performance and integrity? Rumors from a competitor don't count and clean SAM isn't the test. If I land on non-responsible, referral to SBA is mandatory under RFO Part 19 — and a Certificate of Competency, if issued, is conclusive. Friday moves if it has to; an award I can't defend moves nothing.

follow_ups.q: Recite the seven responsibility standards.
follow_ups.h: Money, time, record, character, organization, gear, and eligibility.
follow_ups.d: RFO 9.104: adequate financial resources or the ability to obtain them; ability to comply with the delivery or performance schedule; a satisfactory performance record; a satisfactory record of integrity and business ethics; the necessary organization, experience, accounting and operational controls, and technical skills; the necessary equipment and facilities; and otherwise qualified and eligible under applicable laws.

follow_ups.q: What system checks precede award, and at what threshold?
follow_ups.h: One always; one over the simplified acquisition threshold (SAT).
follow_ups.d: SAM exclusions on every action, no floor — an excluded contractor is ineligible, period. The Federal Awardee Performance and Integrity Information System (FAPIIS) review for actions over the SAT ($350K) — the integrity and performance record system where things like that prior default live. This scenario is exactly why the FAPIIS check exists: it surfaces history a clean SAM search and a fresh Commercial and Government Entity (CAGE) code won't.

follow_ups.q: SBA issues the CoC — can you appeal it?
follow_ups.h: There's a dollar band where you can.
follow_ups.d: A Certificate of Competency conclusively establishes responsibility — you award. There is no dollar band: RFO 19.204(i) makes a COC final on all elements of responsibility, and 19.204(j) says award elsewhere if no COC issues within 15 business days of the referral. For DoD, R-DFARS 219.204 sends me to PGI 219.204 — notify the department OSBP director within 5 working days of SBA Headquarters' written position, appeal file 5 working days after, and the OSBP director decides whether the agency appeals. And either way, the Government's protection shifts to administration: a hard quality assurance surveillance plan (QASP), milestone surveillance, early engagement at the first slip.

scenarios.scenario: A depot needs specialized corrosion-inspection services, estimated $4.5M over three years. The incumbent's contract ends in five months. The program manager (PM) hands you last cycle's market research — dated 26 months ago — showing "only the incumbent responded," plus an email from the incumbent's BD lead helpfully listing why competitors "can't meet the certification requirements." Your specialist mentions two small firms recently won similar work at another command.

facts.why: RFO 10.001 sets no currency clock, but 10.001(b) requires research before the requirements document and the solicitation in front of me — research this old predates both. It can inform, but it can't carry a new strategy. Fresh research is step one.

facts.fact: Incumbent's list of why competitors can't perform
facts.why: Market intelligence authored by the party that benefits from no competition is not market research. Verify independently or discard.

facts.fact: Two small firms winning similar work elsewhere
facts.why: Live evidence of capability — chase it: scope comparability, certifications, capacity. It bears directly on the Rule of Two.
Tight but workable — and "no time to research" is how bad bridges get born. The timeline argues for starting now, not skipping it.

scenarios.board_answer: That research is stale and the most persuasive document in the file was written by the incumbent — I'd run a fresh sources-sought now, engage the two small firms directly, and let the results drive the set-aside and competition decisions. Five months is enough if we start today; if it slips, a short bridge with a real cause beats a sole source built on a competitor's brochure.

coach.qtype: a market-research question — RFO Part 10: evidence before decisions.
coach.smes: the requiring activity's subject-matter experts (SMEs), your Small Business Professional, and industry itself — sources sought, request for informations (RFIs), industry days.
coach.rule: RFO Part 10 research is the evidence; the commerciality, competition, and set-aside calls are decisions built on it. Undocumented research supports nothing downstream — and RFO 10.001(b) ties research to the event it supports (a new requirements document, a solicitation over the simplified acquisition threshold (SAT), an order over the SAT), not to a shelf life.

scenarios.ask: The PM says the research is done and only the incumbent can perform. How do you proceed with five months left?
scenarios.script: This is a market-research question — RFO Part 10: research is the evidence under every decision that follows. My partners here are the requiring activity's engineers, my Small Business Professional, and industry itself. The rules: RFO 10.001(b) ties research to the event it supports rather than to a shelf life, and this file is 26 months old — it predates the requirement I'm about to solicit — worse, its most persuasive document was written by the incumbent. So I'd run a fresh sources-sought today, engage the two small firms directly, and let real results drive the set-aside and competition calls. Five months is enough if we start now. If it slips anyway, a short bridge with a genuine cause beats a sole source built on a competitor's brochure — and the justification and approval (J&A) that research would produce wouldn't survive a protest anyway.

follow_ups.q: What questions must market research answer?
follow_ups.h: Five steps, in priority order — commercial first, nondevelopmental last.
follow_ups.d: RFO 10.001(f) sets the questions, and it sets them in a fixed order of priority. Using the market research results, I determine whether — (1) a commercial product or commercial service on an existing governmentwide contract can meet the requirement; (2) the requirement could be modified so an existing governmentwide contract could be used; (3) a commercial product or commercial service is available from another source; (4) a commercial product or commercial service could be modified to meet the requirement; or (5) the requirement can only be satisfied by a nondevelopmental item. The order is the whole point: 10.001(f) opens by directing agencies to procure commercial to the maximum extent practicable, so nondevelopmental is the last rung, not the first, and 10.001(d) says I must not ask sources for more than the minimum information needed to make those determinations. Research also has to tell me whether small businesses can perform, because that drives the Rule of Two. Bundling and consolidation are not Part 10 questions at all — those determinations live at RFO 7.107.

follow_ups.q: How long is research current, and what document carries it?
follow_ups.h: A shelf life and a report.
follow_ups.d: RFO 10.001 sets no currency period. 10.001(b) ties research to events — before developing a new requirements document, before soliciting over the simplified acquisition threshold (SAT), before a task or delivery order over the SAT — and 10.001(e) requires the results be documented to suit the acquisition's size and complexity. This file's 26-month-old research predates the requirement I'm soliciting, so 10.001(b) requires fresh research on its own terms. And the market research report is the document every downstream decision cites: the J&A, the set-aside determination, the commercial item determination (CID). Research that was never documented can't support any of them — a post-hoc memo is reconstruction, not research.

follow_ups.q: Name five research methods you'd actually run here in the next two weeks.
follow_ups.h: Active outreach beats passive posting.
follow_ups.d: A properly shaped sources-sought (right North American Industry Classification System (NAICS), real title, adequate window); direct request for informations (RFIs) to the two small firms and known integrators; prior-procurement review in the Federal Procurement Data System (FPDS) for who's winning similar work; subject-matter expert (SME) and vendor engagement — actual conversations, documented; and a compressed industry day or one-on-ones if responses warrant. Depth scales to the dollar value: $4.5M with a sole-source question hanging on it deserves all five.

scenarios.scenario: A squadron wants 400 task chairs "identical to the ones facilities bought last year from a local dealer — we already have a quote." Your inventory manager mentions a warehouse annex holding surplus furniture from a recently consolidated unit. The dealer's quote is 8% below the General Services Administration (GSA) schedule price for a comparable chair, and the squadron notes AbilityOne "only makes the fabric panels, not the chairs."

facts.why: Agency inventory and excess sit at the top of the ladder — before anyone's quote matters, that annex gets checked and the result documented.
Attractive, but the ladder isn't priced-ordered — it's priority-ordered. The quote matters only when the buy legitimately reaches the commercial rung (and then it's useful pricing evidence).
Fine — check the procurement list for what's actually covered and document the non-fit. That's the rung working as designed.

scenarios.board_answer: Ladder first: inventory and that annex, then FPI and AbilityOne against the procurement list — but FPI is conditional, not automatic. RFO 8.303 makes me research and write a determination comparing the FPI chair to the private sector on price, quality, and time of delivery, and 8.304(b) sends the buy to competitive procedures if it is not comparable on any one of them. Before any of that, R-DFARS 208.301-70 requires competitive procedures if FPI's share of the DoD market for that federal supply class exceeds 5 percent. Then schedules — and only then the dealer, whose quote becomes price-comparison data, not a shortcut. The file shows each rung and why we moved past it.

coach.qtype: a required-sources question — the RFO Part 8 priority ladder before the open market.
coach.smes: your policy shop, the AbilityOne/UNICOR (Federal Prison Industries) program channels, and the schedule's ordering guide.
coach.rule: Work the RFO Part 8 ladder in order — inventory, excess, UNICOR, AbilityOne, schedules — and mandatory means mandatory; price alone doesn't unlock the open market.

scenarios.ask: The squadron has a quote in hand and wants the chairs ordered this week. What's your buying path?
scenarios.script: This is a required-sources question — the RFO Part 8 priority ladder comes before the open market. My help: the inventory manager, the AbilityOne procurement list, and our policy shop. The rule: RFO 8.103(a) runs in order — Government inventory and that surplus annex first, then FPI, then AbilityOne against the procurement list. But FPI is not an automatic buy. RFO 8.303 requires me to conduct market research and write a determination, with supporting rationale, on whether the FPI chair is comparable to private-sector chairs in price, quality, and time of delivery; and RFO 8.304(b) says that if it is not comparable in any one of those, I acquire the item using competitive procedures and include FPI in the solicitation with a timely offer considered. For DoD there is a gate ahead of that: R-DFARS 208.301-70 requires competitive procedures whenever FPI's share of the DoD market for the federal supply class containing the item is greater than 5 percent, so I check DoD's published list of those supply classes before I treat FPI as mandatory at all. Only once Part 8 is genuinely exhausted do schedules and the open market come into play. The dealer's quote doesn't jump the line; it becomes price-comparison data when and if we lawfully reach the open market. The file shows each rung and why we moved past it — that documentation is what makes the eventual buy defensible, whatever rung it lands on.

follow_ups.q: Recite the supplies priority ladder, top to bottom.
follow_ups.h: What the Government owns, then statute, then schedules, then market.
follow_ups.d: RFO Part 8: (1) existing Government inventory; (2) excess property from other agencies; (3) Federal Prison Industries — UNICOR; (4) AbilityOne procurement-list items; and RFO 8.103(a) stops there — four rungs. Once none of them can fill the need, RFO 8.104 takes over: buy commercial, and use an OFPP-designated “required use” governmentwide contract unless the head of the contracting activity (HCA) grants an exception; other governmentwide vehicles are “should consider.” In order, each rung checked and documented before moving past it. For services the ladder is different again — RFO 8.102 makes AbilityOne procurement-list services the mandatory source, with no inventory, excess or FPI rungs.

follow_ups.q: How does the ladder change for services?
follow_ups.h: One mandatory source, not a ladder.
follow_ups.d: There is no four-rung ladder for services. RFO 8.102 gives one mandatory source: unless otherwise required by law or by 8.101, services on the Procurement List maintained by the Committee must be procured from AbilityOne Participating Nonprofit Agencies under subpart 8.2. Other sources may be used only as prescribed in 41 CFR 101-26.301, and under an unusual and compelling urgency as prescribed in 6.302-2 and 41 CFR 101-25.101-5. Inventory, excess, and FPI are supply rungs — RFO 8.103(a) — and they have no services counterpart. Above 8.102 sits 8.101, which routes specific services to specific procedures: public utility services to part 41, Government printing to subpart 8.5. Everything else is a schedule or open-market choice, not a mandatory rung. And price alone never unlocks the open market.

follow_ups.q: If this lands on a schedule buy — who determines the order price fair and reasonable?
follow_ups.h: GSA priced the schedule. Who prices the order?
follow_ups.d: The ordering contracting officer. GSA's determination established schedule-level ceiling prices — not your quantity, your configuration, or your competitive moment. Compare quotes among schedule holders carrying the item, seek discounts (schedule prices are ceilings), and document the comparison as your price analysis. That documentation is the difference between an order and a defensible order.

scenarios.scenario: A prime's $22M avionics upgrade proposal includes an $8M subsystem the prime bought "commercially" from its own subsidiary. Support: a one-page assertion citing "regular commercial sales," a catalog page with no prices, and a note that "per Part 12, no cost data is required." The subsidiary has sold the subsystem to exactly two customers — both foreign militaries — and your engineer says the Government's configuration adds a hardened chassis and MIL-STD wiring.

facts.why: "Sold to the general public" is the definition's spine — military-only sales history undercuts the assertion at its root. This is the fact to chase first.

Modifications get tested against RFO 2.101(3)(ii): does the change significantly alter the function or essential physical characteristics of the item or component, or change the purpose of a process. Militarization of this scale strains "minor" — and note that 2.101(3)(i), modifications customarily available in the commercial marketplace, is a separate category with no minor-modification test at all.
A catalog proves a brochure exists. Commerciality pricing runs on actual sales at market prices — demand the sales data.

facts.fact: Prime bought from its own subsidiary
facts.why: An affiliated "commercial sale" deserves double scrutiny — the arms-length pricing discipline isn't there.
Backwards — the exception applies only after the determination holds. Assertion isn't determination.

scenarios.board_answer: The Government makes the commerciality call, not the proposal. On these facts — a general-public sales history of two foreign militaries under RFO 2.101(1), and mods measured against the real 2.101(3)(ii) test of significantly altering essential physical characteristics — I'd likely find it non-commercial; the affiliated seller is not part of that, because RFO 2.101(5) preserves commercial status across separate divisions, subsidiaries, and affiliates; and even if some element qualifies, I still require data sufficient to price it, certified or otherwise. The one-page assertion gets returned with a data demand attached.

coach.qtype: a commerciality question — the RFO 2.101 definition, the commercial item determination (CID), and what RFO Part 12 changes.
coach.smes: your pricing office, Legal, and the CID approval level one above you.
coach.rule: Commercial rides the market: the RFO 2.101 definition (including minor mods that keep form, fit, and function) is a documented CID call over the simplified acquisition threshold (SAT), and RFO Part 12 trades certified data for market evidence.

scenarios.ask: The prime says no cost data is required on the $8M 'commercial' subsystem. How do you evaluate this proposal?
scenarios.script: This is a commerciality-and-pricing question — RFO 2.101 and Part 12. My help: my pricing office, Legal, and the commercial item determination (CID) approval level one above me. The rule: the Government makes the commerciality determination — a proposal can assert it, but it can't declare it. On these facts the assertion likely fails on two of the three: a sales history of exactly two foreign militaries is not 'sold, leased, or licensed to the general public' under RFO 2.101(1), and a hardened chassis with MIL-STD wiring looks like it significantly alters the essential physical characteristics of the item, which is the actual RFO 2.101(3)(ii) minor-modification test — not form, fit, or function. The affiliated seller is not one of the two: RFO 2.101(5) expressly preserves commercial status for a product transferred between or among separate divisions, subsidiaries, or affiliates of a contractor, so the subsidiary sale is a pricing-scrutiny problem, not a definitional one. And here's the key move: even if some element qualifies as commercial, that excepts certified data, not data — I still require information sufficient to find the price fair and reasonable. The one-page assertion goes back with a data demand attached.

follow_ups.q: Recite the commercial-item definition for me.
follow_ups.h: Six paragraphs — general public, evolved, two modification branches, combinations, affiliate transfers, NDI.
follow_ups.d: RFO 2.101, commercial product, has six paragraphs: (1) a product of a type customarily used by the general public for nongovernmental purposes that has been sold, leased, or licensed — or offered for sale, lease, or license — to the general public; (2) a product that evolved from a paragraph (1) product and will be available in the commercial marketplace in time to satisfy the delivery requirements; (3) a product that would meet (1) or (2) except for (i) modifications of a type customarily available in the commercial marketplace, or (ii) minor modifications of a type NOT customarily available made to meet Federal Government requirements; (4) combinations of the above customarily combined and sold to the general public; (5) any of (1) through (4) even though transferred between or among separate divisions, subsidiaries, or affiliates of a contractor; and (6) a nondevelopmental item developed exclusively at private expense and sold in substantial quantities competitively to multiple State and local or foreign governments. Two traps live in there. First, the minor-modification test is not form, fit, or function — RFO 2.101(3)(ii) says a minor modification is one that does not significantly alter the function or essential physical characteristics of an item or component, or change the purpose of a process, and (3)(i) is a separate category entirely for modifications the commercial marketplace customarily offers. Second, an affiliate transfer does not break commerciality: paragraph (5) expressly preserves it, and commercial service paragraph (3) says the same for services. What the military-only sales history actually attacks is the general-public element in paragraph (1).

follow_ups.q: What does the written CID require, and who approves it?
follow_ups.h: Over the simplified acquisition threshold (SAT), in writing — and one level up only for certain paragraphs.
follow_ups.d: R-DFARS 212.001-70(c): when using Part 12 procedures above the SAT, I determine in writing that the acquisition meets the RFO 2.101 commercial product or commercial service definition, put that determination in the contract file, and follow PGI 212.001-70(b) for file documentation. Approval one level above the contracting officer is conditional, not universal — 212.001-70(c)(3) requires it only when the determination relies on paragraph (1)(ii), (3), or (4) of the commercial product definition, or paragraph (2) of the commercial service definition. Here the assertion rides on paragraph (3), so one level up applies. Prior determinations run the opposite direction from what people expect: under 212.001-70(b)(1) and 10 U.S.C. 3456(c), if the Commercial Item Database holds a prior commerciality determination — or I have other evidence DoD previously acquired the item under Part 12 — that prior contract MUST serve as the determination, and I document the file accordingly. If I question it and want to buy outside Part 12 anyway, 212.001-70(b)(2) makes me request a review by the head of the contracting activity, who has 30 days to either confirm the prior use was appropriate and still applicable or issue a written determination that it was improper or is no longer appropriate. The determination is the Government's call, made on evidence the vendor supplies.

follow_ups.q: Say it holds up as commercial — what pricing data can you still demand?
follow_ups.h: The exception excepts the certificate, not the data.
follow_ups.d: Data other than certified cost or pricing data, sufficient to determine the price fair and reasonable: sales history to other customers, catalog and market prices, quantity-discount structures, and supporting quotes. Commerciality removes the certification requirement and the defective-pricing remedy — it never removes the CO's duty to price the action on evidence. No data, no deal applies to commercial buys too.

scenarios.scenario: Friday, end of September. The CE squadron brings you four "urgent" buys: $14,800 of hand tools (GPC-ready, they say), another $14,600 of the same catalog's power tools, a $95K generator "only Vendor Z sells with the right output curve," and a request to "set up something so we stop doing paperwork every month" for HVAC filters. The GPC holder mentions the two tool buys "are from the same order the shop chief wrote up — we just split it to keep it simple."

facts.why: Same requirement, same catalog, same write-up: that's a ~$29K buy split to stay under the $15K MPT — the textbook violation. Recombine it into a purchase order, small business first.

Under-simplified acquisition threshold (SAT) sole source: document the single-source rationale (the output-curve requirement) and the price reasonableness — no justification and approval (J&A), but the reasoning goes on paper.
Repetitive, predictable, small: a BPA with established sources is the designed answer.
Fiscal-year pressure doesn't change any lane's rules — it's why the lanes exist. Fast is fine; splitting isn't.

scenarios.board_answer: The tool buys are one requirement — recombining them puts it in the RFO 12.201-1 purchase-order lane, which runs to $9 million for commercial items, not to the $350K SAT. Part 13 isn't the lane at all: 13.001(a)(1) reserves it for needs no commercial product or service can satisfy. The generator is a documented under-SAT sole source. The filters become a commercial BPA under 12.201-1(e)(3). And September doesn't amend any of it.

coach.qtype: a simplified-acquisition question — RFO Part 13: the right lane by dollar band.
coach.smes: your Government Purchase Card (GPC) program coordinator, Small Business Professional, and chief of the contracting office (COCO).
coach.rule: The band picks the RFO Part 13 lane: GPC to $15K, purchase orders to the $350K simplified acquisition threshold (SAT) — reserved for small business under the RFO Part 19 Rule of Two — and splitting a known requirement to stay under a threshold is a bright-line violation.

scenarios.ask: It's the last week of September and the squadron wants all four buys executed now. What's lawful, what isn't, and what's your plan?
scenarios.script: This is a simplified-acquisition question with a fiscal-year costume on, and the first move is picking the right part. RFO 13.000 and 13.001(a) confine Part 13 to noncommercial buys with no required source available; these are catalog commercial items, so the lane is RFO 12.201-1 — an RFQ followed by a purchase order, good to $9 million. My help: the GPC coordinator, my Small Business Professional, and financial management (FM). The rules: splitting one known requirement to stay under the micro-purchase threshold is a bright-line violation — the tool buys are one requirement, so recombined they're a purchase-order action in the small-business-reserved band. The generator can be an under-SAT sole source with a documented single-source rationale and price-reasonableness support — no J&A needed, but documentation absolutely. The recurring filters belong on a BPA. And I'd say it plainly: September doesn't amend the thresholds — expiring money never converts a violation into a technique.

follow_ups.q: What are the three simplified acquisition procedures (SAP) buying methods, and their dollar boundaries?
follow_ups.h: A card, an order, and an account.
follow_ups.d: Pick the part before you pick the method, because Part 13 is narrower than most people teach it. RFO 13.000 scopes it to noncommercial products and services at or below the SAT, and 13.001(a) allows it only if there are no commercial products or commercial services that can satisfy the need and the supplies or services are not available from a required source under Part 8. Everything in this scenario is catalog commercial, so these buys ride Part 12. The methods: the Government Purchase Card for micro-purchases at or under the $15K MPT; a request for quotations followed by a purchase order under RFO 12.201-1(a), which covers commercial acquisitions valued up to $9 million — raised to $15 million by RFO 12.001(c) when the head of the agency determines the buy supports a contingency operation, defense against or recovery from a cyber/nuclear/biological/chemical/radiological attack, international disaster assistance, or response to an emergency or major disaster; and blanket purchase agreements under RFO 12.201-1(e)(3) for repetitive needs from established sources — an account, not a contract, with no obligation until a call is placed. The $350K SAT is not the purchase-order ceiling. It is the Part 13 ceiling, and RFO 13.201 additionally caps each individual purchase under a Part 13 BPA at the SAT.

follow_ups.q: What competition does SAP actually require at these values?
follow_ups.h: Reserved band, local solicitation, synopsis line.
follow_ups.d: The MPT-to-SAT band is reserved for small business under the Rule of Two. Post a presolicitation notice to the governmentwide point of entry for actions expected to exceed $20,000 (RFO 5.101(a)), unless a 5.101(b) exemption applies; and when I solicit quotations directly at or below the SAT, I go to at least three sources and, whenever practicable, to two sources not in the previous solicitation (RFO 12.201-1(c)(2)). Award can be made on price alone, but price reasonableness must always be supportable — quotes, history, catalogs, the independent Government cost estimate (IGCE). Streamlined never means standard-free; it means proportionate documentation.

follow_ups.q: When does an under-SAT sole source need a J&A?
follow_ups.h: It doesn't — but it needs something.
follow_ups.d: Never — the formal J&A machinery starts above the SAT. Under it, a sole source needs a documented single-source rationale (why only Vendor Z's generator meets the need) plus price-reasonableness support. That's the generator's lane here: no J&A, but real documentation. The trap is hearing 'no J&A' as 'no file' — the rationale still has to survive a reviewer.

scenarios.scenario: A $4.7M base supply-chain analytics requirement is ready to solicit. Your predecessor's file shows it was once an 8(a) award "years ago," then competed full-and-open last cycle after "the Small Business Administration (SBA) released it" (no release letter in the file). Research finds one very capable woman-owned small business (WOSB) and one small firm whose capability statement is generic. The program manager (PM) suggests a WOSB sole source "since she's clearly the best," and notes the incumbent large business "will protest anything we do anyway."

facts.why: If the requirement was never properly released from 8(a), its current posture is built on sand — confirm with SBA before any strategy is chosen. The paper matters.

facts.fact: One strong WOSB + one generic small firm
facts.why: The Rule of Two needs a reasonable expectation of two capable offerors — a generic capability statement gets probed, not presumed. The set-aside call turns on this.

facts.fact: "WOSB sole source, she's clearly the best"
facts.why: WOSB sole source has conditions and a ceiling — "best" isn't the test, and at $4.7M it must actually fit the program's sole-source lane ($5.5M other) and its conditions.
Protest fear is not a strategy input — a defensible record is the protest strategy.

scenarios.board_answer: First I'd confirm the 8(a) release with SBA — that decides whose requirement this even is. Then the Rule of Two on real capability evidence: if the second small firm doesn't hold up, a WOSB sole source is only available if the program's conditions and ceiling genuinely fit at $4.7M — otherwise compete it and let the record carry the protest.

coach.qtype: a small-business question — RFO Part 19: the Rule of Two and the program lanes.
coach.smes: your Small Business Professional and the Small Business Administration (SBA) PCR; DD Form 2579 documents the coordination.
coach.rule: RFO Part 19: a reasonable expectation of two or more capable small businesses at fair market prices → set it aside. The rule tests the expectation at strategy time, not the final offer count.

scenarios.ask: How do you structure the competition — and does the 8(a) history change what you're allowed to do?
scenarios.script: This is a small-business-programs question — RFO Part 19, with an RFO 19.108 8(a) trap inside it. My first calls: my Small Business Professional and the SBA district office, plus Legal. The controlling rule: once a requirement enters the 8(a) program it stays there unless SBA agrees to release it — and there's no release letter in this file, so before anything else I confirm that release with SBA, because it decides whose requirement this even is. Then the Rule of Two on real capability evidence: if two capable small firms hold up at fair market prices, it's a set-aside. A WOSB sole source only enters if the program's conditions and caps genuinely fit at $4.7M. Otherwise compete it and let the documented record carry any protest.

follow_ups.q: When does an 8(a) sole source need a justification and approval (J&A)?
follow_ups.h: There's a dollar line, and it's high for DoD.
follow_ups.d: For DoD, not below $100M ($30M for civilian agencies) — below those lines the program's statutory basis is the competition authority, the 'authorized by statute' lane, no J&A required. SBA must approve the contract. Above the lines, a J&A enters. Know the pair: $100M DoD / $30M civilian is a favorite board number.

follow_ups.q: Where does competitive 8(a) begin?
follow_ups.h: Same number family as the HUBZone and WOSB caps.
follow_ups.d: Competitive 8(a) when at least two eligible firms are expected and the value exceeds $8.5M for manufacturing or $5.5M for everything else. Below those, sole source within the program is available. The $8.5M/$5.5M pair recurs across HUBZone and WOSB sole-source caps (SDVOSB runs $8.5M/$5M) — learn it once as a family and the board can't rattle you with any of them.

follow_ups.q: One more wrinkle: what changed in the 8(a) program recently that you'd verify before relying on it?
follow_ups.h: Eligibility standards shifted in early 2026.
follow_ups.d: As of January 2026, SBA moved the program to strictly race-neutral eligibility standards following litigation — admissions dropped sharply and many participants were affected. Before building a strategy on 8(a), verify the firm's current program status with SBA and your Small Business Professional. It's also a model board answer: naming a live regulatory shift shows you're current, and 'I'd verify before relying' is always the right closing note.

scenarios.scenario: A program manager (PM) bursts in: her ground-station modernization needs a new encryption module integrated "immediately — the wing commander is asking weekly." The incumbent integrator says it can start Monday. She's drafted a memo titled "Sole Source Justification — Urgent" for your signature, and adds that since the module rides on the incumbent's existing $60M integration contract, "we can probably just add it as a mod anyway." The module work is estimated at $2.8M. The existing contract's statement of work (SOW) covers "integration of communications and crypto subsystems as identified in the modernization baseline" — and this module is in the approved baseline.

facts.why: Pressure language pulling you toward a 6.103-2 urgency justification and approval (J&A). Command interest is not unusual and compelling urgency — no quantified harm, no mission stoppage.

facts.fact: The drafted "Sole Source Justification — Urgent" memo
facts.why: Someone else picked your authority before you analyzed the action. The board wants you to re-derive it.

facts.fact: SOW covers crypto subsystems in the approved baseline
facts.why: This is the fact that decides it: the work is arguably in scope of the existing contract. Run the scope analysis (Part 43 thinking: would offerors have anticipated it? cumulative impact?). If it's in scope, it's the M in SAMO — the Competition in Contracting Act (CICA) doesn't apply and there is no J&A to write.

If scope analysis says it's new work, the action is over simplified acquisition threshold (SAT) → full and open unless a 6.103 exception holds, and at $2.8M your J&A approver would be the Competition Advocate.

scenarios.board_answer: Before I talk exceptions, I'd do a scope review with Legal — if this module is within the existing contract's scope, CICA doesn't govern and we execute a mod. If it's out of scope, competition is the default at $2.8M, and I'd need market research to support any 6.103-1 justification — command interest alone won't carry a 6.103-2 urgency.

coach.qtype: a competition question — the Competition in Contracting Act (CICA) and RFO Part 6: the default and the exception ladder.
coach.smes: the Competition Advocate, Legal, and fresh market research to test the premise.
coach.rule: Full and open is the default over the simplified acquisition threshold (SAT) (RFO 6.101). 'Other than' takes one of the seven RFO 6.103 exceptions in a justification and approval (J&A) approved at the RFO 6.104 tier — and 'we've always used them' is not one of the seven.

scenarios.ask: The PM has the sole-source memo drafted and the commander is asking weekly. What's your answer?
scenarios.script: This is a competition question — CICA and RFO Part 6 — but scope comes first. My help: Legal on the scope review, then the Competition Advocate if we end up in exception territory. The order of analysis matters and I'd say it in this order: first, if this encryption module is within the existing contract's scope under RFO Part 43, CICA doesn't even govern — we execute a modification and we're done. If it's out of scope, it's a new $2.8M requirement and full and open competition is the default. A 6.103-1 one-source justification needs market research that would survive a competitor's lawyer, and command interest alone won't carry 6.103-2 urgency — urgency is about mission harm, quantified, not about who's asking.

follow_ups.q: By the way — name all seven exceptions to full and open competition.
follow_ups.h: One source, urgency, mobilization… keep going to seven.
follow_ups.d: RFO 6.103: (1) only one responsible source; (2) unusual and compelling urgency; (3) industrial mobilization, or engineering/developmental/research capability; (4) international agreement; (5) authorized or required by statute — UNICOR (Federal Prison Industries), AbilityOne, 8(a); (6) national security; (7) public interest — extremely rare, agency-head level. Recite them cold: this is the single most-asked list at the board.

follow_ups.q: Walk me up the J&A approval ladder.
follow_ups.h: Four rungs, and the DoD line at the top differs.
follow_ups.d: RFO 6.104, at October 2025 values: to $900K, the contracting officer's certification is the approval; above $900K to $20M, the Competition Advocate; above $20M to $90M — $150M for DoD — the Head of the Procuring Activity or program executive officer (PEO); above that, the Senior Procurement Executive. Post the J&A to SAM.gov within 14 days of award, 30 for urgency. This $2.8M action, if it goes sole source, sits with the Competition Advocate.

follow_ups.q: And when does CICA not apply at all?
follow_ups.h: Four carve-outs — the mod lane is the one in play here.
follow_ups.d: CICA doesn't govern: simplified acquisitions under Part 13; actions under statutory authorities like the Federal Supply Schedules; in-scope modifications under Part 43; and task or delivery orders under existing indefinite-delivery/indefinite-quantitys (IDIQs), which run on RFO 16.507 fair opportunity instead (Other Transactions also sit outside). That's why the scope review comes first in this scenario — if the module is in scope, we're in the mod lane and the whole exceptions conversation never starts.

follow_ups.q: Say urgency is real — what must the J&A quantify, and what limits ride with it?
follow_ups.h: Harm, breadth, duration, and a posting clock.
follow_ups.d: An RFO 6.103-2 urgency J&A quantifies the serious harm to the Government — mission failure, safety, unacceptable operational delay — not the commander's interest level. Limits: solicit as many sources as practicable even under urgency; duration limited to about one year; and the J&A may follow the award but must be posted within 30 days. Urgency buys speed, never silence.

scenarios.scenario: Tradeoff selection, $45M, discussions closed, final proposal revisions (FPRs) in. Offeror A: slightly lower rated, price well below the Government's probable cost. Offeror B: modestly better ratings, much higher price. The source selection evaluation board (SSEB) chair worries B "will protest if they lose." Then you learn the source selection authority (SSA) — without you — called Offeror A, told them their price "is way out of line with our probable cost," flagged conflicts between their EN responses and their FPR, and "gave them three ways to fix it."

facts.why: That call was discussions — after FPRs, with one offeror, inviting revision. Unequal exchanges with a single offeror after close is about as serious as Part 15 problems get. Stop everything; Legal now.

facts.fact: "Three ways to fix it" — compounds it
facts.why: Coaching one offeror toward award is disparate treatment on the record — the remedy has to be structural, not cosmetic.
Legitimately handled through the evaluation itself (realism on cost-type; risk assessment otherwise) — it never justified an off-record call.
Protest fear caused this mess. The cure is a clean record, and now likely: document the breach, reopen discussions with all offerors in the range, fresh FPRs — done with Legal's hand on the wheel.

scenarios.board_answer: My concerns are unequal discussions after close and disclosure of our probable cost to one offeror. I'd halt award, document the exchange, and with Legal likely reopen discussions with every offeror in the range and take new FPRs — the only fix for unequal treatment is restored equal treatment, on the record.

coach.qtype: a source-selection question — RFO Part 15: fair process, documented judgment.
