For consulting services the DoD overlay is higher still — R-DFARS 209.503-70 puts waiver approval with the Secretary of Defense, USD(A&S), or the assistant secretaries of the military departments, with no delegation below a Presidentially appointed, Senate-confirmed official.

coach.qtype: an organizational-conflict-of-interest question — RFO 9.5: the type drives the remedy.
coach.smes: Legal (JA) and your reviewing chain; a waiver runs to the agency head or a designee and is never delegated below the head of the contracting activity (HCA) (RFO 9.503).
coach.rule: Identify the type first — unequal access, impaired objectivity, biased ground rules — then avoid, neutralize, or mitigate under RFO 9.5, in that order. A firewall can't fix ground rules already written. On a significant potential conflict the contracting officer (CO) analyses and recommends; the chief of the contracting office approves, modifies, or rejects the course of action in writing before the solicitation issues (RFO 9.506(b)-(c)).

scenarios.ask: The contractor proposes a firewall and the affiliate wants to bid. What's your call?
scenarios.script: This is an organizational-conflict-of-interest question — RFO 9.5 biased ground rules, the hardest type. My help: Legal, the organizational conflict of interest (OCI) review chain, and the HCA if anyone breathes the word waiver. The rule: type drives remedy. A firewall manages information flow — it does nothing about test criteria the contractor is drafting for a competition its new affiliate will enter; that influence is already in the documents. So: the contractor comes off the criteria work now, the Government independently develops or scrubs what they touched, and the record documents exactly what their people authored. If the affiliate wants to compete, it competes on ground rules it provably didn't shape. And I own the analysis and the recommendation, not the decision: RFO 9.506(b) makes me submit the written analysis, the recommended course of action, the draft solicitation provision and any proposed clause to the chief of the contracting office before issuing the solicitation, and 9.506(c)(3) has that approving official approve, modify, or reject the recommendations in writing. Before award I resolve the conflict consistent with the approval or other direction by the head of the contracting activity (9.506(d)(3)).

scenarios.scenario: On your advisory and assistance services (A&AS) multiple-award indefinite-delivery/indefinite-quantity (IDIQ), Holder A's analysts maintain the program's requirements database. A new task order competition opens to all five holders — and Holder A's proposal cites specific unfunded requirements from that database as 'anticipated growth' no other holder mentions.
baits: Holder A did nothing overtly wrong — they used what they knew
The insight makes their proposal genuinely better
key_moves: Unequal access to non-public information — no bad act required; the imbalance is the conflict
Options: neutralize (share the same data with all holders and allow revisions) or address Holder A's access in the evaluation, with Legal
Fix the structure: database-support roles need OCI clauses and data walls before the next competition

follow_ups.q: Can you cure this mid-competition? How?
follow_ups.h: Mid-competition cures level the field — what levels information?
follow_ups.d: Yes — the classic cure for unequal access is equal access: release the same database extract (scrubbed appropriately) to all five holders, extend the response date, and allow proposal revisions so everyone competes on the same picture. Alternatives: neutralize Holder A's advantage by excluding the tainted content from evaluation, or in a bad case exclude Holder A from this order. Document whichever cure you pick and why it restores fairness — the record is what survives the ombudsman.

follow_ups.q: What contract language prevents this on support task orders?
follow_ups.h: The fix for next time lives in the support task order's own terms.
follow_ups.d: Support task orders should carry OCI clauses tailored to the access the work creates: firewall and nondisclosure obligations, restrictions on using program information in the holder's own proposals, screening or recusal duties when competitions open, and — where the access is structural — an agreed mitigation plan as a condition of the support work. The time to price and paper those terms is when the support order is placed, not when the first tainted proposal arrives.

coach.qtype: an organizational-conflict-of-interest question — RFO 9.5: the type drives the remedy.
coach.smes: Legal (JA) and your reviewing chain; a waiver runs to the agency head or a designee and is never delegated below the head of the contracting activity (HCA) (RFO 9.503).
coach.rule: Identify the type first — unequal access, impaired objectivity, biased ground rules — then avoid, neutralize, or mitigate under RFO 9.5, in that order. A firewall can't fix ground rules already written. On a significant potential conflict the contracting officer (CO) analyses and recommends; the chief of the contracting office approves, modifies, or rejects the course of action in writing before the solicitation issues (RFO 9.506(b)-(c)).

scenarios.ask: Holder A's proposal is quoting the requirements database it maintains. Can this competition proceed?
scenarios.script: This is an RFO 9.5 organizational conflict of interest (OCI) question inside an RFO 16.507 fair-opportunity competition — unequal access to nonpublic information. My help: Legal and the vehicle procuring contracting officer (PCO). The rule: the imbalance is the conflict — Holder A citing unfunded requirements from a database it maintains for the Government is competing on information the other four holders can't see. No bad act required. The cure that keeps the competition alive: give everyone the same picture — release the scrubbed data to all holders, extend the clock, allow revisions. If the taint runs deeper, neutralize or exclude, documented. And going forward, the support order itself gets OCI terms — firewalls, use restrictions, screening duties — because this conflict was foreseeable the day we let a holder run the requirements database.

scenarios.scenario: Your apparent awardee on a $700K paving contract lists an office address that turns out to be a mailbox store, has no equipment in its own name ('we lease everything per job'), and its listed superintendent also appears full-time on another company's website. Price is excellent and references check out by phone.
baits: Good references and price pull toward award
Leasing equipment is legitimately common in construction
key_moves: Run the standards on facts: organization, equipment access, key personnel actually available — a pre-award survey fits here
Leasing is fine IF the lease commitments are real — ask for them
If it nets to non-responsible and they're small: SBA referral for the CoC decision, not a quiet pass-over

follow_ups.q: Which of the seven standards are in play?
follow_ups.h: Map each fact to a standard: organization, equipment, personnel.
follow_ups.d: In play: adequate organization and experience (a mailbox office and no visible operation), necessary equipment and facilities or the ability to obtain them (leasing is legitimate — IF lease commitments exist for this job), and key personnel actually available (a superintendent already employed full-time elsewhere fails the availability test unless there's a real transition plan). None of these facts is disqualifying alone; each demands verification. A pre-award survey is the right tool at this dollar value and doubt level.

follow_ups.q: What does a CoC do to your determination?
follow_ups.h: The referral is mandatory; the certificate is conclusive.
follow_ups.d: If the offeror is small and you determine non-responsibility, the referral to SBA is mandatory — and a Certificate of Competency, if SBA issues one, conclusively establishes responsibility: you award. The contracting officer's (CO) protection then shifts to administration — surveillance, milestones, early engagement. There is no dollar band and no appeal in the RFO — 19.204(i) makes a COC final on all elements of responsibility, and if no COC issues within 15 business days of the referral I award elsewhere (19.204(j)). For DoD, R-DFARS 219.204 routes me to PGI 219.204: notify the department OSBP director within 5 working days of SBA Headquarters' written position, appeal file 5 working days after — and the OSBP director, not the CO, decides whether the agency appeals.

coach.qtype: a responsibility question — the seven RFO 9.104 standards, applied to today's facts.
coach.smes: your contracting chain, Legal, and the Small Business Administration (SBA) — a small-business referral is mandatory under RFO Part 19, and a CoC is conclusive.
coach.rule: Doubt cuts in the Government's favor — doubt means no. But the 'no' must stand on the RFO 9.104 standards and documented facts, never on undocumented distrust.

scenarios.ask: Mailbox address, leased-everything, moonlighting superintendent. Award, or not — and on what?
scenarios.script: This is a responsibility question — the seven RFO 9.104 standards on today's documented facts. My help: my chain, a pre-award survey, and the Small Business Administration (SBA) if this goes where it might. The rule: doubt cuts in the Government's favor, but doubt must stand on facts, so I verify before I judge: demand the equipment lease commitments for this job, the superintendent's actual availability and transition plan, and evidence of an operating organization behind the mailbox. Leasing is a legitimate model — undocumented leasing is not. If the facts hold up, award. If they don't, non-responsibility on the standards — and because they're small, mandatory referral to SBA, whose Certificate of Competency, if issued, I honor and then protect the Government through hard-nosed administration.

scenarios.scenario: A contractor you terminated for default eight months ago is the apparent low offeror on a new solicitation — bidding through a newly formed LLC with the same owners, same address, and a fresh Commercial and Government Entity (CAGE) code. Your evaluator says 'new entity, clean slate, we can't hold the past against them.'
baits: 'New entity' formalism
Fear that considering history is prejudice
key_moves: Responsibility looks through paper: same owners and operations means the performance and integrity record follows them
The T4D is exactly the kind of documented history the standards exist to weigh — considering it is the job, not prejudice
Document the affiliation facts; if small and heading to 'no,' SBA referral still applies

follow_ups.q: What distinguishes a legitimate fresh start from evasion?
follow_ups.h: What separates reorganization from costume change?
follow_ups.d: A legitimate fresh start shows substantive change: new capital, new management, corrected root causes of the failure, and a track record — however short — under the new structure. Evasion shows continuity wearing new paper: same owners, same operations, same address, new CAGE code. Responsibility looks through the paper to the people and the operation; a shell that exists to shed a default record is itself an integrity fact under the standards.

follow_ups.q: What system checks reveal the connection?
follow_ups.h: The systems are built for exactly this connection — think beyond a clean SAM search on the new name.
follow_ups.d: FAPIIS and CPARS searched by the principals, not just the entity; SAM exclusion records checked against owners and key individuals (exclusions attach to people too); state incorporation records showing officers and addresses; and the prior contract file itself. A new CAGE code resets none of it. Over the simplified acquisition threshold (SAT), the FAPIIS review is mandatory — and the connection this scenario hands you is precisely what that review exists to surface.

coach.qtype: a responsibility question — the seven RFO 9.104 standards, applied to today's facts.
coach.smes: your contracting chain, Legal, and the Small Business Administration (SBA) — a small-business referral is mandatory under RFO Part 19, and a CoC is conclusive.
coach.rule: Doubt cuts in the Government's favor — doubt means no. But the 'no' must stand on the RFO 9.104 standards and documented facts, never on undocumented distrust.

scenarios.ask: Same owners, new LLC, low offer. Does the default history follow them?
scenarios.script: This is a responsibility question — RFO 9.104 — about continuity. My help: Legal and the record systems — the Federal Awardee Performance and Integrity Information System (FAPIIS), the Contractor Performance Assessment Reporting System (CPARS), SAM, searched by the people, not just the new entity. The rule: responsibility looks through paper. Same owners, same address, same operations means the performance and integrity record follows them — my own termination for default (T4D) eight months ago is exactly the documented history the standards exist to weigh. 'New entity, clean slate' is true for the CAGE code and false for the humans. So: evaluate the fresh-start claim on substance — new capital, new management, root causes fixed — and if it's a costume, determine non-responsibility on documented facts. If they're small, the Small Business Administration (SBA) referral follows. What doesn't happen is the low price laundering the history.

scenarios.scenario: For a niche electronic-warfare training service, your sources-sought draws zero responses. The program manager (PM) takes it as proof only the incumbent can perform and asks you to start the justification and approval (J&A). The notice ran 10 days over a holiday period, used the program's internal acronym in the title, and posted under a generic North American Industry Classification System (NAICS).
baits: Zero responses looks like market absence
The PM's conclusion matches what the program wants anyway
key_moves: Zero responses to a badly shaped notice proves nothing — fix the title, NAICS, period, and do direct outreach
A J&A built on defective research is protest bait — the market-research section is its spine
Document round two either way; absence must be demonstrated, not inferred

follow_ups.q: What makes a sources-sought effective?
follow_ups.h: A notice nobody qualified could find proves what, exactly?
follow_ups.d: An effective sources-sought is findable and answerable: right NAICS and product service code (PSC) codes, a title that says what the work is, a response window that doesn't die over a holiday, a description with enough substance to let a capable firm self-identify, and direct outreach to the firms research already suggests. Zero responses to a mis-coded, badly-timed notice measures the notice, not the market — and a J&A whose market-research section rests on it inherits the defect.

follow_ups.q: How much research is enough for a $10M sole source?
follow_ups.h: Scale the evidence to a $10M sole-source claim.
follow_ups.d: For a $10M sole source, the research has to support the strongest claim in contracting: nobody else can do this. That means a properly shaped notice AND direct industry outreach, trade channels, adjacent-NAICS sweeps, other services' experience, and documented conversations — an effort a competitor's lawyer will read line by line. The J&A's market-research section is its spine; thin research is the number-one way sole-source justifications die at review or protest.

coach.qtype: a market-research question — RFO Part 10: evidence before decisions.
coach.smes: the requiring activity's subject-matter experts (SMEs), your Small Business Professional, and industry itself — sources sought, request for informations (RFIs), industry days.
coach.rule: RFO Part 10 research is the evidence; the commerciality, competition, and set-aside calls are decisions built on it. Undocumented research supports nothing downstream — and RFO 10.001(b) ties research to the event it supports (a new requirements document, a solicitation over the simplified acquisition threshold (SAT), an order over the SAT), not to a shelf life.

scenarios.ask: Zero responses, and the PM wants the J&A started. Is the market really empty?
scenarios.script: This is a market-research question — RFO Part 10 — and the evidence doesn't say what the PM thinks it says. My help: my Small Business Professional, industry channels, and the requiring activity to fix the requirement description. The rule: research is the evidence; the J&A is a conclusion the evidence must earn. Zero responses to a notice with the wrong codes, a holiday window, and a vague title proves the notice failed — not that the market is empty. So: reshape and rerun it — right NAICS, real title, adequate window — plus direct outreach to plausible performers. If genuine absence emerges, the J&A writes itself on solid ground. If competition surfaces, we just avoided a protest. Either way, the file shows we measured the market, not our own noise.

scenarios.scenario: The program wants a custom-built environmental test chamber and has written a 40-page spec. Your research finds three commercial chamber makers whose catalog units meet every parameter except one vibration profile — which two vendors say they routinely add as a factory option.
baits: The 40-page spec presumes custom development
'Except one parameter' feels like disqualification
key_moves: Research exists to reshape requirements: a catalog unit plus a routine factory option is likely a commercial product with minor modification
Rewrite toward performance terms; a commercial determination unlocks Part 12 streamlining
Document the comparison analysis — it becomes the CID's core

follow_ups.q: What makes a modification 'minor'?
follow_ups.h: "Minor modification" is a defined term at RFO 2.101 — and this probably isn't one.
follow_ups.d: RFO 2.101 splits this in two, and the split is the answer. Paragraph (3)(i) covers modifications of a type customarily available in the commercial marketplace. Paragraph (3)(ii) covers minor modifications of a type NOT customarily available in the commercial marketplace, made to meet Federal Government requirements — and a minor modification is one that does not significantly alter the function or essential physical characteristics of the item. So a factory-offered vibration option that two of the three makers already sell isn't a minor modification at all; it is (3)(i), customarily available. The label matters because the DoD ceiling on the certified-cost-or-pricing-data exemption is written against (3)(ii), not (3)(i). The determination is a facts-and-engineering call documented in the CID, not a gut call — and 'we wrote a 40-page spec' doesn't make an item noncommercial.

follow_ups.q: What does Part 12 change about this buy?
follow_ups.h: Part 12 changes the data you can demand, the clauses, and the termination machinery.
follow_ups.d: Commercial procedures mean: no certified cost or pricing data (price on market evidence — catalogs, competition among the three makers), streamlined commercial terms with a firm-fixed-price (FFP) preference, customary commercial data rights only, and termination under the commercial clause rather than Part 49. Under the $9M streamlined ceiling this buy moves fast. One DoD caveat the panel will reach for: the certified-data exemption for a paragraph (3)(ii) minor modification is capped. RFO 15.403-2(c)(3)(iii)(B)-(C) exempts such modifications for DoD, NASA, and the Coast Guard only while the total price of all of them under the contract action stays at or below the greater of the 15.403-3(a) threshold or 5 percent of the total price of the contract at award — above that line the exemption stops and certified cost or pricing data are back on the table. (For DoD the 15.403-3(a) figure is displaced by R-DFARS 215.403-3(a).) None of that bites here if the option rides in as a 2.101(3)(i) commercial modification. The trade: less Government-unique protection — which is exactly right for a catalog product with three competing makers.

coach.qtype: a market-research question — RFO Part 10: evidence before decisions.
coach.smes: the requiring activity's subject-matter experts (SMEs), your Small Business Professional, and industry itself — sources sought, request for informations (RFIs), industry days.
coach.rule: RFO Part 10 research is the evidence; the commerciality, competition, and set-aside calls are decisions built on it. Undocumented research supports nothing downstream — and RFO 10.001(b) ties research to the event it supports (a new requirements document, a solicitation over the simplified acquisition threshold (SAT), an order over the SAT), not to a shelf life.

scenarios.ask: Three catalog makers cover everything but one vibration profile. Custom build, or commercial with a mod?
scenarios.script: This is an RFO Part 10 market-research question that becomes an RFO 2.101 commerciality call. My help: the program engineers, my pricing office, and the commercial item determination (CID) approver one level up. The rule: research exists to reshape requirements, not just to document them. Three catalog makers cover every parameter but one vibration profile — and two offer that profile as a factory option. That's a commercial product under RFO 2.101(3)(i) — a modification of a type customarily available in the commercial marketplace — not a 2.101(3)(ii) minor modification, which is the branch for modifications NOT customarily available made to meet Federal Government requirements. The difference isn't pedantry: the DoD cap on the certified-data exemption at RFO 15.403-2(c)(3)(iii)(B)-(C) attaches to (3)(ii). So I'd push the requirement toward performance terms, write the CID on the comparison analysis, and compete it among the three makers under commercial procedures — market pricing, no certified data, fast. The 40-page custom spec buys a slower, costlier chamber and a thinner industrial base. The catalog buys the mission.

scenarios.scenario: A unit orders custodial supplies monthly from a commercial e-commerce site using the Government Purchase Card (GPC) because 'it's cheaper than the mandatory source and delivery is faster.' Annual spend across the unit: about $140K, in individual orders that never top $3K.
baits: Each swipe is legitimately under the MPT
Cheaper-and-faster feels like good stewardship
key_moves: Mandatory sources (AbilityOne procurement-list items especially) aren't price-optional — check what's actually covered
$140K of predictable annual demand is one requirement wearing 50 swipes — structure it (BPA/consolidated buy) through the source ladder
Fix the unit's process, not just this order

follow_ups.q: Walk the supplies priority ladder
follow_ups.h: Walk it: what the Government owns, then statute, then schedules, then market.
follow_ups.d: Supplies ladder, in order: existing Government inventory; excess from other agencies; Federal Prison Industries (UNICOR); AbilityOne procurement-list items. RFO 8.103(a) stops there — four rungs, not seven. Once none of them can fill the need, RFO 8.104 governs: buy commercial, and use an OFPP-designated “required use” governmentwide contract unless the head of the contracting activity grants an exception; other governmentwide vehicles are “should consider.” Each rung is checked and documented before moving past it — and for procurement-list items, AbilityOne isn't a suggestion. Price alone never unlocks the next rung; fit and availability problems are worked through the program channels, on the record.

follow_ups.q: When does GPC use become splitting?
follow_ups.h: Fifty swipes, one predictable annual demand — what's the requirement, really?
follow_ups.d: Splitting happens whenever a known requirement is fragmented to stay under a threshold — intent to evade isn't required for the pattern to be a violation. $140K of predictable custodial demand is one annual requirement; buying it as 50 GPC swipes both evades the MPT and bypasses the mandatory sources. The structural fix: a BPA or purchase-order arrangement against the right source, sized to the real annual demand, with the GPC reserved for genuine micro-purchases.

coach.qtype: a required-sources question — the RFO Part 8 priority ladder before the open market.
coach.smes: your policy shop, the AbilityOne/UNICOR (Federal Prison Industries) program channels, and the schedule's ordering guide.
coach.rule: Work the RFO Part 8 ladder in order — inventory, excess, UNICOR, AbilityOne, schedules — and mandatory means mandatory; price alone doesn't unlock the open market.

scenarios.ask: The unit says the e-commerce site is cheaper and faster than the mandatory source. What do you fix, and how?
scenarios.script: This is an RFO Part 8 required-sources question compounded by RFO Part 13 splitting. My help: the GPC program coordinator, the AbilityOne program office, and my policy shop. Two rules: the supplies ladder is mandatory and runs in priority order — and price alone doesn't unlock the open market; if these items sit on the procurement list, AbilityOne is the source, cheaper e-commerce notwithstanding. Second: $140K of predictable annual demand is one requirement wearing fifty swipes — that's splitting, and it evades both the micro-purchase threshold (MPT) and the mandatory sources. The fix: structure the real demand into a blanket purchase agreement (BPA) or purchase orders against the correct source, retrain the unit's cardholders, and document the transition. Faster delivery is a requirement to work through the program — not a license to shop.

scenarios.scenario: Your customer wants specific network switches 'exactly like the General Services Administration (GSA) Advantage shows, from Vendor Q's schedule listing, $290K.' A quick eBuy check shows four other schedule holders carry the same original equipment manufacturer (OEM) line, two with published prices 6-9% lower.
baits: 'GSA already negotiated the price' — schedule fair-and-reasonable ≠ order fair-and-reasonable
The customer's vendor preference
key_moves: On schedules, the ordering CO still determines the order price fair and reasonable — compare holders, seek discounts
Four holders with the same line = easy comparison; document the quotes and the basis
Vendor preference without a differentiator is steering

follow_ups.q: What does GSA's determination actually cover?
follow_ups.h: GSA priced the schedule; who prices the order?
follow_ups.d: GSA's determination establishes schedule-level ceiling prices as fair and reasonable — for the schedule, not for your order. The ordering contracting officer (CO) independently determines the ORDER price fair and reasonable: comparing holders carrying the same line, seeking discounts (schedule prices are ceilings, discounts are expected), and documenting the comparison. Four holders with published prices 6-9% apart is a comparison begging to be run.

follow_ups.q: When can you limit consideration to one schedule holder?
follow_ups.h: Limiting sources on a schedule buy has its own justification lane.
follow_ups.d: An order can be limited to one schedule holder only on a documented basis — a logical follow-on to a schedule order, urgency, only-one-holder-carries-it, or an item peculiar to one vendor — written and kept in the file (the schedule equivalent of a brand-name justification). 'The customer likes Vendor Q's listing' isn't a basis. When multiple holders carry the same OEM line, competition among them is both the default and the easiest path to a defensible price.

coach.qtype: a required-sources question — the RFO Part 8 priority ladder before the open market.
coach.smes: your policy shop, the AbilityOne/UNICOR (Federal Prison Industries) program channels, and the schedule's ordering guide.
coach.rule: Work the RFO Part 8 ladder in order — inventory, excess, UNICOR, AbilityOne, schedules — and mandatory means mandatory; price alone doesn't unlock the open market.

scenarios.ask: The customer wants Vendor Q's listing bought as-is at $290K. What does a defensible schedule order look like?
scenarios.script: This is an RFO Part 8 schedules question about what GSA's pricing actually covers. My help: the schedules' eBuy tools and my own comparison file. The rule: GSA established schedule-level prices as fair and reasonable — the order-level determination is mine, and it doesn't come free with the listing. Four holders carry the same OEM line, two visibly cheaper. So: request for quotations (RFQ) among the holders, seek discounts — schedule prices are ceilings, not floors — and document the comparison as my price analysis. If the customer wants Vendor Q specifically, that takes a written justification naming a real basis, and 'we liked their listing' isn't one. Ten minutes of eBuy competition is the difference between a defensible order and a $290K habit.

scenarios.scenario: A vendor proposes its 'commercially available' logistics-analytics platform for $4.2M. Digging in: the platform has one prior sale — to a foreign navy — and the proposal's 'catalog' was created last month. The vendor stresses the underlying database engine is genuinely commercial off-the-shelf (COTS) with millions of users.
baits: The genuinely-COTS engine launders the whole platform
A 'catalog' document exists
key_moves: Commerciality is determined at the level of what you're buying — the platform, not its ingredients
One military sale + a fresh catalog ≠ sold to the general public; the assertion likely fails
Component-level analysis may still except real COTS pieces; the rest needs data to price

follow_ups.q: What evidence establishes 'of a type' sold commercially?
follow_ups.h: 'Of a type' still needs a market — whose purchases prove one exists?
follow_ups.d: Evidence that establishes commerciality: actual sales, leases, or licenses to the GENERAL PUBLIC — commercial customers, at market prices, in ordinary volumes — or an item evolved from such a product and available in time. Catalogs corroborate; they don't substitute. One sale to a foreign navy is a government sale, and a catalog created last month for this proposal is advocacy, not evidence. The determination is the Government's, made on the record the vendor supplies — and the burden of supporting the assertion sits with the vendor.

follow_ups.q: What data can you demand if it's non-commercial?
follow_ups.h: Non-commercial at $4.2M sole source — what does the pricing lane become?
follow_ups.d: If the item is non-commercial, the Part 12 shortcuts fall away: at $4.2M the action is above the simplified acquisition threshold (SAT) but below the certified-data trigger, so you demand data other than certified cost or pricing data — cost element detail, sales history, supporting quotes — sufficient for a fair-and-reasonable determination, with price analysis always and cost analysis as needed. The vendor's refusal to provide adequate data becomes its own answer: no data, no deal.

coach.qtype: a commerciality question — the RFO 2.101 definition, the commercial item determination (CID), and what RFO Part 12 changes.
coach.smes: your pricing office, Legal, and the CID approval level one above you.
coach.rule: Commercial rides the market: the RFO 2.101 definition (including minor mods that keep form, fit, and function) is a documented CID call over the simplified acquisition threshold (SAT), and RFO Part 12 trades certified data for market evidence.

scenarios.ask: One foreign military sale and a month-old catalog. Does the commercial assertion survive — and what happens to the buy either way?
scenarios.script: This is a commerciality question — RFO 2.101 — and the Government makes the call, not the proposal. My help: my pricing office, Legal, and the commercial item determination (CID) approver one level up. The rule: commercial means sold, leased, or licensed to the general public — or evolved and available in time. One sale to a foreign navy is a government sale; a catalog created last month is a prop. On these facts the assertion likely fails, and my CID says so with the comparison analysis written down. Then the buy continues honestly: non-commercial, $4.2M, sole source — I demand data other than certified sufficient to price it, run price analysis plus cost analysis as needed, and if the vendor won't support its own price, that refusal is my answer. No data, no deal.

scenarios.scenario: A commercial-items contract for fleet telematics is going badly — units fail in cold weather. The program manager (PM) asks you to 'send a cure notice and start the termination for default (T4D) like we did on the radar contract.' The contract was awarded under Part 12 with the standard commercial clause.
baits: The radar-contract playbook feels transferable
'Cure notice / T4D' vocabulary is muscle memory
key_moves: Part 49 machinery doesn't run commercial contracts — the commercial clause's termination-for-cause framework does
Rights and remedies come from the clause: notice, opportunity, cause standards — with Legal on the specifics
The performance record and re-procurement logic still matter; the procedure differs

follow_ups.q: How does termination-for-cause differ from T4D in effect?
follow_ups.h: Same failure, different clause — what machinery actually runs a Part 12 contract?
follow_ups.d: Termination for cause under the commercial clause reaches the same destination as T4D — the Government doesn't pay for nonconforming performance and can pursue reprocurement exposure — but the road differs: RFO 12.304(a) says to follow that section and the termination paragraphs of the clause at 52.212-4, and not to use the procedures in part 49. Careful with the cure notice, though — it is not Part 49 muscle memory you leave behind. RFO 12.304(b)(1) requires a cure notice before terminating for cause unless the reason for the termination is late delivery, and 52.212-4(m) says the same thing in the clause. What replaces Part 49's machinery is the notice content prescribed at 12.304(b)(2): a statement that the contract is terminated for cause, the reasons, which remedies the Government intends to seek or a date by which it will say, and a statement that the notice is the contracting officer's final decision with the right to appeal under the Disputes clause. Citing 49.x procedures on a commercial contract invites the conversion argument that the termination itself was procedurally defective.

follow_ups.q: What does the Government owe on a commercial convenience termination?
follow_ups.h: Commercial convenience settlements are narrower than Part 49's.
follow_ups.d: On a commercial termination for convenience, the Government owes the percentage of work performed at the contract price plus reasonable charges resulting from the termination — a leaner formula than Part 49's cost-plus-settlement machinery, with no anticipatory profit either way. The contractor's records support the charges. Knowing the two formulas apart — and which contract carries which — is precisely the seam this scenario tests.

coach.qtype: a commerciality question — the RFO 2.101 definition, the commercial item determination (CID), and what RFO Part 12 changes.
coach.smes: your pricing office, Legal, and the CID approval level one above you.
coach.rule: Commercial rides the market: the RFO 2.101 definition (including minor mods that keep form, fit, and function) is a documented CID call over the simplified acquisition threshold (SAT), and RFO Part 12 trades certified data for market evidence.

scenarios.ask: The PM wants a cure notice and a T4D 'like the radar contract.' What's different here?
scenarios.script: This is a terminations question on a commercial contract — RFO 12.304 territory, not RFO Part 49 — and the seam is the whole answer. My help: Legal before any notice, and the contracting officer's representative's (COR) cold-weather failure record. The rule: Part 49 doesn't run Part 12 contracts — RFO 12.304(a) says do not use the procedures in part 49. But the PM is half right, and I'd say so: the cure notice is required, not a habit. RFO 12.304(b)(1) and the clause at 52.212-4(m) both direct a cure notice before terminating for cause unless the reason is late delivery. What's actually different is the label and the machinery — termination for cause under the commercial clause with the notice content prescribed at 12.304(b)(2), not a Part 49 termination for default, and convenience under the clause's leaner settlement formula. So: document the cold-weather failures against the requirement, give the clause's notice honestly, and if we terminate for cause, do it under the right authority with the right words — because citing 49.x machinery on a commercial award hands the contractor a procedural-defect argument. Same destination as the radar contract; different road, and the road matters.

scenarios.scenario: An exercise planner needs 30 days of portable toilets, fencing, and light towers across three sites — about $120K total. A staff sergeant already collected one quote per item from 'the companies we used last year' and asks you to cut three POs today so setup can start Monday.
baits: Pre-collected single quotes feel like completed legwork
Monday deadline
key_moves: The band is small-business reserved — confirm the vendors' size or solicit competitors
One quote per item at $120K needs price-reasonableness support: add quotes or comparison evidence fast
SAP can absolutely hit Monday — done properly it's hours, not weeks

follow_ups.q: How many quotes is 'enough' under SAP?
follow_ups.h: Check which part you're in before you answer — the commercial lane puts a number on it.
follow_ups.d: Start by refusing the premise. Portable toilets, fencing, and light towers are commercial, so this isn't a Part 13 buy at all — RFO 13.001(a)(1) says those procedures may be used only if there are no commercial products or commercial services that can satisfy the need. RFO Part 12 governs, and it does put a number on it: under RFO 12.201-1(c)(2), when the contracting officer solicits quotations directly at or below the simplified acquisition threshold (SAT), post a presolicitation notice in the Governmentwide Point of Entry unless an exception at 5.101(b) applies, solicit quotations from at least three sources, and whenever practicable solicit from two sources not included in the previous solicitation — which is exactly what "the companies we used last year" fails. The "no magic number, the documentation defends the award" answer is real, but it belongs to RFO 13.101 and to noncommercial simplified acquisitions. And whichever lane you're in, the price-reasonableness determination still has to stand on evidence — history, catalogs, an independent Government cost estimate (IGCE).

follow_ups.q: Could a BPA serve the recurring exercise cycle?
follow_ups.h: Same sites, same gear, every exercise cycle — what structure fits recurring demand?
follow_ups.d: Yes — a BPA against the recurring exercise cycle: negotiated up front with one or more small-business sources, priced terms, then each exercise's needs placed as fast calls without re-soliciting. It converts an annual fire drill into an account with discipline — and the calls stay inside the BPA's scope and the band's rules. The structural fix is what prevents next year's staff sergeant from collecting one quote per item under deadline.

coach.qtype: a simplified-acquisition question — RFO Part 13: the right lane by dollar band.
coach.smes: your Government Purchase Card (GPC) program coordinator, Small Business Professional, and chief of the contracting office (COCO).
coach.rule: The band picks the RFO Part 13 lane: GPC to $15K, purchase orders to the $350K simplified acquisition threshold (SAT) — reserved for small business under the RFO Part 19 Rule of Two — and splitting a known requirement to stay under a threshold is a bright-line violation.

scenarios.ask: One quote per item, award by Friday. What does this buy actually need?
scenarios.script: This is a commercial simplified-purchase question — RFO Part 12, not RFO Part 13: 13.001(a)(1) lets you use Part 13 only when no commercial product or service can satisfy the need, and portable toilets, fencing, and light towers are catalog commercial services. That matters immediately, because RFO 12.201-1(c)(2) tells me to solicit from at least three sources and, whenever practicable, from two sources not in the previous solicitation. My help: my Small Business Professional and the exercise planners on the real recurring demand. The rules: this is a commercial buy, so the small-business obligation runs through RFO 19.104-1(a) — set it aside above the micro-purchase threshold when two or more responsible small businesses will offer at a fair market price (RFO 13.102's band language is the noncommercial Part 13 rule) — so the first check is the vendors' size status — and price reasonableness rides on evidence, not on Friday. One quote per item at $120K is thin: I'd quickly solicit competitors or support the quotes with history and catalog comparisons; simplified acquisition procedures (SAP) is streamlined, not standard-free. Then the structural answer: this same requirement recurs every exercise cycle, so it belongs on a blanket purchase agreement (BPA) — negotiated once, called quickly forever after. That's how Friday deadlines stop producing one-quote files.

scenarios.scenario: September 28th. A flight has $47K of expiring operation and maintenance (O&M) and a wish list: two years of software licenses ($22K), a training course occurring in November ($9K), and 'stocking up' on toner and cables ($16K). 'Just get it obligated by Friday.'
baits: Everything is under the SAT so it feels easy
Use-or-lose framing
key_moves: Two years of licenses on one-year money fails Time — current-year period only
November training: bona fide need analysis (when does the need arise?) with FM
Reasonable stock replenishment is fine; hoarding isn't — document the consumption basis

follow_ups.q: When can a current-year obligation serve next-year performance?
follow_ups.h: The question is when the need arises, not when the money dies.
follow_ups.d: A current-year obligation serves next-year performance only when the need is bona fide to the current year: severable services within their 12-month window may cross fiscal years; delivery lead times can justify ordering now for later arrival; reasonable stock replenishment is current-year need. What never works: obligating simply because money expires — for a November course, the analysis is when the training need genuinely arises, worked with FM, not the color of September's calendar.

follow_ups.q: What's the severability of a license term?
follow_ups.h: A license term is a service period — measure it like one.
follow_ups.d: Software licenses are generally severable services measured by their term: a 12-month license on current-year O&M works (and may cross fiscal years); a 24-month term on one-year money fails Time — the second year is next year's need bought with this year's appropriation. The lawful shapes: buy the one-year term now and next year's separately, or structure a base-plus-option that lets each year's money fund each year's term.

coach.qtype: a simplified-acquisition question — RFO Part 13: the right lane by dollar band.
coach.smes: your Government Purchase Card (GPC) program coordinator, Small Business Professional, and chief of the contracting office (COCO).
coach.rule: The band picks the RFO Part 13 lane: GPC to $15K, purchase orders to the $350K simplified acquisition threshold (SAT) — reserved for small business under the RFO Part 19 Rule of Two — and splitting a known requirement to stay under a threshold is a bright-line violation.

scenarios.ask: It's September 28th with $47K expiring. What survives the fiscal test, and what doesn't?
scenarios.script: This is a fiscal-law question — Time, Purpose, Amount under the appropriations statutes, applied item by item. My help: financial management (FM) first and always — the Government Accountability Office (GAO) Red Book and DoD FMR are the references behind every call here. The wish list, sorted: two years of licenses on one-year money fails Time — buy the 12-month term, structure the rest; the November course gets a bona fide need analysis — when does the need actually arise? — worked with FM rather than assumed; and reasonable toner-and-cable replenishment is legitimate current-year need, while 'stocking up' beyond reasonable levels is next year's need wearing this year's money. And I'd say the quiet part: expiring funds create urgency, never authority. The test is the need's year — not the money's expiration date.

scenarios.scenario: Market research for a $3.1M cyber-hygiene assessment shows five interested firms: three small (one 8(a), one woman-owned small business (WOSB), one plain small) and two large incumbents from predecessor work. The customer worries small firms 'can't handle the clearances' — though all three hold facility clearances per DISS.
baits: The clearance worry is asserted, and disproven, in the same breath
Incumbent gravity
key_moves: Rule of Two is met on documented capability — set-aside required posture, and check the socioeconomic programs before the plain set-aside
The clearance objection died in DISS; record it as resolved
Wrong-direction pressure gets answered with the file, DD 2579 coordinated

follow_ups.q: Order of precedence among 8(a)/HUBZone/service-disabled veteran-owned small business (SDVOSB)/WOSB and total set-asides?
follow_ups.h: One of these is a must and the rest are mays — don't invert them.
follow_ups.d: Don't put the program lanes ahead of the set-aside — the RFO grades them differently. RFO 19.101(b)(3) says contracting officers must set aside contracts valued at more than the micro-purchase threshold for small businesses in certain circumstances, and RFO 19.104-1(a) supplies those circumstances: set the contract aside if there is a reasonable expectation of offers from two or more responsible small business concerns that are competitive in terms of fair market prices, quality, and delivery. RFO 19.101(b)(4)-(7) says contracting officers may set aside or sole source under the HUBZone, SDVOSB, WOSB, and 8(a) programs, and 19.104-1(e) is permissive on its face — the set-aside requirement "does not preclude" awarding under those programs. So the total small-business set-aside is the obligation; the program lanes are the options you weigh alongside it, in coordination with your Small Business Professional (DD 2579). There's no universal mandatory ranking among the programs — what's mandatory is considering them deliberately and documenting the path chosen.

follow_ups.q: What breaks a Rule-of-Two expectation legitimately?
follow_ups.h: The expectation breaks on evidence, not anxiety.
follow_ups.d: A Rule-of-Two expectation legitimately breaks when documented research shows fewer than two capable small businesses likely to offer at fair market prices — capability gaps proven against the actual requirement, not presumed from size; past small-business failure on THIS work; or market changes since research. Customer nervousness, clearance myths, and incumbent preference break nothing. If the expectation stands, the set-aside posture is required — and the file carries the evidence either way.

coach.qtype: a small-business question — RFO Part 19: the Rule of Two and the program lanes.
coach.smes: your Small Business Professional and the Small Business Administration (SBA) PCR; DD Form 2579 documents the coordination.
coach.rule: RFO Part 19: a reasonable expectation of two or more capable small businesses at fair market prices → set it aside. The rule tests the expectation at strategy time, not the final offer count.

scenarios.ask: Five interested firms, three of them small, and a nervous customer. What's your set-aside call?
scenarios.script: This is a small-business question — the RFO Part 19 Rule of Two on documented capability. My help: my Small Business Professional and the Small Business Administration (SBA), with the DD 2579 papering the coordination. The rule: a reasonable expectation of two or more capable small businesses at fair market prices means set-aside — and three interested small firms with relevant past performance is a textbook expectation. The customer's clearance worry died in the facility-clearance database; I'd record it as resolved, not let it haunt the strategy. The plain set-aside is the must here — RFO 19.101(b)(3) with the Rule of Two at 19.104-1(a); the program lanes at 19.101(b)(4)-(7) are mays I weigh alongside it, and 19.104-1(e) says the set-aside requirement doesn't preclude going 8(a) or WOSB instead. Then we compete it small, and the record carries any protest. Nervousness isn't evidence; the research is.

scenarios.scenario: An 8(a) firm has performed your base's grounds maintenance for six years across two competed-in-8(a) awards. The follow-on estimate is $5.8M. The district the Small Business Administration (SBA) office is slow answering emails, and the program manager (PM) suggests 'just doing it full-and-open this time — more competition is always better, right?'
baits: 'More competition is always better' sounds virtuous
SBA slowness invites unilateral action
key_moves: Once in 8(a), the requirement stays unless SBA releases it — full-and-open without release is a program violation, not extra competition
$5.8M exceeds the competitive-threshold family → competitive 8(a) is the likely lane
Chase the release question through channels, documented

follow_ups.q: When is release from 8(a) appropriate to request?
follow_ups.h: Release is SBA's call — when would the Government even ask?
follow_ups.d: Requesting release from 8(a) is appropriate when the requirement has genuinely outgrown the program's purpose — mandatory sources changed, the requirement transformed, or long-term strategy (like consolidations) needs the flexibility — and SBA weighs the program's development interest in the incumbent community. And release is one of three exits, not the only one: RFO 19.108-11(a) keeps any follow-on in the 8(a) program unless there is a mandatory source (8.101 through 8.103), or the follow-on will be set aside under the HUBZone, SDVOSB, or WOSB programs, or SBA agrees to release it. When release is the route, 19.108-11(b) names the approver — a written request to, and concurrence from, the SBA Associate Administrator for Business Development, not the district office — and 19.108-11(c) fixes what the request must say: whether the agency met its small disadvantaged business goal, whether it met its HUBZone, SDVOSB, WOSB, or small business goals, and whether the requirement is critical to the business development of the incumbent 8(a) firm. It's a deliberate, documented request worked through your Small Business Professional — not a workaround for slow email, and never a unilateral contracting officer (CO) decision.

follow_ups.q: Competitive vs. sole-source 8(a) — what sets the line?
follow_ups.h: Find the line the $5.8M estimate crosses.
follow_ups.d: Competitive 8(a) begins at $8.5M for manufacturing and $5.5M for everything else. At $5.8M, this services follow-on exceeds the competitive threshold — so it competes among eligible 8(a) firms rather than going sole source. Sole-source 8(a) below the thresholds needs no justification and approval (J&A) (DoD's statutory lane runs to $100M); above them, competition inside the program is the design. Know the family: $8.5M/$5.5M is the same pair that caps HUBZone and WOSB sole source.

coach.qtype: a small-business question — RFO Part 19: the Rule of Two and the program lanes.
coach.smes: your Small Business Professional and the Small Business Administration (SBA) PCR; DD Form 2579 documents the coordination.
coach.rule: RFO Part 19: a reasonable expectation of two or more capable small businesses at fair market prices → set it aside. The rule tests the expectation at strategy time, not the final offer count.

scenarios.ask: SBA is slow and the PM wants it competed full-and-open. What controls this follow-on?
scenarios.script: This is a small-business programs question — RFO 19.108-11, the 8(a) follow-on trap. My help: my Small Business Professional and the SBA district office, escalated past the slow inbox. The rule: once SBA accepts a requirement into 8(a), RFO 19.108-11(a) keeps the follow-on there unless one of three things is true — a mandatory source applies, the follow-on will be set aside under HUBZone, service-disabled veteran-owned small business (SDVOSB), or woman-owned small business (WOSB), or SBA agrees to release it — six years and two in-program awards make this unmistakably an 8(a) requirement, and full-and-open without a release letter is a program violation, not extra competition. At $5.8M we're over the $5.5M services line, so the lawful path is competitive 8(a) among eligible firms. If the program genuinely wants out of 8(a) someday, that's a written request to, and concurrence from, the SBA Associate Administrator for Business Development under RFO 19.108-11(b), carrying the goal and business-development content at 19.108-11(c) — not a decision made by an unanswered email.

scenarios.scenario: A depot needs original equipment manufacturer (OEM)-proprietary calibration of 12 test stands. The OEM quotes $480K. Your predecessor's file contains three identical annual justifications and approvals (J&As) citing 'only one responsible source,' each noting 'the Government intends to develop organic capability' — which never happened.
baits: Three approved J&As feel like precedent
The OEM lock may be genuinely real
key_moves: Repetition weakens, not strengthens: each J&A promised barrier-removal actions that never occurred — this year's must address that honestly
Attack the barrier: data/licensing for organic or third-party calibration priced as a line of effort
If the lock is real this year, the J&A can still be truthful — about the failure too

follow_ups.q: What does 6.104-1 require about overcoming barriers?
follow_ups.h: The J&A has a required section about knocking the barrier down — read the last three.
follow_ups.d: A one-source justification must describe the actions the agency will take to overcome the barriers to competition — data purchases, qualification of second sources, organic capability. When three consecutive J&As promised the same actions and nothing happened, this year's justification must confront that record honestly: what was promised, why it didn't occur, and what concrete funded steps change it now. Reviewers and protesters both read the file backward — a fourth copy-paste is where sole-source cases go to die.

follow_ups.q: Who approves at $480K?
follow_ups.h: $480K sits in a specific rung of the ladder.
follow_ups.d: At $480K the J&A sits in the lowest band of RFO 6.104-2(a) — $900,000 or below, approved by the contracting officer, accomplished by the certification required in the justification's own content at 6.104-1(a)(12). There is no chief of the contracting office (COCO) rung on this ladder; don't invent one. Know the rest of it anyway, because the panel will climb it: above $900,000 to $20 million, the advocate for competition, not delegable; above $20 million to $90 million — $150 million for DoD, NASA, and the Coast Guard — the head of the procuring activity, delegable only to a general or flag officer or a civilian above GS-15; above that, the senior procurement executive, not delegable except for USD(A&S) acting as DoD's senior procurement executive. Tier questions are the board's favorite second ask.

coach.qtype: a competition question — the Competition in Contracting Act (CICA) and RFO Part 6: the default and the exception ladder.
coach.smes: the Competition Advocate, Legal, and fresh market research to test the premise.
coach.rule: Full and open is the default over the simplified acquisition threshold (SAT) (RFO 6.101). 'Other than' takes one of the seven RFO 6.103 exceptions in a justification and approval (J&A) approved at the RFO 6.104 tier — and 'we've always used them' is not one of the seven.

scenarios.ask: Three identical J&As in the file and a fourth on your desk. What does this year's have to say?
scenarios.script: This is a competition question — RFO 6.103-1 — about repetition. My help: Legal, the Competition Advocate's office, and the program on the barrier itself. The rule: each J&A must be true when written — and repetition weakens rather than grandfathers it. Three identical justifications each promised barrier-removal that never happened; a fourth copy-paste is protest bait. So this year's J&A confronts the record: what was promised, why it didn't happen, and the funded, dated plan that actually attacks the barrier — buying the calibration data or licensing, qualifying a second source, or building organic capability. At $480K the approval sits low, but the credibility question sits high. The OEM can win this year honestly; the Government just can't keep buying the same excuse.

scenarios.scenario: A lab wants to award a $2M 'study extension' to the university that just finished a basic-research grant, sole source, 'to preserve research continuity.' The work statement reads like applied development with deliverable prototypes. The lab argues grants don't need justifications and approvals (J&As) so neither should this.
baits: Grant history blurs the instrument question
'Continuity' as an all-purpose justification
key_moves: Name the instrument first: prototype deliverables for Government benefit = acquisition (contract), not assistance — competition rules attach
Continuity can support a 6.103-1 case only with market research showing unique capability
If it's genuinely basic research, a BAA or assistance lane may fit — but the SOW says otherwise

follow_ups.q: Acquisition vs. assistance — the test?
follow_ups.h: Who principally benefits — the public purpose or the Government's own need?
follow_ups.d: The test is principal purpose: assistance instruments (grants, cooperative agreements) transfer support for a public purpose — the Government stimulates research it doesn't primarily consume. Acquisition (a contract) obtains supplies or services for the Government's direct benefit. Deliverable prototypes serving a Government capability need are acquisition, whatever the paperwork was last time — and acquisition brings CICA, competition, and Part 6 with it.

follow_ups.q: Could a BAA have covered this from the start?
follow_ups.h: The BAA's lane is ideas competed against a standard — could this work have started there?
follow_ups.d: Yes — applied research with varying technical approaches is the BAA's home turf: broad announcement, stated criteria, independent scientific merit review, proposals evaluated against the standard rather than head-to-head. A BAA from the start would have made every award competitive by design, including follow-on phases within its scope. The lesson to say out loud: instrument choice at the beginning determines the competition posture years later.

coach.qtype: a competition question — the Competition in Contracting Act (CICA) and RFO Part 6: the default and the exception ladder.
coach.smes: the Competition Advocate, Legal, and fresh market research to test the premise.
coach.rule: Full and open is the default over the simplified acquisition threshold (SAT) (RFO 6.101). 'Other than' takes one of the seven RFO 6.103 exceptions in a justification and approval (J&A) approved at the RFO 6.104 tier — and 'we've always used them' is not one of the seven.

scenarios.ask: A sole-source 'study extension' that reads like prototype development. What instrument — and what process?
scenarios.script: This is a research and development (R&D)-authorities question — RFO Part 35 against the assistance instruments — name the instrument before anything else. My help: Legal, the agreements officer channel, and the lab's program office. The test: principal purpose. Deliverable prototypes for a Government capability need are acquisition — a contract — no matter how the last award was papered; and acquisition means the Competition in Contracting Act (CICA) attaches. So the $2M 'extension' either competes or stands on a real RFO 6.103-1 justification with market research behind it — 'research continuity' is an argument, not an authority. Going forward, I'd point the lab at the broad agency announcement (BAA) lane: applied research with varied approaches competed against a published standard is exactly what BAAs exist for, and starting there makes the follow-on question disappear.

scenarios.scenario: Mid-evaluation on a trade-off selection, the source selection evaluation board (SSEB) discovers every offeror misread an ambiguous performance work statement (PWS) paragraph the same way — pricing 24/7 coverage the Government never intended. The source selection authority (SSA) wants to 'just evaluate what they offered and fix it with the winner after award.'
baits: Uniform misreading feels evaluable ('same playing field')
Fixing post-award avoids schedule slip
key_moves: A materially defective solicitation isn't cured by consistent confusion — amend, and give offerors a chance to revise
'Fix it with the winner' = negotiating scope after award: pricing shifts, protest exposure, scope questions
Amendment now costs weeks; the alternative costs the competition

follow_ups.q: When does an amendment require proposal revisions?
follow_ups.h: Materiality decides between a clarifying answer and an amendment with revisions.
follow_ups.d: An amendment requires proposal revisions when it changes what offerors priced or how they'd technically respond — a materially different coverage requirement is exactly that. Minor clarifications that don't affect price or approach can be answered without revisions. Here, every offeror priced 24/7 coverage the Government doesn't want: the amendment changes the deal, so offerors get the amendment and the chance to revise — anything less evaluates proposals against a requirement nobody was asked to meet. And there's a third tier above both of those, and it's mandatory, not discretionary: RFO 15.106(e)(2) says contracting officers must cancel the RFP and issue a new one, regardless of the stage of the acquisition, if an amendment is proposed after offers have been received and, in the contracting officer's judgment based on market research or otherwise, the requirement change is so substantial that it exceeds what prospective offerors reasonably could have anticipated and additional sources likely would have submitted offers had the change been in the RFP. Cutting 24/7 down to the coverage the Government actually wanted is exactly the change that test is aimed at, so I'd make that call on the record instead of assuming an amendment cures it.

follow_ups.q: What if the ambiguity surfaced after award instead?
follow_ups.h: Post-award, the same fix becomes a scope-and-competition problem.
follow_ups.d: If the ambiguity surfaced after award, the 'fix' becomes a modification reducing coverage — a price-relevant change the losers never got to compete. That invites the descoping protest ('we'd have bid differently at 12-hour coverage') and a scope analysis with an honest consideration adjustment. The comparison is instructive for the panel: pre-award, an amendment cures it cleanly; post-award, the same facts become protest exposure plus a negotiated mod. Timing is everything — which is why you fix it now.

coach.qtype: a source-selection question — RFO Part 15: fair process, documented judgment.
coach.smes: the source selection authority (SSA), your source selection evaluation board (SSEB) chairs, Legal, and the pricing office for the cost/price side.
coach.rule: The solicitation is the contract of the competition: evaluate exactly as Section M promised, keep RFO Part 15 exchanges in their lanes — clarifications under 15.202(a)(2), which never permit a proposal revision, and competitive negotiations under 15.204-2, which must at minimum surface each offeror's deficiencies and significant weaknesses.

scenarios.ask: Every offeror priced coverage the Government never wanted. The SSA says evaluate as-is and fix it with the winner. Your call?
scenarios.script: This is a source-selection question — RFO Part 15 — about a defective solicitation. My help: Legal and the SSA — who I'd respectfully redirect. The rule: proposals are evaluated against the solicitation as written, and this solicitation misstates the requirement — every offeror priced 24/7 coverage the Government never intended. Consistent confusion doesn't cure a defect; it proves it. 'Fix it with the winner' is negotiating scope after award: the price shifts, the losers protest, and they'd be right. So: amend the solicitation, state the real coverage requirement, and give all offerors the chance to revise — after running the test at RFO 15.106(e)(2), which makes cancelling the request for proposals (RFP) and issuing a new one mandatory, regardless of the stage, when an amendment proposed after receipt of offers changes the requirement so substantially that it exceeds what prospective offerors reasonably could have anticipated and additional sources likely would have offered. It costs two weeks now. The alternative costs a sustained protest, a descoping mod, and the program's credibility later.

scenarios.scenario: After award, the losing offeror's debrief question list includes: their own weaknesses (fine), the winner's proposed staffing plan, the winner's price broken out by contract line item number (CLIN), and 'all evaluator notes mentioning our company.' The program manager (PM) wants to 'give them everything so they feel heard and don't protest.'
baits: Generosity as protest-avoidance strategy
'Feeling heard' conflated with disclosure
key_moves: Debriefs disclose the requester's own evaluation, the evaluated award result and rationale — never the winner's proposal details or CLIN pricing
Over-disclosure creates the next problem (winner's proprietary data released)
A quality debrief is thorough about THEM — that's what actually prevents protests

follow_ups.q: What must a post-award debrief include?
follow_ups.h: The debrief discloses their evaluation and the outcome's rationale — whose proposal stays sealed?
follow_ups.d: A post-award debrief must include: the requester's own evaluation — significant weaknesses and deficiencies — the overall evaluated cost/price and technical rating of requester and awardee, past-performance conclusions on the requester, rankings where used, the award rationale, and answers to reasonable questions about whether procedures were followed. For a commercial product, RFO 15.301-1(c)(1)(v) adds the make and model the winner will deliver. And for DoD it goes past "the level of the SSDD's reasoning": R-DFARS 215.301-170(a) makes a debriefing mandatory on request for awards valued at $15 million or more, and (b) puts the source selection decision document itself in play — redacted to protect other offerors' confidential and proprietary information, optional at the requester's election on awards over $15 million and not over $150 million to a small business or nontraditional defense contractor, and required on awards over $150 million. Then R-DFARS 215.301-270: the offeror gets 2 business days after the debriefing to submit additional written questions, I have 5 business days to answer in writing, and the debriefing is not concluded until that written response is delivered. It's a real accounting of THEIR result and WHY the winner won — not the winner's papers.

follow_ups.q: What's releasable about the awardee?
follow_ups.h: The winner's information has an owner.
follow_ups.d: About the awardee, releasable: identity, total evaluated price, overall ratings, and the comparative rationale for selection. Not releasable: their staffing plan, technical approach, CLIN-level pricing, or anything revealing proposal content — that's contractor bid and proposal information, protected, and over-disclosure creates the next integrity problem (the winner's own protest, or a the Procurement Integrity Act (PIA) issue). The discipline: explain the decision, guard the proposals.

coach.qtype: a source-selection question — RFO Part 15: fair process, documented judgment.
coach.smes: the source selection authority (SSA), your source selection evaluation board (SSEB) chairs, Legal, and the pricing office for the cost/price side.
coach.rule: The solicitation is the contract of the competition: evaluate exactly as Section M promised, keep RFO Part 15 exchanges in their lanes — clarifications under 15.202(a)(2), which never permit a proposal revision, and competitive negotiations under 15.204-2, which must at minimum surface each offeror's deficiencies and significant weaknesses.

scenarios.ask: The loser wants the winner's staffing plan and CLIN prices. What does their debrief contain?
scenarios.script: This is a debrief question — RFO Part 15's disclosure lines — and a good debrief is protest prevention, not a document fight. My help: Legal on the disclosure lines, the source selection evaluation board (SSEB) record for the substance. The rule: the loser gets a full, honest accounting of their own evaluation — weaknesses, deficiencies, their ratings and evaluated price, the rankings, and the rationale for the award — plus the winner's identity, total evaluated price, and overall ratings. What they don't get: the winner's staffing plan, approach, or CLIN pricing — that's protected proposal information, and releasing it trades one protest for another. So I'd run the debrief generously inside those lines: answer questions, show the process was fair, take feedback. And I'd run the DoD machinery deliberately — R-DFARS 215.301-170 makes the debriefing mandatory on request at $15 million or more and can put the redacted source selection decision document itself on the table by dollar value, and R-DFARS 215.301-270 keeps the debriefing open until I answer: 2 business days for their additional written questions, 5 business days for my written response, and the debriefing is not concluded until that response is delivered. That last point is the one the protest clock hangs on. Offerors protest mysteries far more often than they protest explanations.

scenarios.scenario: Negotiating a $16M sole-source sustainment mod (awarded July 2026), the contractor certifies its data. Three weeks after agreement on price — before the mod is signed — their sweep surfaces a vendor quote 22% below the one in the proposal for a major material item.
baits: 'We already agreed on price'
The sweep feels like good faith that shouldn't be punished
key_moves: Pre-award discovery: use the corrected data — adjust the price downward before signature
The certificate speaks as of the date of agreement; incorporating the correction protects both sides
Document the adjustment in the PNM; good-faith sweeps are exactly why the process works

follow_ups.q: Same facts discovered 6 months after award — what changes?
follow_ups.h: Six months post-award, the same quote becomes a different animal with a remedy attached.
follow_ups.d: Discovered after award, that undisclosed quote is defective pricing: the certified data wasn't accurate, complete, and current at agreement. The Government becomes entitled to a price reduction plus interest (and profit on the delta) through the defective-pricing clause — with Legal driving, and a unilateral mod if the contractor won't settle. Same facts, different timing: before signature it's a correction; after award it's a remedy. That contrast is the whole lesson.

follow_ups.q: All five defective-pricing elements?
follow_ups.h: Run the five elements against these exact facts.
follow_ups.d: The five: (1) the vendor quote is cost or pricing data — yes; (2) it existed before agreement on price — yes, the sweep found it in their files; (3) it wasn't disclosed to the contracting officer (CO) — yes; (4) the Government relied on the data submitted — yes, the negotiation priced the higher quote; (5) reliance increased the price — yes, by the delta. All five hold, which is what makes the pre-signature correction so valuable: it resolves cleanly what would otherwise be a textbook defective-pricing case.

coach.qtype: a pricing question — RFO 15.403 on what data you're owed, RFO 15.404 on the analysis the file needs.
coach.smes: your pricing office, the Defense Contract Management Agency (DCMA) for field pricing and rates, the Defense Contract Audit Agency (DCAA) for audit, and Legal on defective-pricing exposure.
coach.rule: Price analysis always (RFO 15.404-1). Certified data only past the threshold with the RFO 15.403-2 CLAWM exceptions checked first — and no award without a documented fair-and-reasonable determination.

scenarios.ask: The sweep surfaced a 22% cheaper vendor quote after agreement but before signature. What happens to the price?
scenarios.script: This is a pricing question — the 10 U.S.C. §§3701–3708 certified-data machinery at the sweep seam. My help: my pricing office and Legal on the exposure math. The rule: the certificate speaks as of the date of agreement on price, and we haven't signed — so the corrected data gets used now. The price adjusts downward for the 22% quote before signature, the price negotiation memorandum (PNM) is updated to tell the true story, and the certificate is executed against accurate, complete, current data. I'd also credit the contractor's sweep — that's the system working. And I'd say the contrast out loud for the panel: caught today, it's a correction; caught six months after award, it's defective pricing — price reduction plus interest, with Legal. Same quote, different day, very different meeting.

scenarios.scenario: A contractor offers to 'save everyone time' on a $14M sole-source development action: they'll accept firm-fixed-price (FFP) if the Government skips 'the whole certified data exercise,' arguing the fixed price transfers all risk so the data doesn't matter.
baits: Risk-transfer logic sounds economically clever
Everyone loves skipping the exercise
key_moves: Contract type is not a CLAWM exception — over threshold, sole source, non-commercial = certified data, period
An FFP priced without data analysis just locks in an unanalyzed number — risk transfer at an unknown premium
Separately evaluate whether FFP even fits development-grade uncertainty

follow_ups.q: Recite CLAWM
follow_ups.h: Recite the exceptions — is contract type on the list?
follow_ups.d: CLAWM: Commercial items; prices set by Law or regulation; Adequate price competition; Waiver by the head of the contracting activity (HCA); commercial-item Modifications. That's the list. Contract type appears nowhere on it — FFP is a risk allocation, not a data exception. Over the threshold, sole source, non-commercial: certified cost or pricing data is required regardless of type, and offering FFP doesn't buy out of it.

follow_ups.q: Why is unanalyzed FFP worse than analyzed cost-type here?
follow_ups.h: What does the fixed price actually lock in if nobody analyzed the number?
follow_ups.d: An unanalyzed FFP locks in an unanalyzed number — if it's padded 30%, the Government pays the padding with certainty, every unit, no remedy. Analyzed cost-type at least buys visibility: costs are auditable, fee is negotiated on known risk, and overruns are seen as they happen. Risk transfer only has value when the price transferring the risk was priced right — which is precisely what the data exists to establish. 'FFP protects us' without analysis protects the contractor's margin.

coach.qtype: a pricing question — RFO 15.403 on what data you're owed, RFO 15.404 on the analysis the file needs.
coach.smes: your pricing office, the Defense Contract Management Agency (DCMA) for field pricing and rates, the Defense Contract Audit Agency (DCAA) for audit, and Legal on defective-pricing exposure.
coach.rule: Price analysis always (RFO 15.404-1). Certified data only past the threshold with the RFO 15.403-2 CLAWM exceptions checked first — and no award without a documented fair-and-reasonable determination.

scenarios.ask: FFP in exchange for skipping certified data — 'the fixed price transfers all the risk anyway.' Deal?
scenarios.script: This is a pricing question wearing a contract-type disguise. My help: my pricing office, the Defense Contract Management Agency (DCMA) on rates, Legal if this gets creative. The rule: RFO 15.403-2's CLAWM — commercial, law, adequate competition, waiver, commercial mods — and contract type is not on the list. A $14M sole-source, non-commercial development action over the threshold requires certified cost or pricing data whatever the type. And I'd dismantle the pitch itself: an FFP priced without analysis just locks in an unanalyzed number — if it's padded, we pay the padding with certainty. Risk transfer has value only when the transferring price was priced right. So: certified data comes in, we analyze, we negotiate — and then FFP may well be the right answer, at a defensible number.

scenarios.scenario: A program manager (PM) wants cost-plus-fixed-fee (CPFF) for a follow-on production lot of 200 proven units, 'because the contractor says material prices are volatile and won't hold a firm price.' Cost history from three prior firm-fixed-price (FFP) lots is extensive and stable except for two commodity metals.
baits: Contractor preference presented as necessity
Real-but-narrow volatility inflated into type-wide uncertainty
key_moves: Mature production with deep cost history is FP territory — the named risk is two commodities, not the effort
FFP with economic price adjustment scoped to those indices prices the actual risk
CPFF on stable production shifts all cost risk to the Government for no reason — and check the E.O. 14402 justification implications of going non-FFP

follow_ups.q: How does an EPA clause get structured?
follow_ups.h: An EPA clause prices a named risk — name it, index it, bound it.
follow_ups.d: Start with the use test: RFO 16.203-3 allows a fixed-price contract with economic price adjustment only if the contracting officer determines it is necessary to protect the contractor and the Government against significant fluctuations in labor or material costs. Then pick the instrument the commodities actually call for. For basic steel, aluminum, brass, bronze, or copper mill products bought fixed-price where an established catalog or market price exists, R-DFARS 216.203-470(a)(1)(i) puts the clause at 252.216-7000, Economic Price Adjustment—Basic Steel, Aluminum, Brass, Bronze, or Copper Mill Products, in the solicitation, with the representation provision at 252.216-7007; (a)(1)(ii) is the limit to remember — do not exceed the 10 percent figure in paragraph (d)(1) of the clause unless approved at a level above the contracting officer. If the metals don't fit that clause, RFO 16.203-1(a) gives the three families — adjustments based on established prices, on actual costs of labor or material, or on cost indexes — and a defensible index clause identifies the specific cost elements exposed (the two volatile commodities), names the published index, sets a trigger band so routine noise doesn't adjust anything, applies ceilings and floors, and defines the adjustment math and timing. It surgically prices the actual risk while everything else stays firm — protecting both parties from the named volatility without converting the whole lot to cost-plus.

follow_ups.q: When would production legitimately be cost-type?
follow_ups.h: When would production honestly need cost-type?
