follow_ups.d: Rarely — and only when genuine cost uncertainty pervades the effort: first articles after major redesign, production restart after a long break with a broken supplier base, or configuration instability that makes quantities and processes honestly unpriceable. Mature, stable, repeatedly-priced production is the opposite of that. The type question always returns to requirement definition: uncertainty you can name and bound gets priced with an instrument; uncertainty that pervades gets cost-type. Two commodities have names.

coach.qtype: a contract-type question — RFO Part 16: who carries the cost risk, and why.
coach.smes: your pricing office, the program manager (PM) on requirement certainty, and your reviewing chain for the acquisition plan, and the head of the contracting activity (HCA) for any incentive- or award-fee determination and findings (D&F).
coach.rule: RFO Part 16 matches risk to definition: firm-fixed-price (FFP) when the work prices firmly; cost-type when it can't — gated by RFO 16.301-3 on an acquisition plan approved one level above the contracting officer (CO), an accounting system that can segregate, accumulate and allocate costs, and sufficient Government resources including a designated contracting officer's representative (COR). The HCA-signed D&F belongs to incentive- and award-fee contracts (RFO 16.401-2(a)), not to cost-type. Forcing FFP onto the unknowable is risk denial, not risk transfer — and E.O. 14402 makes other-than-FFP a justified decision (RFO 16.104).

scenarios.ask: CPFF for a proven production lot because 'material prices are volatile.' What type does this work actually take?
scenarios.script: This is a contract-type question — RFO Part 16: match the type to where the risk actually lives. My help: my pricing office and the cost history from three prior lots. The facts: mature production, deep stable actuals, and the named risk is two commodities — not the effort. That's fixed-price territory: FFP with an economic price adjustment clause scoped to those two commodities — RFO 16.203-3 is the use test, significant fluctuations in material costs, and for basic steel, aluminum, brass, bronze, or copper mill products with an established catalog or market price, R-DFARS 216.203-470(a)(1) names the instrument: clause 252.216-7000, with the 10 percent figure in its paragraph (d)(1) not exceeded without approval above me. CPFF would hand back the entire cost risk of a proven production line to cure a problem two indices can carry — and RFO 16.301-3's gates would have to be cleared for a type the work doesn't need — an acquisition plan approved one level above me, an accounting system that can segregate, accumulate and allocate costs, and enough Government resources including a designated contracting officer's representative (COR). Price the real risk surgically; keep the rest firm. The contractor's volatility concern is legitimate; their prescription isn't.

scenarios.scenario: On a fixed-price incentive (firm target) (FPIF) negotiation — target cost $20M, target profit $1.6M, ceiling 125%, share 80/20 — the contractor's final position quietly moves the ceiling to 135% 'to reflect supply-chain reality' while leaving everything else unchanged. The program manager (PM) thinks that's harmless 'since we only pay actuals plus profit anyway.'
baits: 'We only pay actuals' misunderstands FPIF
One parameter moving 'quietly' among four
key_moves: The ceiling is the Government's hard protection — raising it moves the PTA and extends Government exposure by $2M
Run the PTA math both ways and show the delta; price any real supply-chain risk explicitly instead
Every FPIF element is negotiated geometry; nothing moves 'quietly'

follow_ups.q: Compute PTA before and after
follow_ups.h: Run PTA = (Ceiling − Target Price) ÷ Gov share + Target Cost, both ways.
follow_ups.d: Target price is $21.6M (target cost $20M + target profit $1.6M). At a 125% ceiling ($25M): PTA = (25 − 21.6) ÷ 0.8 + 20 = $24.25M. At 135% ($27M): PTA = (27 − 21.6) ÷ 0.8 + 20 = $26.75M. The quiet edit moved the point of total assumption $2.5M to the right and raised the Government's maximum exposure by $2M — the contractor stays on the shared-risk gravy longer before bearing full cost risk. Run the math at the board; the delta IS the argument.

follow_ups.q: What happens to contractor behavior past PTA?
follow_ups.h: After PTA, whose money funds each additional dollar of cost?
follow_ups.d: Past the PTA, every additional cost dollar comes out of the contractor's profit until the ceiling, where the contractor bears everything — effectively firm-fixed-price (FFP) from PTA to ceiling. That's why PTA placement drives behavior: a contractor operating below PTA shares overruns with the Government (20 cents on the dollar here); past it, cost discipline suddenly gets personal. Raising the ceiling delays that discipline — which is exactly why they proposed it quietly.

coach.qtype: a contract-type question — RFO Part 16: who carries the cost risk, and why.
coach.smes: your pricing office, the program manager (PM) on requirement certainty, and your reviewing chain for the acquisition plan, and the head of the contracting activity (HCA) for any incentive- or award-fee determination and findings (D&F).
coach.rule: RFO Part 16 matches risk to definition: firm-fixed-price (FFP) when the work prices firmly; cost-type when it can't — gated by RFO 16.301-3 on an acquisition plan approved one level above the contracting officer (CO), an accounting system that can segregate, accumulate and allocate costs, and sufficient Government resources including a designated contracting officer's representative (COR). The HCA-signed D&F belongs to incentive- and award-fee contracts (RFO 16.401-2(a)), not to cost-type. Forcing FFP onto the unknowable is risk denial, not risk transfer — and E.O. 14402 makes other-than-FFP a justified decision (RFO 16.104).

scenarios.ask: The contractor quietly moved the ceiling from 125% to 135%. What did that change, and what's your response?
scenarios.script: This is a contract-type question — RFO Part 16 FPIF mechanics, and the ceiling is the Government's hard protection. My help: my pricing office, with the PTA math on one page. The move: raising the ceiling from 125% to 135% shifts the PTA from $24.25M to $26.75M and adds $2M of Government exposure — the contractor rides the 80/20 share longer before cost discipline gets personal. 'Supply-chain reality' may be genuine, but the cure isn't a quiet ceiling raise — if there's a real, nameable risk, we price it explicitly: adjust the target cost on evidence, or scope an economic price adjustment (EPA)-style protection to the named exposure. My response: the ceiling stays, the math goes on the table, and any real risk gets priced in daylight.

scenarios.scenario: On a 4-holder engineering indefinite-delivery/indefinite-quantity (IDIQ), the program shapes a new task order around a proprietary modeling tool that only Holder C owns — the requirement literally names the tool. Asked why, the program manager (PM) says 'their engineer demoed it and it's exactly what we need.'
baits: Naming the tool feels like precision, not steering
The demo genuinely was impressive
key_moves: A requirement written around one holder's proprietary product is steering wearing a spec costume — restate to performance terms
If only the tool truly satisfies the need, that's an 'only one capable' exception argument — made honestly in a Justification for an Exception to Fair Opportunity, not smuggled in
Fair opportunity means the other three get a real shot at the actual need

follow_ups.q: What belongs in the justification if the tool is genuinely unique?
follow_ups.h: The justification for a genuinely unique tool still has required content — evidence, not enthusiasm.
follow_ups.d: A defensible only-one-capable justification documents: the performance need the tool satisfies, the market check across the OTHER holders (what they were asked, what they answered), why alternatives genuinely can't meet the need in time, the price-reasonableness plan absent competition, and — like a justification and approval (J&A) — what the Government will do to open future orders. Approved at the tier the dollars demand, posted. 'Their engineer demoed it and it's exactly what we need' appears nowhere in that outline.

follow_ups.q: How does this differ from a brand-name justification in open competition?
follow_ups.h: Same disease, different venue — how does the open-market version of this get justified?
follow_ups.d: In open competition, naming a product is a brand-name justification: a documented explanation of the particular feature-need only that product meets, with market research behind it, approved and made public with the solicitation. At the order level the controlling rule is RFO 16.507-7: a brand-name item, even if available on more than one contract, is an item peculiar to one manufacturer, so it needs its own brand-name justification in the 16.507-6(d)-(e) format, approved when the requirement is determined — and for an order over $40,000, posted or provided to all contract awardees with the solicitation. The shared lesson: requirements stated as performance outcomes preserve competition in both venues; requirements stated as product names must earn the restriction in writing.

coach.qtype: a fair-opportunity question — RFO 16.507: every holder's real chance, or a documented exception.
coach.smes: the vehicle's procuring contracting officer (PCO) and ordering guide, the Competition Advocate for over-simplified acquisition threshold (SAT) justifications, and the ombudsman lane for holder complaints.
coach.rule: RFO 16.507-2 makes fair opportunity the default on multiple-award vehicles; exceptions (16.507-6) ride a written Justification for an Exception to Fair Opportunity — the document the RFO names — up the same approval ladder as justifications and approvals (J&As), and consideration must be genuine — not rotation paperwork.

scenarios.ask: The order names Holder C's proprietary tool by name. How do you handle the requirement — and the demo-driven enthusiasm?
scenarios.script: This is an RFO 16.507 fair-opportunity question — a requirement written around one holder's product. My help: the vehicle procuring contracting officer (PCO), Legal, and the program engineers on what the mission actually needs. The rule: fair opportunity is the default, and a spec that names Holder C's tool is steering wearing a requirements costume. First move: restate the requirement in performance terms — what must the modeling produce, to what fidelity, by when — and ask the other three holders the capability question directly. If the honest answer is that only the tool satisfies the need in time, then the exception is real: an only-one-capable Justification for an Exception to Fair Opportunity on evidence, approved at tier, posted. The demo enthusiasm goes in a drawer; the performance requirement and the market answers go in the file.

scenarios.scenario: A $9M task order for logistics software support is at month 30 of 36. The program wants to add data-migration work for a completely different system owned by another program executive officer (PEO) — 'the vehicle's ceiling has room and the contractor is willing.'
baits: Ceiling room framed as authority
Contractor willingness framed as feasibility
key_moves: Ceiling is capacity, not scope — test the new work against the IDIQ's scope and this order's
Another PEO's unrelated system is a new requirement: fair opportunity on this vehicle (if in scope) or a new procurement (if not)
Out-of-scope orders are protestable at any dollar value as improper sole-source awards

follow_ups.q: Who protests an out-of-scope order and where?
follow_ups.h: An improper order is a competition someone was denied — who complains, and to whom?
follow_ups.d: An out-of-scope order is effectively a sole-source award of new work: the other vehicle holders (denied fair opportunity) complain to the task-order ombudsman at any dollar value — and at the Government Accountability Office (GAO), an order that exceeds the scope, period, or ceiling of the underlying contract is protestable at ANY value, by holders or even by contractors outside the vehicle whose competitive universe was bypassed. Scope growth is the exception that unlocks GAO's door below the dollar thresholds.

follow_ups.q: What analysis documents an in-scope conclusion?
follow_ups.h: The in-scope memo has two layers — the vehicle's four corners and this order's.
follow_ups.d: The analysis documents both levels: does the work fit the IDIQ's scope statement (the enterprise every holder signed up to compete within), and does it fit THIS order's scope (what this order's competition anticipated)? Corners: nature of the work versus the scope statement, period, cumulative value, and what the original order competition reasonably anticipated. A different PEO's unrelated system fails at both levels — and writing the honest analysis now is cheaper than writing the protest response later.

coach.qtype: a fair-opportunity question — RFO 16.507: every holder's real chance, or a documented exception.
coach.smes: the vehicle's procuring contracting officer (PCO) and ordering guide, the Competition Advocate for over-simplified acquisition threshold (SAT) justifications, and the ombudsman lane for holder complaints.
coach.rule: RFO 16.507-2 makes fair opportunity the default on multiple-award vehicles; exceptions (16.507-6) ride a written Justification for an Exception to Fair Opportunity — the document the RFO names — up the same approval ladder as justifications and approvals (J&As), and consideration must be genuine — not rotation paperwork.

scenarios.ask: Ceiling room exists and the clock is running. Can the migration work ride this task order?
scenarios.script: This is an RFO 16.507 fair-opportunity question about scope — and ceiling is capacity, not permission. My help: the vehicle procuring contracting officer (PCO) and Legal on the scope analysis. The test runs at two levels: does data migration for a different PEO's unrelated system fit the indefinite-delivery/indefinite-quantity's (IDIQ) scope statement, and does it fit this order's own scope? On these facts it fails both — it's a new requirement, not growth of this one. So the lawful paths: compete it among the vehicle's holders as a new order if the vehicle's scope truly covers it, or take it to its proper vehicle or a new competition if it doesn't. Riding the ceiling because 'the contractor knows our environment' is a sole source without a justification — and out-of-scope orders are protestable at any dollar value. That's a door I'm not opening.

scenarios.scenario: Exercising option year 2 of a lab-services contract, you discover the option contract line item number (CLIN) was never priced at award — the schedule says 'TBD, to be negotiated.' The contracting officer's representative (COR) has already emailed the contractor that 'the option is being picked up' and performance continues seamlessly in three weeks.
baits: Seamless continuity pressure
The COR's email creating apparent momentum
key_moves: An unpriced 'option' isn't an option — there's no unilateral right to exercise; it's a negotiation (and its competition posture needs Legal now)
The COR email binds nothing but complicates the negotiation — correct it in writing
Bridge honestly if needed while the real path (negotiate/compete) is worked

follow_ups.q: What made the option invalid at award — evaluation or pricing?
follow_ups.h: An option's power comes from what happened at award — what has to have happened?
follow_ups.d: A real option was priced at award and evaluated in the source selection — that's what makes later exercise a unilateral right and shields it from being a new sole-source procurement. 'TBD, to be negotiated' fails the pricing half: there's nothing to exercise, only something to negotiate. And a negotiated continuation with the incumbent is a new procurement action wearing an option's label — its competition posture needs Legal immediately.

follow_ups.q: What are the Government's lawful continuity tools here?
follow_ups.h: Continuity tools exist — each with its own clock and justification.
follow_ups.d: The lawful kit: negotiate a bilateral extension with the incumbent supported by an honest justification and price analysis; use the extension-of-services mechanism (up to 6 months) if the clause is in the contract; or bridge via a properly justified short sole-source while competing the follow-on. In parallel: start the recompete NOW, because every continuity tool is a rented month, not a strategy — and document why the defective option wasn't caught at award, because that finding is coming.

coach.qtype: an options question — RFO Part 17: the exercise gates, applied to today.
coach.smes: Financial management (FM) for funds, the contracting officer's representative (COR) and program manager (PM) on performance and continuing need, and Legal if the notice window slipped.
coach.rule: Exercise only through the RFO 17.204-1(b) gates: timely written notice, funds available, an existing requirement, synopsized or exempt, no active SAM exclusion, acceptable performance, a fair and reasonable price in the Government's best interest, and part 6 compliance — and for DoD, R-DFARS 217.204-170 adds an active and accurate SAM record plus SPRS verification of the NIST SP 800-171 score and a current CMMC certificate. Miss the notice window and the unilateral right lapses into a bilateral negotiation.

scenarios.ask: The option CLIN says 'TBD.' The COR already promised exercise. Where does this leave you?
scenarios.script: This is an RFO Part 17 options question where the option turns out not to exist. My help: Legal, immediately, and financial management (FM) on the continuity gap. The rule: an option is a unilateral right because it was priced and evaluated at award — a 'TBD' CLIN was never an option, just an agreement to negotiate later. So there's nothing to exercise: continuing with the incumbent is a negotiation, and its competition posture has to be sorted with Legal before anything is signed. The COR's email binds nothing — but I correct that channel today in writing. Then continuity honestly: a justified bilateral extension or the extension-of-services clause buys months, the recompete starts now, and the award-time failure that let 'TBD' through gets documented so it never recurs.

scenarios.scenario: An option must be exercised by 15 September for a performance period starting 1 October. Financial management (FM) says the new fiscal year's funds obviously don't exist yet, and the program manager (PM) concludes 'so we legally can't exercise until October — the contractor will just have to gap two weeks.'
baits: The fiscal logic sounds airtight
A two-week gap normalized as inevitable
key_moves: The availability-of-funds mechanism exists for exactly this: exercise subject to availability, obligation upon funds
Missing the 15 September date kills the unilateral right — that's the real risk in the room
Coordinate the clause mechanics with FM now; no gap required

follow_ups.q: What does the funds-availability clause actually promise the contractor?
follow_ups.h: The clause promises obligation when funds arrive — what does it let you do before?
follow_ups.d: The availability-of-funds mechanism lets the Government exercise on time, subject to availability — the exercise preserves the unilateral right and the contractor's obligation to perform, while the Government's obligation attaches when funds become available. But it is fenced: RFO 32.703-2(a) lets the contracting officer initiate a contract action chargeable to new-fiscal-year funds before those funds are available only if the contract includes the clause at 52.232-18, Availability of Funds, and only for operation and maintenance and continuing services (e.g., rentals, utilities, and supply items not financed by stock funds) that are (1) necessary for normal operations and (2) for which Congress previously had consistently appropriated funds — unless specific statutory authority exists for other requirements. Confirm this option sits inside that fence before relying on the mechanism. And under 32.703-2(c) the Government will not accept supplies or services until the contracting officer has given the contractor notice, confirmed in writing, that funds are available. The notice says what it must: exercised subject to availability, obligation upon funds — and FM coordinates the funding document the moment the appropriation lands.

follow_ups.q: What if funds never materialize?
follow_ups.h: If the appropriation never comes, what protects each party?
follow_ups.d: If funds never materialize, the Government isn't obligated — that's the clause's core protection; no Anti-Deficiency exposure, and the contractor was on notice from the exercise language. The contractor's protection is honesty and speed: prompt notice if availability fails, so it isn't holding capacity for a ghost. The Government then faces the real consequences — no option year, a continuity gap, possibly a termination for convenience (T4C) of the exercised period — which is why availability exercises ride actual appropriation expectations, not hope.

coach.qtype: an options question — RFO Part 17: the exercise gates, applied to today.
coach.smes: Financial management (FM) for funds, the contracting officer's representative (COR) and program manager (PM) on performance and continuing need, and Legal if the notice window slipped.
coach.rule: Exercise only through the RFO 17.204-1(b) gates: timely written notice, funds available, an existing requirement, synopsized or exempt, no active SAM exclusion, acceptable performance, a fair and reasonable price in the Government's best interest, and part 6 compliance — and for DoD, R-DFARS 217.204-170 adds an active and accurate SAM record plus SPRS verification of the NIST SP 800-171 score and a current CMMC certificate. Miss the notice window and the unilateral right lapses into a bilateral negotiation.

scenarios.ask: Exercise is due 15 September; the money arrives 1 October. Is the PM right that you're stuck?
scenarios.script: This is an RFO Part 17 options question at the fiscal seam — and the PM has it backwards. My help: FM on the funding mechanics and Legal on the notice language. The rule: missing the 15 September date kills the unilateral right — after that, continuation is a bilateral negotiation where the contractor holds the leverage. The seam is what the availability-of-funds mechanism exists for — inside its limits: RFO 32.703-2(a) allows it only for operation and maintenance and continuing services necessary for normal operations and for which Congress previously had consistently appropriated funds, and only with the clause at 52.232-18 in the contract. So the first question is whether this option is that kind of work; if it is, exercise on time, expressly subject to availability, with the obligation attaching when the new year's money arrives — and we accept nothing until I give written notice that funds are available (32.703-2(c)). So: run the gates, issue the notice by the 15th with the availability language, and have FM ready to obligate on 1 October. Waiting for the money to feel real is how the Government converts its own right into the contractor's negotiation.

scenarios.scenario: An outfit wants to send $3.2M to another agency's 'rapid-tech marketplace' office, which promises award in 30 days through 'pre-competed innovation vehicles.' The one-page flyer doesn't identify the underlying contracts, the fee is 6%, and the program manager (PM) says 'everyone at the symposium uses them.'
baits: Speed and social proof
'Pre-competed' as a magic word
key_moves: Identify the actual vehicles and authority before a dollar moves — 'marketplace' is marketing, not analysis

Over SAT to a non-DoD shop → RFO 17.603(a) compliance certification from the nondefense agency head, then the R-DFARS 217.670 review: best interest of DoD (requirements, schedule, cost effectiveness including fees, contract administration), scope, funding
Assisted acquisition needs the signed interagency agreement; our fiscal rules travel with the money

follow_ups.q: What makes the 6% fee acceptable or not?
follow_ups.h: A fee buys services — which ones, at what value?
follow_ups.d: The fee question is answered inside the R-DFARS 217.670(a)(3) factor — cost effectiveness taking into account discounts and fees, following the total-fee procedures at PGI 217.670(a)(3) — and if the order rides the Economy Act rather than a more specific authority, RFO 17.502-2(c)(4) is a hard cap: the servicing agency must not charge, and we must not pay, any fee exceeding the actual (or estimated) cost of entering into and administering the contract. So: what does 6% buy — real acquisition expertise, vehicle access, administration — and is that value reasonable against alternatives, including buying it ourselves? A fee isn't inherently improper; an unexamined fee is. If the marketplace's value is speed we could achieve in-house, the fee fails the best-interest-of-DoD analysis; if it's genuine capability we lack on a real timeline, it can pass — documented, not assumed.

follow_ups.q: Direct vs. assisted here — which is this?
follow_ups.h: Who awards the eventual contract decides which lane you're in.
follow_ups.d: This is assisted acquisition: the marketplace office would award and administer on our behalf — which triggers the RFO 17.502-1(a)(1) written interagency agreement — signed by both the servicing and the requesting agency before the solicitation issues, covering acquisition-planning roles, contract execution, and administration and management — plus our unique terms passed to them (or written notice there are none), and, over the SAT, the RFO 17.603(a) nondefense-agency compliance certification and my component's R-DFARS 217.670 review and approval. If the order rides the Economy Act rather than a more specific authority, add the RFO 17.502-2(b) determination and findings (D&F) — best interest of the Government, and the supplies or services cannot be obtained as conveniently or cheaply by contracting directly with a private source — approved by a contracting officer (CO) of ours with authority to buy this, and sent to the servicing agency with the order request. Direct acquisition would be our CO placing orders on their vehicles ourselves — no agreement required, but then their office isn't doing the work. The flyer's vagueness about who actually awards is itself the first question to resolve.

coach.qtype: an interagency question — RFO Part 17 interagency acquisition and the Economy Act (31 U.S.C. 1535): direct vs. assisted, and whose rules travel with the money.
coach.smes: Financial management (FM) (the fiscal rules travel with the funds), Legal, and the servicing agency's contracting office.
coach.rule: Pick the lane deliberately: direct (our contracting officer (CO) orders on their vehicle) vs. assisted (their CO buys for us under a signed agreement). The Economy Act applies only absent a more specific authority — military interdepartmental purchase request (MIPR) plus determination and findings (D&F).

scenarios.ask: $3.2M to a 'rapid-tech marketplace' promising 30-day awards. What has to be true before that military interdepartmental purchase request (MIPR) moves?
scenarios.script: This is an interagency question — RFO Part 17 assisted acquisition — and a one-page flyer isn't an acquisition strategy. My help: financial management (FM), Legal, and the servicing office itself, on the record. Before a dollar moves: identify the actual underlying vehicles and their authority — 'marketplace' is marketing, and I can't verify scope, competition posture, or fee reasonableness against a brochure. Then the lane: they'd award for us, so it's assisted acquisition — written interagency agreement, signed, defining roles, before funds transfer. Over the simplified acquisition threshold (SAT) to a non-DoD shop, two real gates apply. RFO 17.603(a): a DoD acquisition official may ask a nondefense agency to conduct an acquisition on our behalf above the SAT only if the head of that agency has certified compliance with applicable procurement requirements for that fiscal year — unless waived under 17.603(e) — and the certifications are posted, so I check before the MIPR moves. Then R-DFARS 217.670: my component's review-and-approval procedures for orders over the SAT under non-DoD contracts, evaluating whether use of a non-DoD contract is in the best interest of DoD — satisfying customer requirements, schedule, cost effectiveness taking into account discounts and fees, and contract administration — plus scope of the contract to be used and funding within appropriation limitations. If the vehicles are real and the analysis holds, fine, we proceed with eyes open. If it's a flyer and a fee, we just bought ourselves a finding.

scenarios.scenario: Last September your office MIPRed $1.5M of operation and maintenance (O&M) to a servicing agency for a training-support task. It's now July; their contracting officer (CO) reports $410K will go unspent when the task ends next month, and their program office suggests 'rolling the remainder into a follow-on task so the funds don't go to waste.'
baits: 'Don't go to waste' — the eternal siren
The servicing agency's helpfulness
key_moves: Unobligated MIPR balances come home — they don't become the servicing agency's seed corn
The FY25 O&M is expiring; a new follow-on task is a new (current-year) need
Recover the funds, close the agreement cleanly, fund any follow-on properly

follow_ups.q: What happens to the recovered funds now?
follow_ups.h: Whose money is it once the task ends?
follow_ups.d: Unobligated MIPR balances return to the requesting agency — they don't become the servicing agency's working capital. And the returning funds keep their identity: FY25 O&M, now expiring or expired, available only for adjustments to the original obligations, not for new work. 'Rolling it forward' converts prior-year money into a new-year need — a Time violation dressed as efficiency. Recover the balance, report it to FM, and let the new need compete for current-year funds honestly.

follow_ups.q: Who tracks interagency balances — and how often should you?
follow_ups.h: This surprise was avoidable — what does routine interagency management look like?
follow_ups.d: The requesting agency tracks its own interagency balances: the agreement should require periodic financial reporting; the procuring contracting officer (PCO) or program office reconciles obligation and expenditure status quarterly at minimum (monthly near year-end), asks for burn-rate data, and triggers early recovery of excess. Discovering $410K in July for an August-ending task means nobody was watching for three quarters — the finding isn't the balance, it's the silence.

coach.qtype: an interagency question — RFO Part 17 interagency acquisition and the Economy Act (31 U.S.C. 1535): direct vs. assisted, and whose rules travel with the money.
coach.smes: Financial management (FM) (the fiscal rules travel with the funds), Legal, and the servicing agency's contracting office.
coach.rule: Pick the lane deliberately: direct (our contracting officer (CO) orders on their vehicle) vs. assisted (their CO buys for us under a signed agreement). The Economy Act applies only absent a more specific authority — military interdepartmental purchase request (MIPR) plus determination and findings (D&F).

scenarios.ask: $410K will go unspent, and the servicing agency suggests 'rolling it into' a new task. Your answer?
scenarios.script: This is an interagency-fiscal question — 31 U.S.C. 1535 machinery — and the money comes home. My help: financial management (FM) immediately, and the servicing agency's CO for the reconciliation. The rules: unobligated military interdepartmental purchase request (MIPR) balances return to us, and they return as what they are — FY25 O&M, expiring, good for adjustments to the original task and nothing new. A 'rolled' follow-on task is a new need, and new needs take current-year money; the suggestion fails Time no matter how efficient it sounds. So: recover the $410K now, reconcile the task's final costs, and if the follow-on is real, fund it properly and compete it properly. Then I'd fix the process — quarterly balance reconciliation in the agreement — because finding this in July means we weren't watching.

scenarios.scenario: A small business on a firm-fixed-price (FFP) production contract asks for progress payments, then mid-year requests the rate be raised 'to the max allowed' and asks whether the Government can also pay for a materials stockpile it wants to pre-buy against future orders that aren't on contract yet.
baits: Small-business sympathy
'Max allowed' framed as an entitlement
key_moves: Progress payments follow the clause rates; customary financing is fine — but payments attach to THIS contract's performance
Financing a stockpile for hoped-for future orders isn't contract financing — it's an advance against nothing
If cash flow is the real issue, performance-based payments or delivery scheduling may honestly help

follow_ups.q: Order of preference for financing methods?
follow_ups.h: Walk the ladder — where do progress payments sit and what outranks them?
follow_ups.d: RFO 32.106 sets five rungs, and the contracting officer (CO) must consider them in order unless an exception is in the Government's best interest in the specific case: (a) private financing without Government guarantee — though the CO must not require the contractor to obtain it at unreasonable terms or from other agencies; (b) customary contract financing other than loan guarantees and certain advance payments — where progress payments and performance-based payments live, approvable by the CO in the normal course; (c) loan guarantees; (d) unusual contract financing (32.114), which requires higher approval; and (e) advance payments last, the least preferred, most heavily approved. PBPs are preferred over cost-based progress payments where events can be defined. The rates themselves come from the clause and current class deviations — they're set, not negotiated upward on request.

follow_ups.q: What protects the Government in progress payments (title, liquidation)?
follow_ups.h: The Government pays early — what does it hold in exchange?
follow_ups.d: Two protections: title — under the progress-payments clause, title to work-in-process, materials, and inventory allocable to the contract vests in the Government as payments are made; and liquidation — progress payments are recovered by liquidation against delivery invoices, so the financing unwinds as performance completes. Both attach to THIS contract's performance, which is exactly why financing a stockpile for hoped-for FUTURE orders doesn't fit: no contract, no allocability, no title, no liquidation path.

coach.qtype: a fiscal-law question — Time, Purpose, Amount under the appropriations statutes, with RFO Part 32 carrying the financing side.
coach.smes: Financial management (FM)/Comptroller first and always, then Legal; the Government Accountability Office (GAO) Red Book and DoD FMR are the references.
coach.rule: Run T-P-A on every dollar: the right-year money for a bona fide need of that period, the appropriated purpose (31 U.S.C. 1301), within the available amount — Anti-Deficiency violations are the serious, reportable kind.
coach.cite: RFO Part 32 · GAO Red Book / DoD FMR · Vol. 2, Fiscal

scenarios.ask: Max progress-payment rates plus financing for a stockpile 'for future orders.' What do you approve?
scenarios.script: This is a contract-finance question — RFO Part 32 customary financing, at clause rates, for this contract's work. My help: financial management (FM), the Defense Contract Management Agency (DCMA) on the payment administration, and the clause itself. The rules: progress payments ride the clause and the current class deviation — as a DoD small business they already get the favorable rate; 'raise it to the max' isn't a negotiation, the rate is the rate. The stockpile ask fails differently: progress payments finance costs allocable to this contract, with title vesting and liquidation against deliveries. Materials for hoped-for future orders have no contract, no allocability, no title path — that's asking the Government to bank speculation. If cash flow is the real issue, performance-based payments on defined events are the preferred structure — and I'd offer to build exactly that.

scenarios.scenario: A contractor delivers the final technical data package for a missile-handling trailer — every drawing stamped with limited-rights legends, including drawings the Government watched them create under this fully Government-funded contract. 'Standard company template,' their data manager shrugs, offering to 'sort it out during sustainment.'
baits: 'Template' minimization
Deferral to sustainment (when leverage is gone)
key_moves: Government-funded development = unlimited rights; the legends are nonconforming markings — challenge/correct now, in writing
'Sort it later' means competing sustainment against markings you accepted silently
The assertion list from award is the yardstick — unasserted restrictions carry the contractor's burden

follow_ups.q: The marking-challenge sequence?
follow_ups.h: Challenge in writing, honor the markings meanwhile — walk the clock.
follow_ups.d: The sequence: written challenge notice stating the grounds; contractor has 60 days to respond with justification; unresolved, the contracting officer (CO) issues a final decision; contractor may appeal — 90 days to the agency board of contract appeals, 12 months to the Court of Federal Claims (RFO 33.205-6). Challenges run within six years after final payment or six years after delivery of the data or software, whichever is later, and there is no time limit at all where the data are publicly available without restriction, were provided to the United States without restriction, or the restriction was fraudulently asserted (R-DFARS 227.7103-13(d)(1)). Critical discipline: until appeals resolve, honor the markings — using challenged data as if unrestricted converts your challenge into their claim. The Government's leverage is the process, not self-help.

follow_ups.q: What if some drawings genuinely mixed in private-expense heritage?
follow_ups.h: Mixed heritage doesn't rescue a blanket stamp.
follow_ups.d: If some drawings genuinely mix private-expense heritage, rights resolve at the component level: the contractor identifies which elements derive from private development — with records proving it, since the burden of supporting restrictions is theirs — and those elements carry limited rights while Government-funded portions stay unlimited. The blanket stamp fails precisely because it asserts nothing specific: an assertion list with evidence, drawing by drawing, is what the challenge process forces into existence.

coach.qtype: a data-rights question — R-DFARS 227: the funding source drives the license.
coach.smes: Legal (IP counsel), the program engineers on the component map, and the Defense Contract Management Agency (DCMA) on assertion administration.
coach.rule: R-DFARS 227: who paid for development answers most of it — Government funds → unlimited, mixed → Government purpose rights (GPR), private → limited/restricted. The contractor proves the restriction — the assertion list comes from the provision at 252.227-7992, Identification and Assertion of Use, Release, or Disclosure Restrictions (DEVIATION 2026-O0036), inserted under R-DFARS 227.7103-6(g)(2); 252.227-7017 is the legacy pre-deviation provision. Honor the markings until a challenge resolves.

scenarios.ask: Every drawing arrived stamped limited-rights — including ones we watched them create on contract. What now?
scenarios.script: This is an R-DFARS 227 data-rights question — nonconforming markings on Government-funded work. My help: IP counsel in Legal and the Defense Contract Management Agency (DCMA) on assertions administration. The rule: development funded entirely by the Government yields unlimited rights, and legends don't rewrite funding history — but the remedy is process, not self-help. So: written challenge now, stating the grounds — this was Government-funded development under this contract; the contractor gets their 60 days to justify with records, because the burden of proving any restriction is theirs. Where genuine private-expense heritage exists at the component level, those pieces get their proper legends; everything else gets corrected. And until it resolves, we honor the markings — because sorting this at sustainment competition time means competing against our own paid-for drawings.

scenarios.scenario: A small firm's Small Business Innovation Research (SBIR) Phase II produced a promising power-management module. Years later, your program wants the design data to second-source production. The firm asserts SBIR data rights; your engineer argues 'the protection must be expired by now,' and the program manager (PM) suggests just reverse-engineering it from delivered units.
baits: 'Must be expired' — assumed, not verified
Reverse-engineering framed as a clean workaround
key_moves: SBIR protection runs long — verify the actual window from the contract and delivery dates before anyone acts
Reverse-engineering has its own legal limits and practical costs; it's a Legal conversation, not a shop decision
The durable fix is negotiating rights or a license priced against the second-source business case

follow_ups.q: What do SBIR rights protect during the period?
follow_ups.h: During the protection window, what can the Government do with SBIR data?
follow_ups.d: During the SBIR protection period, the Government holds SBIR rights — it can use the data for Government purposes within the Government, but cannot release it for competitive procurement or disclose it outside without the firm's permission. The window is long (20 years under current policy) and runs from defined trigger dates in the contract. It exists to let small firms commercialize without the Government handing their innovation to competitors — that's the program's bargain.

follow_ups.q: What happens to the rights when the window closes?
follow_ups.h: When the window closes, the default rights story resumes.
follow_ups.d: After the SBIR period ends, the Government's rights transition toward the ordinary framework — the protection lapses and the Government's license broadens per the clause. Verify the actual window and trigger dates from the contract and delivery records before planning anything. And the planning lesson: if second-sourcing was foreseeable, the time to negotiate specially-tailored rights or buy a license was when the Government had leverage — at Phase III award — not years later at the sustainment cliff.

coach.qtype: a data-rights question — R-DFARS 227: the funding source drives the license.
coach.smes: Legal (IP counsel), the program engineers on the component map, and the Defense Contract Management Agency (DCMA) on assertion administration.
coach.rule: R-DFARS 227: who paid for development answers most of it — Government funds → unlimited, mixed → Government purpose rights (GPR), private → limited/restricted. The contractor proves the restriction — the assertion list comes from the provision at 252.227-7992, Identification and Assertion of Use, Release, or Disclosure Restrictions (DEVIATION 2026-O0036), inserted under R-DFARS 227.7103-6(g)(2); 252.227-7017 is the legacy pre-deviation provision. Honor the markings until a challenge resolves.

scenarios.ask: SBIR rights on the module, and your engineer wants to 'just reverse-engineer it.' What's your counsel?
scenarios.script: This is a data-rights question — R-DFARS 227 SBIR rights, the long-protection species. My help: IP counsel and the contract file for the actual trigger dates. The rules: SBIR protection runs long — verify the real window from the contract before anyone acts on a guess — and during it, the Government can't release the data for competitive reprocurement without the firm's agreement. On reverse-engineering: it has its own legal limits and real costs, and 'engineering around' data we hold under restriction is litigation bait — that path gets sized honestly with counsel, not tossed off in a meeting. The constructive paths: negotiate a license or specially-tailored rights with the firm — they may sell what we can't take — or plan the second source for when the window actually closes. Leverage lives at award time; we spend what's left of it deliberately.

scenarios.scenario: A firm-fixed-price contract delivers training courseware in English. Partway through, the customer asks to add Spanish and Portuguese versions — roughly 40% more content-hours — and the contractor cheerfully offers a 'no-cost mod' in exchange for a 10-month period extension and relief from two quality metrics.
baits: 'No-cost' hides the real price (time + quality relief)
Contractor cheerfulness
key_moves: Nothing about this is no-cost — schedule and metric relief ARE consideration; price the exchange honestly
New-language versions at +40% effort: run the four-corner scope test; this may be out-of-scope new work
If out of scope: competition or a justified exception — a mod can't carry it

follow_ups.q: What counts as consideration in a mod?
follow_ups.h: Consideration isn't only money — price what the Government is giving up.
follow_ups.d: Consideration is anything of value exchanged: schedule extensions, relaxed performance metrics, waived remedies — all are Government givings with real value. A 'no-cost' mod that trades 40% more work for schedule and metric relief is a priced exchange with the price hidden. Papering it honestly means valuing both sides: what the added work is worth, what the relief costs the Government, and whether the exchange is fair — documented, so the file shows a bargain, not a favor swap.

follow_ups.q: How does the anticipation test apply to added languages?
follow_ups.h: Would the original competitors have bid differently on a three-language contract?
follow_ups.d: The anticipation test asks what the original competition reasonably contemplated. A courseware contract competed in English, growing 40% in content-hours to add two languages, is at least at the scope boundary: translation and localization could change who would have bid and how they'd have priced. Run the four corners — competition anticipation, type, period, cumulative cost — and if the honest answer is 'this is new work,' it competes or rides a justification. The contractor's cheerfulness doesn't move the scope line.

coach.qtype: a scope question — RFO Part 43: a modification, or a new procurement in disguise.
coach.smes: Legal, the procuring contracting officer (PCO) chain, and the original competition record itself.
coach.rule: The test is what the original competitors reasonably anticipated — judged against the original contract with all mods cumulative. In scope: modify under RFO Part 43. Beyond it: compete it or justify it under RFO Part 6.

scenarios.ask: Forty percent more content for 'no cost' — in exchange for schedule and metric relief. How do you paper this?
scenarios.script: This is a modifications question — RFO Part 43: scope first, then honest consideration. My help: Legal on the scope analysis and my pricing office on valuing the exchange. Two rules: nothing here is 'no cost' — schedule relief and relaxed metrics ARE consideration, and the exchange gets priced and papered as the bargain it is. And scope: 40% more content-hours adding two languages gets the four-corner test against the original competition — would the field have bid differently on a trilingual contract? If it's in scope, we negotiate a bilateral mod that values both sides honestly. If it's beyond, it's new work: competed or justified, not absorbed. Cheerful offers deserve the same analysis as hostile ones — sometimes more.

scenarios.scenario: During a base network upgrade, the Government's fiber-conduit maps prove wrong in six buildings — the contractor reroutes on the fly at the contracting officer's representative's (COR) verbal 'keep moving, we'll square up.' Four months later a consolidated $340K request for equitable adjustment (REA) arrives. The program manager (PM) objects: 'they never got a mod authorizing any of that.'
baits: 'No mod = no entitlement' — exactly backwards here
The consolidated lump obscures per-building facts
key_moves: Government-caused changes (bad maps + directed continuation) are constructive changes — the missing mod is the Government's paperwork failure, not the contractor's entitlement bar
Evaluate entitlement building-by-building, then quantum with technical support
Settle bilaterally with a release; and fix the direction channel

follow_ups.q: REA vs. claim consequences if this stalls?
follow_ups.h: If this stalls unresolved, which lane's consequences attach?
follow_ups.d: Today this is an REA, so none of the CDA machinery is running: no interest, no decision clock, no appeal rights. It gets worked as a negotiated bilateral supplemental agreement (RFO 43.203(a)(1)) closed with the 43.304(c) release. If the contractor converts it, they must certify the claim under FAR subpart 33.2 — R-DFARS 243.371(c) is explicit that this is a different certification from the 10 U.S.C. 3862(a) REA certification in clause 252.243-7002 — and only then does the machinery run: interest from the CO's receipt of the claim (RFO 33.205-3(a)(1)), a written final decision on the RFO 33.205-6(c) clock or a deemed denial under 33.205-6(g), and appeal rights — Board in 90 days, the U.S. Court of Federal Claims (COFC) in 12 months. Once converted, delay costs the Government interest and initiative — which is why working entitlement promptly beats hoping it goes away.

follow_ups.q: Who had authority to say 'keep moving' — and what does that change?
follow_ups.h: Authority analysis changes the theory, not the entitlement.
follow_ups.d: The COR lacked authority to direct changes — but Government conduct is bigger than one email: defective Government-furnished maps plus continued direction to perform is a constructive-change theory that doesn't depend on the COR's warrant. The authority failure changes the Government's internal story (channel discipline broke) more than the contractor's entitlement. What the COR's role does affect: your prevention plan — direction flows through the CO, and that gets fixed in writing regardless of how the claim resolves.

coach.qtype: a scope question — RFO Part 43: a modification, or a new procurement in disguise.
coach.smes: Legal, the procuring contracting officer (PCO) chain, and the original competition record itself.
coach.rule: The test is what the original competitors reasonably anticipated — judged against the original contract with all mods cumulative. In scope: modify under RFO Part 43. Beyond it: compete it or justify it under RFO Part 6.

scenarios.ask: Bad Government maps, a COR's 'keep moving,' and a $340K consolidated REA. How do you work it?
scenarios.script: This is a disputes question — the Contract Disputes Act — built on our own paperwork failure. My help: Legal early, the COR's records, and the Defense Contract Management Agency (DCMA) if the quantum needs support. The frame: defective Government maps plus 'keep moving' direction is a constructive-change case — the missing mods are the Government's failure, not the contractor's entitlement bar. And it is an REA, not a claim: no Contract Disputes Act interest, no decision clock, no appeal rights — RFO 33.205-3(a)(1) starts interest when the CO receives the claim, and no claim has been submitted. So my output is a negotiated bilateral modification under RFO 43.203(a)(1), papered with a 43.304(c) release. I run the R-DFARS 243.371(b) arithmetic — absolute values of every increase and decrease — before concluding a $340K request sits under the $350,000 simplified acquisition threshold (SAT) and doesn't need the 252.243-7002 certification; and 243.371(c) is the trap: the 10 U.S.C. 3862(a) REA certification is a different certification from the 41 U.S.C. 7103 disputes certification, so if they convert, they must certify under FAR subpart 33.2 and the CDA clocks start then. So: entitlement element by element — the reroutes trace to the bad maps; quantum gets a real technical and cost review rather than resentment; and I'd negotiate hard toward a global settlement with a release. Then the internal fix: direction flows through the CO, in writing, and the mapping failure gets reported where it can't recur. The contractor did the work; the Government does the honest math.

scenarios.scenario: Closing out a five-year research and development (R&D) contract, the property report lists 212 Government-furnished items; the contractor can locate 168. Of the missing 44, they say 30 were 'consumed in testing years ago' (no records), 9 are 'probably at the subcontractor,' and 5 are simply unknown. They propose closing out now and 'reconciling later.'
baits: 'Consumed in testing' as an unverifiable catch-all
Closeout momentum
key_moves: No closeout with an open property reconciliation — the leverage ends at closeout
Loss/damage/destruction process per the clause: investigation, liability determination under the risk allocation, records
Subcontractor-held property is still the prime's accountability

follow_ups.q: Who adjudicates property loss — and on what standard?
follow_ups.h: The clause has a process and a standard — who runs it and against what?
follow_ups.d: Property loss runs through the clause machinery: the contractor reports and investigates each loss; the property administrator manages the process; and the contracting officer (CO) determines liability under the contract's risk allocation — on a cost-type contract the contractor typically bears loss only where its managers were at fault or the property system failed. 'Consumed in testing, no records' isn't an outcome — it's an unproven claim the investigation either substantiates or converts into liability.

follow_ups.q: What does the contractor's property-management-system status change?
follow_ups.h: The property system's approval status shifts the burden.
follow_ups.d: An approved property management system creates confidence records exist and losses were managed — individual determinations proceed against a working system. A disapproved or deficient system flips the posture: systemic recordkeeping failure is itself contractor fault, supporting broader liability and corrective demands. Forty-four unaccounted items out of 212 suggests the system, not just the items, needs the look — and DCMA's property specialists are the ones to give it.

coach.qtype: a Government-property question — RFO Part 45: the default rule and the four-part exception.
coach.smes: the property administrator, the Defense Contract Management Agency (DCMA), and the program manager (PM) — who owes the written justification.
coach.rule: RFO Part 45: contractors furnish property. Government-furnished property (GFP) only when all four parts hold — best interest, benefit over burden, no substantial risk shift, not otherwise satisfiable — and furnishing it puts the Government's own performance on the schedule.

scenarios.ask: 212 items furnished, 168 found, and the contractor wants closeout. What happens first?
scenarios.script: This is an RFO Part 45 Government-property question at the worst possible moment — closeout, where the leverage ends. My help: the property administrator, the Defense Contract Management Agency's (DCMA) property specialists, and Legal on liability. The rule: no closeout with an open property reconciliation. Each of the 44 missing items runs the clause machinery — report, investigate, liability determination under the contract's risk allocation. 'Consumed in testing, no records' gets tested against the property system's records, and if the system itself failed, that failure is contractor fault with broader consequences. Closeout happens when the record is reconciled and liabilities are resolved — not when the contractor is tired of the contract.

scenarios.scenario: To help a struggling firm-fixed-price (FFP) contractor meet schedule, the program manager (PM) wants to lend them a Government CNC machine 'for a few months, informally — putting it on contract takes too long and they only need it for one part run.'
baits: Informality justified by brevity
Helping-the-schedule urgency
key_moves: No informal property loans — on contract with the property clause set or not at all
Furnishing property to an FFP contractor shifts risk and may found an REA if it's late or faulty — price/paper the arrangement deliberately
The four-part GFP justification still applies, brief or not

follow_ups.q: What happens if the informal machine breaks mid-run?
follow_ups.h: Mid-run failure with no clause set — trace where every cost lands.
follow_ups.d: If the informal machine breaks mid-run: no property clause allocates the loss, so the Government and contractor litigate ownership of the damage from a paperwork vacuum; the contractor claims Government-caused delay on the FFP schedule (the machine was the Government's, informally provided); the part run stops; and nobody's insurance clearly answers. The 'few months informal' loan becomes a request for equitable adjustment (REA), a property dispute, and a schedule slip — all purchasable for the price of one modification.

follow_ups.q: How does Government-furnished property (GFP) alter FFP's risk story?
follow_ups.h: GFP hands the Government a role in an FFP story it wasn't supposed to have.
follow_ups.d: FFP's clean allocation — contractor bears cost risk, Government pays the price — assumes the contractor controls its means of production. Furnish property and the Government joins the performance path: late, faulty, or broken GFP is Government-caused delay and REA exposure, and the four-part justification plus clause set exists to make that trade deliberate. Helping a struggling FFP contractor with Government property can be right — but it's a priced, papered decision, because it moves risk back to the Government that FFP had transferred away.

coach.qtype: a Government-property question — RFO Part 45: the default rule and the four-part exception.
coach.smes: the property administrator, the Defense Contract Management Agency (DCMA), and the program manager (PM) — who owes the written justification.
coach.rule: RFO Part 45: contractors furnish property. Government-furnished property (GFP) only when all four parts hold — best interest, benefit over burden, no substantial risk shift, not otherwise satisfiable — and furnishing it puts the Government's own performance on the schedule.

scenarios.ask: An informal loan of a Government CNC machine 'for a few months.' What do you tell the PM?
scenarios.script: This is an RFO Part 45 Government-property question — and 'informal' is the problem, not the timeline. My help: the property administrator and the PM, who owes the justification if we do this at all. The rule: no informal property loans, ever — on contract with the full clause set, or not at all. If lending the CNC machine is genuinely in the Government's interest, the PM documents the four findings, the machine goes on contract with marking, condition baselined, and the property clauses allocating risk. And I'd tell the PM what the shortcut actually costs: furnishing property to an FFP contractor moves schedule risk back to us — if that machine breaks mid-run with no clause set, we own a dispute, a delay claim, and a stopped part run simultaneously. The mod takes days. The vacuum takes a year.

scenarios.scenario: An undefinitized contract action (UCA) for aircraft battle-damage repair was issued at a $30M not-to-exceed (NTE). The qualifying proposal arrives at $41M with a letter explaining 'actual damage exceeded initial survey.' The contractor requests the NTE be raised to match 'so definitization can proceed on real numbers.'
baits: 'Real numbers' framing makes the raise sound like accuracy
Definitization urgency used as leverage
key_moves: The NTE is the Government's liability ceiling — it doesn't float up to meet proposals
Is the extra damage in-scope growth (negotiate within/adjust deliberately with approvals) or new work (new action, new approvals)?
Definitize what was ordered; obligations stay inside the caps meanwhile

follow_ups.q: What approvals would an NTE increase require?
follow_ups.h: An NTE increase is a deliberate Government decision with a chain — whose?
follow_ups.d: Raising a UCA's NTE isn't a negotiating concession — it's a formal Government decision requiring the head of the contracting activity's (HCA) approval. R-DFARS 217.7404-1 makes that flat: the contracting officer (CO) obtains approval from the HCA before entering into a UCA and, at (c), before modifying the scope of a UCA when performance has already begun — no dollar tiering, no delegate named below the HCA. And it rests on a documented scope analysis: is the 'extra damage' in-scope growth of this repair or new work needing its own action and justification? Funds must exist for any increase, and the definitization schedule presses on regardless. The contractor's proposal doesn't move the ceiling; the Government's deliberate process might.

follow_ups.q: How do the 50/75% caps apply during this fight?
follow_ups.h: The caps ride the NTE — run the arithmetic through the fight.
follow_ups.d: The obligation caps key to the NTE: R-DFARS 217.7404-4(a) bars obligating more than 50 percent of the NTE before definitization, and the 75 percent step is conditional, not automatic — it is available only if the contractor submitted a qualifying proposal before 50 percent of the NTE had been obligated, and even then the limitation "may be increased to no more than 75 percent," which is discretion I exercise, not an entitlement they earn by proposing. On a $30M NTE that's $15M, and $22.5M only if the condition is met and I decide to go there — and neither number floats with the contractor's $41M. If actual in-scope work genuinely exceeds the NTE, the Government's deliberate increase would move the caps with it; until then, obligations stay inside the existing arithmetic, which is precisely the leverage that makes the contractor negotiate rather than perform indefinitely on an open tab.

coach.qtype: an undefinitized contract action (UCA) question — R-DFARS 217.74: undefinitized work and decaying negotiation leverage.
coach.smes: your pricing office, the clearance authority, and Legal; the Defense Contract Management Agency (DCMA) for actuals once performance starts.
coach.rule: R-DFARS 217.74 makes UCAs the exception: obligations capped at 50% of the not-to-exceed price, raised to no more than 75% only if the qualifying proposal arrives before that 50% point (217.7404-4(a)); definitization by the earlier of 180 days after the qualifying proposal or the date obligations pass 50% of the NTE (217.7404-3(a)); clearance at definitization — and neither poor planning nor administrative convenience ever justifies one.

scenarios.ask: The proposal came in at $41M against a $30M NTE, and the contractor wants the ceiling raised. What's your negotiating position?
scenarios.script: This is a UCA question — R-DFARS 217.74: the NTE is the Government's liability ceiling, and it doesn't float. My help: my pricing office on the actuals, the UCA approval authority, and Legal on scope. The position: the qualifying proposal starts definitization; it doesn't reprice the ceiling. First, scope: is the 'extra damage' growth of this repair — negotiable within a deliberately, formally increased NTE if the evidence supports it — or new work needing its own action? Second, the caps hold against the existing NTE: 50 percent under R-DFARS 217.7404-4(a), and the 75 percent step only if their qualifying proposal arrived before 50 percent had been obligated — and even then it "may be increased," which is my discretion, not their entitlement. Either way the arithmetic runs on thirty million, not forty-one. Third, the actuals cut our way on fee — months of incurred cost mean burned-down risk, and weighted guidelines will show it. We definitize on evidence, on schedule, at a ceiling the Government chooses deliberately — not one proposed to us.

scenarios.scenario: Definitizing a 9-month-old undefinitized contract action (UCA), the contractor proposes forward rates for the remaining work but resists providing actual incurred costs for the months already performed — 'the certified proposal covers everything going forward, and actuals would just confuse the comparison.'
baits: 'Certified forward proposal' sounds complete
'Confuse the comparison' — the confusion is the point
key_moves: Work performed has actuals — they're exactly what definitization pricing must use for the performed portion
Certified data spans the action; incurred costs are cost or pricing data
Fee reflects the burned-down risk in weighted guidelines — actuals are how you see it

follow_ups.q: Why does fee typically drop at definitization?
follow_ups.h: Definitization prices two different time zones — which one has facts instead of estimates?
follow_ups.d: Fee drops at definitization because weighted guidelines price RISK, and months of performance burned much of it down: the cost uncertainty the fee would have compensated has partly become known actuals. Pricing the performed portion on estimates when facts exist would pay risk premium for risk already retired. The forward work keeps its honest risk pricing; the performed work gets priced on what happened — that split is the intellectual core of definitizing a mature UCA.

follow_ups.q: What audit support fits here?
follow_ups.h: Match the audit tool to the dollars and the dispute.
follow_ups.d: For incurred-cost visibility on a UCA definitization: DCMA field pricing support for rates and forward-pricing positions, DCAA for incurred-cost and proposal audits at the dollar thresholds — and the contractor's resistance itself is a flag worth an auditor's attention. The ask is targeted: actuals for the performed months, current rate agreements, and reconciliation of the proposal's forward estimates against the performance record to date. No visibility, no agreement — and the caps hold while they decide.

coach.qtype: an undefinitized contract action (UCA) question — R-DFARS 217.74: undefinitized work and decaying negotiation leverage.
coach.smes: your pricing office, the clearance authority, and Legal; the Defense Contract Management Agency (DCMA) for actuals once performance starts.
coach.rule: R-DFARS 217.74 makes UCAs the exception: obligations capped at 50% of the not-to-exceed price, raised to no more than 75% only if the qualifying proposal arrives before that 50% point (217.7404-4(a)); definitization by the earlier of 180 days after the qualifying proposal or the date obligations pass 50% of the NTE (217.7404-3(a)); clearance at definitization — and neither poor planning nor administrative convenience ever justifies one.

scenarios.ask: The contractor resists providing incurred costs — 'the certified proposal covers everything going forward.' What do you require?
scenarios.script: This is a UCA-pricing question — R-DFARS 217.74 meeting RFO 15.403: actuals versus estimates. My help: the Defense Contract Management Agency (DCMA) on rates, the Defense Contract Audit Agency (DCAA) if the audit thresholds or the resistance warrant, my pricing office throughout. The rule: certified cost or pricing data spans the whole action, and incurred costs for nine months of performed work ARE cost or pricing data — 'the proposal covers going forward' is a scope argument against their own certificate. So I require the actuals: the performed portion gets priced on facts, the remaining work on honestly-priced estimates, and fee follows the risk actually remaining — which the actuals will show has burned down. If they won't open the books, the caps hold, the definitization clock presses, and no agreement happens on estimates where facts exist. That's not hardball; that's what definitization means.

scenarios.scenario: Your negotiation team reaches a handshake deal Friday on a $60M sole-source action — inside the objective. The contractor's CEO emails Monday asking to 'paper it this week before our quarter closes.' Clearance is scheduled in twelve days. The program manager (PM) asks if you can sign now and 'ratify through clearance after.'
baits: Deal inside the objective feels pre-blessed
CEO/quarter pressure
key_moves: No award before contract clearance — the review is the approval, not a receipt
'Ratify after' inverts the design: independent eyes before commitment
Ask the clearance shop to accelerate on merits; that's the lawful fast path

follow_ups.q: What does the clearance authority review in the PNM?
follow_ups.h: The PNM is the reviewer's window — what story must it tell?
follow_ups.d: The clearance authority reads the PNM for the whole negotiation: objectives versus outcome and why they moved, the facts behind each significant position change, price analysis supporting fair-and-reasonable, profit basis, data relied on, and compliance. A handshake inside the objective still needs the story told — 'we did well' isn't documentation. The PNM is finished and honest BEFORE clearance, because the review is of the record, not the vibe.

follow_ups.q: What if clearance directs a position change after your handshake?
follow_ups.h: A directed change after handshake tests your professionalism, not your loyalty.
follow_ups.d: If clearance directs a position change, the handshake yields — the deal was always subject to approval, and the negotiation reopens on the directed point with the contractor told honestly that final Government approval required it. This is why you never let a contractor believe a handshake is an award: manage that expectation up front ('agreement subject to clearance'), and the CEO's quarter-close pressure becomes his planning problem, not your integrity problem.

coach.qtype: a clearance question — the Department of the Air Force (DAF) clearance procedures: independent review before the Government commits.
coach.smes: the clearance authority itself, your chief, and Legal on any compliance flags.
coach.rule: Two gates catching two failures: business clearance blesses the strategy before release; contract clearance blesses the negotiated result before award. The selector never approves the selection.

scenarios.ask: Handshake Friday, CEO wants it papered this week, clearance is 12 days out. What do you tell everyone?
scenarios.script: This is a clearance question — the Department of the Air Force (DAF) clearance procedures: independent review before commitment, and a calendar can't override it. My help: the clearance authority's shop, my chief, and a finished price negotiation memorandum (PNM). The rule: no award before contract clearance — the review is the approval, not a receipt stamp. And a handshake was always 'agreement subject to Government approval'; I'd confirm the contractor understood that Friday. What I can do honestly: ask the clearance shop to accommodate an earlier review if the file is truly ready — the PNM telling the full story, inside-objective or not. What I won't do is invert the design and paper first, ratify later. The CEO's quarter is real; so is the reason an independent set of eyes comes before the Government commits sixty million dollars.

scenarios.scenario: Day 40 of a the Government Accountability Office (GAO) protest on your IT award, agency counsel concludes the evaluation record has a genuine defect — one factor was scored against an unstated standard. GAO's decision is 60 days away; the program manager (PM) wants to 'ride it out since we might still win.'
baits: 'Might still win' gambling with a known defect
Sunk-cost momentum
key_moves: Voluntary corrective action on a real defect beats a sustain: faster, cheaper, and you control the remedy scope
Riding out a known defect risks paying protester's costs on top of losing
Define the correction precisely (re-evaluate the factor, revised SSDD) — not a panicked full redo

follow_ups.q: What corrective actions are available?
follow_ups.h: Corrective action is the Government prescribing its own remedy — what's on the menu?
follow_ups.d: The menu scales to the defect: reopen the evaluation and re-score against stated criteria; amend the solicitation and take revised proposals if the criteria themselves were defective; reopen discussions if they were flawed; terminate the award and re-award if the outcome changed. The Government chooses the narrowest action that genuinely cures the defect — controlled, scoped, and documented — versus a sustain where GAO recommends and the agency implements under a deadline anyway.

follow_ups.q: How does GAO treat corrective action taken mid-protest?
follow_ups.h: GAO's response to mid-protest correction is the system working.
follow_ups.d: When the agency takes corrective action addressing the protest's core, GAO typically dismisses the protest as academic — the remedy is happening without a decision. Timing matters for costs: correcting promptly after the defect became clear avoids reimbursing protest costs; riding a known defect to a sustain invites paying the protester's costs and attorney fees on top of the same corrective action. Early, honest correction is both cheaper and faster — and it keeps the remedy in the agency's hands.

coach.qtype: a protest question — RFO Part 33 and the Competition in Contracting Act (CICA): venue, stay math, and the record you built months earlier.
coach.smes: Legal drives; the Government Accountability Office (GAO) or the U.S. Court of Federal Claims (COFC) counsel through Legal; the head of the contracting activity (HCA) owns any override decision.
coach.rule: Know the stay machinery cold — RFO 33.105-3(b)(1) is the government-wide 10-day/5-day rule, but for DoD R-DFARS 233.105-370 substitutes a four-part whichever-is-later test in its place, and there are three venues with different powers — and remember the real defense was built earlier: criteria stated, followed, and documented.
coach.cite: RFO 33.104 · RFO 33.105 · R-DFARS 233.105-370 · CICA · Vol. 2, Protests

scenarios.ask: Day 40, real defect found, decision 60 days away. Ride it out or act — and how?
scenarios.script: This is an RFO Part 33 protest question where our own record failed. My help: agency counsel — who found it — plus the source selection authority (SSA) and the evaluation team for the fix. The math: riding out a known defect for 60 more days buys a probable sustain, GAO-directed remedy on GAO's terms, protest costs on top, and a program 60 days later than honest correction would put it. So: voluntary corrective action now — scoped to the actual defect. One factor was scored against an unstated standard, so we reopen that evaluation and re-score against the stated criteria, amending only if the criteria themselves were the problem. GAO dismisses as academic, we control the remedy, and the program moves. The PM's 'we might win' is hope arguing with a record — and the record already told us who wins.

scenarios.scenario: A holder on your MA-indefinite-delivery/indefinite-quantity (IDIQ) emails a formal-looking 'protest' of a $4M task order award (DoD), citing unfair evaluation. It's below the Government Accountability Office (GAO) order-protest threshold and doesn't allege scope growth. The contractor CCs your senior contracting official (SCO) and threatens 'escalation to GAO and the Court' within five days.
baits: Formal formatting and CC-intimidation
The five-day ultimatum
key_moves: Under $35M with no scope allegation: GAO lacks jurisdiction — the lane is the task-order ombudsman
Treat it seriously anyway: review the order file, respond through the ombudsman process
No stay attaches; performance continues while the complaint is worked

follow_ups.q: What DOES get an order to GAO?
follow_ups.h: Two doors to GAO for orders — dollars, or growth.
follow_ups.d: A task or delivery order reaches GAO two ways: value over the threshold ($35M DoD / $10M civilian), or an allegation that the order exceeds the scope, period, or maximum value of the underlying contract — the growth theory, protestable at any dollar value because it alleges work escaped the vehicle's competed boundaries. This complaint alleges neither growth nor crosses the threshold, so GAO's door is closed — which makes the ombudsman the lane, not a loophole.

follow_ups.q: What does the ombudsman actually do?
follow_ups.h: The ombudsman is review, not decoration.
follow_ups.d: The task-order ombudsman — senior, independent of the procuring contracting officer (PCO) — reviews complaints that holders weren't afforded fair opportunity: examines the order file, the evaluation, and the consideration record, and can recommend corrective action to the contracting activity. It's the deliberate substitute Congress built for order-level GAO protests. Engage it seriously: a real review with a documented response either fixes an actual fairness failure or creates the record that ends the complaint.

coach.qtype: a protest question — RFO Part 33 and the Competition in Contracting Act (CICA): venue, stay math, and the record you built months earlier.
coach.smes: Legal drives; the Government Accountability Office (GAO) or the U.S. Court of Federal Claims (COFC) counsel through Legal; the head of the contracting activity (HCA) owns any override decision.
coach.rule: Know the stay machinery cold — RFO 33.105-3(b)(1) is the government-wide 10-day/5-day rule, but for DoD R-DFARS 233.105-370 substitutes a four-part whichever-is-later test in its place, and there are three venues with different powers — and remember the real defense was built earlier: criteria stated, followed, and documented.
coach.cite: RFO 33.104 · RFO 33.105 · R-DFARS 233.105-370 · CICA · Vol. 2, Protests

scenarios.ask: A $4M order 'protest' lands, below GAO's threshold, CC'd to your SCO. How do you handle it?
scenarios.script: This is a protest-jurisdiction question — the RFO 16.508 order-protest rules — and the answer is a lane, not a shrug. My help: Legal, the vehicle's ombudsman, and my own order file. The rule: under $35M with no scope-growth allegation, GAO lacks jurisdiction over a DoD task-order complaint — the lane Congress built is the task-order ombudsman. So I'd respond in writing, correctly and respectfully: naming the right lane, committing to a genuine ombudsman review, and meaning it — the order file, the evaluation, the consideration record all get an honest look, because if fair opportunity actually failed, I want to fix it before the ombudsman tells me to. The SCO on copy gets a heads-up from me first with the facts. Jurisdiction answers the venue question; it doesn't answer the fairness question — I owe both.

scenarios.scenario: A contractor's $85K request for equitable adjustment (REA) for Government-caused test-range delays has sat in your predecessor's inbox for seven months unanswered. The contractor's new letter converts it to a certified claim 'for $85K plus interest from the original submission' and demands a final decision in 60 days.
baits: Interest 'from the original submission' — check the actual trigger
Seven months of silence feels indefensible (it is, but it's not entitlement)
key_moves: Interest runs from receipt of the certified CLAIM, not the earlier REA — correct the math while owning the delay
Under $100K certification isn't required, but as submitted the decision clock is real: decide or settle within the window
