sat.a: Generally conclusive — except for latent defects, fraud, gross mistakes amounting to fraud, or as otherwise provided in the contract.
sat.x: Conclusive is the default; the exceptions — latent defects, fraud, gross mistakes amounting to fraud, contract carve-outs — are the whole exam. Note what's not on the list: a patent defect you simply failed to catch. Acceptance closes the door on everything a reasonable inspection would have found.
d: Yes — acceptance is absolutely final in every case.
No — the Government may revoke acceptance for any defect found within one year.
It becomes final only when the warranty period expires.

cite.quote: Acceptance shall be conclusive, except for latent defects, fraud, gross mistakes amounting to fraud, or as otherwise provided in the contract.

sat.q: What inspection does the Government normally perform for contracts at or below the SAT?
sat.a: Inspection at destination, and only for type and kind; quantity; damage; operability (if readily determinable); and preservation, packaging, packing, and marking. DoD reinforces it from the other side: do not require quality assurance at source at or below the SAT unless the 246.402 criteria are met.
sat.x: Below the SAT the inspection is deliberately shallow: at destination, five checks — type and kind, quantity, damage, operability if readily determinable, packaging and marking. DoD guards the other flank: no quality assurance at source at or below the SAT unless 246.402's criteria are met. Demanding source inspection on a simple buy is gold-plating.

cite.quote: the Government must inspect contracts at or below the simplified acquisition threshold at destination and only for type and kind; quantity; damage; operability (if readily determinable); and preservation, packaging, packing, and marking, if applicable.

dod.quote: Do not require Government contract quality assurance at source for contracts or delivery orders valued at or below the simplified acquisition threshold unless the criteria at 246.402 have been met.

sat.q: What is a claim?
sat.a: A written demand or written assertion by one of the contracting parties seeking, as a matter of right, payment of money in a sum certain, the adjustment or interpretation of contract terms, or other relief arising under or relating to the contract. Two carve-outs travel with the definition: a contractor demand for money exceeding $100,000 is not a claim until certified, and a routine, undisputed voucher or invoice is not a claim — though it can become one if it is later disputed as to liability or amount, or is not acted on in a reasonable time.
sat.x: Three elements — written, as a matter of right, sum certain (or contract terms, or other relief) — and two carve-outs: over $100K nothing is a claim until certified, and a routine invoice isn't one until disputed or ignored. Status matters because it starts the machinery: interest runs from the CO's receipt of a proper claim.

cite.quote: Claim means a written demand or written assertion by one of the contracting parties seeking, as a matter of right, the payment of money in a sum certain, the adjustment or interpretation of contract terms, or other relief arising under or relating to the contract. However, a written demand or written assertion by the contractor seeking the payment of money exceeding $100,000 is not a claim under 41 U.S.C. chapter 71, Contract Disputes, until certified as required by the statute. A voucher, invoice, or other routine request for payment that is not in dispute when submitted is not a claim.

sat.q: At what dollar value must a contractor certify a claim?
sat.a: Over $100,000 — a money demand exceeding $100,000 is not even a claim under the Disputes statute until certified.
sat.x: Over $100,000 — and the consequence is sharper than 'attach a certificate.' An uncertified demand over the line isn't a claim at all: no interest accrues, no decision obligation attaches. The figure people reach for is the SAT; the Disputes statute keeps its own threshold.
d: Over the simplified acquisition threshold.

cite.quote: a written demand or written assertion by the Contractor seeking the payment of money exceeding $100,000 is not a claim under 41 U.S.C. chapter 71 until certified

sat.q: How long does the contracting officer have to decide a contractor claim?
sat.a: For claims of $100,000 or less: if the contractor requests a decision in writing, render it within 60 days of the request. For certified claims over $100,000: within 60 days, either decide the claim or tell the contractor the date by which the decision will be made.
sat.x: Two clocks keyed to $100K. At or under: 60 days, but only if the contractor requests a decision in writing. Over: 60 days to decide or to name the date you will. That second option is the practical lever — on a complex claim the CO controls the schedule by committing to a date, not by going quiet.

cite.quote: For Contractor claims of $100,000 or less, the Contracting Officer must, if requested in writing by the Contractor, render a decision within 60 days of the request. For Contractor-certified claims over $100,000, the Contracting Officer must, within 60 days, decide the claim or notify the Contractor of the date by which the decision will be made.

sat.q: A contractor threatens to stop work until a dispute is resolved. What does the Disputes clause require?
sat.a: The contractor must proceed diligently with performance pending final resolution, and comply with the contracting officer's decision.
sat.x: Perform now, argue in parallel. The Disputes clause obligates diligent performance pending final resolution and compliance with the CO's decision — stopping work over a dispute is its own breach. The desk move: the moment the threat is made, restate the obligation in writing, citing the clause.
d: The contractor may suspend performance until the dispute is decided.
Work continues only if the Government first pays the undisputed amount.
The CO must issue a stop-work order while the claim is resolved.

cite.quote: The Contractor must proceed diligently with performance of this contract, pending final resolution of any request for relief, claim, appeal, or action arising under the contract.

sat.q: Who may execute contract modifications?
sat.a: Only contracting officers acting within the scope of their authority. Other Government personnel must not act in a way that makes the contractor believe they can bind the Government.
sat.x: Only contracting officers, inside the warrant — and the second sentence is the operational half: everyone else must avoid even appearing able to bind the Government, because acting the part is how unauthorized commitments get made. Modifications are where authority discipline is won or lost.

cite.quote: Only contracting officers acting within the scope of their authority may execute contract modifications on behalf of the Government.

sat.q: What is the difference between a bilateral and a unilateral modification?
sat.a: Bilateral (supplemental agreement) — signed by both the contractor and the contracting officer, e.g., negotiated equitable adjustments. Unilateral — signed only by the contracting officer, e.g., administrative changes, change orders, termination notices.
sat.x: Bilateral: both signatures — supplemental agreements, negotiated equitable adjustments. Unilateral: the CO's alone — administrative changes, change orders, termination notices. The classic confusion is the change order: it's unilateral by design, and the bilateral paper shows up afterward, in the equitable adjustment that prices it.

cite.quote: A bilateral modification (supplemental agreement) is a contract modification that is signed by the contractor and the contracting officer.

sat.q: Does an in-scope modification require a new competition?
sat.a: No. Part 6 competition requirements do not apply to modifications within the scope of the contract, including exercising priced options evaluated in the original competition.
sat.x: Scope is the competition question. An in-scope mod — including a priced option evaluated in the original competition — needs no new part 6 analysis. Flip it and the trap appears: an out-of-scope change is a new procurement wearing a mod's clothing, and it needs its own competition or its own justification.

cite.quote: Contract modifications that are within the scope of the contract, including exercising priced options that were evaluated as part of the original competition (see part 17)

sat.q: Before exercising an option, what must the contracting officer determine about the price?
sat.a: That the option price is fair and reasonable based on current market conditions and that exercising the option is in the Government's best interest — after written notice to the contractor and confirming funds are available. For DoD, R-DFARS 217.204-170 adds pre-exercise gates — an active, accurate SAM record and current SPRS entries (a NIST SP 800-171 assessment score and a CMMC certificate, each not more than 3 years old) — and, for firm-fixed-price contracts containing spare parts, PGI 217.204-170 requires cost or price analysis of the spares before any option is exercised.
sat.x: The civilian checklist — notice, funds, fair-and-reasonable at current market, best interest — is half the DoD answer. Boards listen for the R-DFARS gates: an active, accurate SAM record and current SPRS entries (NIST 800-171 score, CMMC certificate, each within 3 years), plus spares cost or price analysis on FFP contracts. An option exercise is a new obligation, not a formality.

cite.quote: After reviewing price and other factors, the option price is fair and reasonable based on current market conditions and exercise of the option is in the Government's best interest

dod.quote: See PGI 217.204-170 for the requirement to perform cost or price analysis of spare parts prior to exercising any option for firm- fixed-price contracts containing spare parts.

sat.q: What does the Anti-Deficiency Act prohibit?
sat.a: Creating or authorizing an obligation in excess of available funds, or in advance of appropriations, unless otherwise authorized by law.
sat.x: The ADA polices amount and timing: obligations over the funds available, or before the appropriation exists. The classic cross-wire is with purpose — spending the right amount of the wrong pot is a different fiscal violation. This is also why funds availability is one of the CO's two pre-signature assurances.
d: Spending appropriated funds on a purpose Congress did not authorize.
Obligating expired funds for a new requirement.
Committing funds before Financial Management certifies their availability.

cite.quote: No officer or employee of the Government may create or authorize an obligation in excess of the funds available, or in advance of appropriations (Anti-Deficiency Act, 31 U.S.C. 1341), unless otherwise authorized by law.

sat.q: May a severable services contract cross fiscal years?
sat.a: Yes. A contract, option, or order for severable services may begin in one fiscal year and end in the next as long as the period does not exceed one year, and the first year's funds may be obligated for the total amount. In DoD the authority sits with the contracting officer under R-DFARS 232.703-3(b) (10 U.S.C. 3133), rather than with the head of the executive agency as FAR 32.703-3(b) frames it.
sat.x: Yes — the period may cross the fiscal-year line so long as it doesn't exceed one year, and first-year funds may cover the whole of it. Two nuances: the cap is twelve months, not 'through the next FY,' and in DoD the 10 U.S.C. 3133 authority sits with the contracting officer, not the agency head the civilian text names.

cite.quote: for severable services for a period that begins in one fiscal year and ends in the next fiscal year if the period of the contract awarded, option exercised, or order placed does not exceed one year

dod.quote: The contracting officer may enter into a contract, exercise an option, or place an order under a contract for severable services for a period that begins in one fiscal year and ends in the next fiscal year if the period of the contract awarded, option exercised, or order placed does not exceed 1 year (10 U.S.C. 3133).

sat.q: When is an invoice payment due under the Prompt Payment rules?
sat.a: The later of two dates: the 30th day after the designated billing office receives a proper invoice, or the 30th day after Government acceptance of the supplies or services. For computing any interest penalty, acceptance is deemed to occur constructively on the 7th day after delivery or performance absent a dispute. DoD note: the contracting officer may extend a constructive acceptance period, but shorter than the 7-day (or 14-day construction) period is not authorized.
sat.x: The due date is the later of the two 30-day paths — later is the word that flips answers. For interest math, acceptance happens constructively on the 7th day after delivery absent a dispute. DoD's wrinkle: the CO may lengthen a constructive-acceptance period, but shortening below the 7 days (14 for construction) is not authorized.

cite.quote: The later of the following two events: (i) The 30th day after the designated billing office receives a proper invoice from the contractor (except as provided in paragraph (b)(3) of this section). (ii) The 30th day after Government acceptance of supplies delivered or services performed.

dod.quote: A constructive acceptance period of less than the cited 7 or 14 days is not authorized.

sat.q: What has to be in place before the Government pays a contractor's invoice?
sat.a: Two things: receipt of a proper invoice and satisfactory contract performance. A proper invoice carries the contractor's name and address, invoice date and number, contract number, the description, quantity, and price of what was delivered, shipping and payment terms, and correct EFT banking data. A defective invoice goes back with the reasons within 7 days — but 3 days for meat, meat food products, or fish, and 5 days for perishable agricultural commodities, dairy, and edible fats or oils. Miss the clock and the payment-due date slips by the extra days taken.
sat.x: Payment stands on two legs: a proper invoice and satisfactory performance. The clock discipline is on your side of the desk — a defective invoice goes back with reasons within 7 days, but 3 for meat and fish, 5 for perishables, dairy, and edible fats, and the due-date math moves by every extra day the office sits on it.

cite.quote: Payment will be based on receipt of a proper invoice and satisfactory contract performance.

sat.q: Must a contractor ask for interest when the Government pays late?
sat.a: No. The designated payment office pays the interest penalty automatically, without any request from the contractor, once a proper invoice was received, the receiving report cleared with no disagreement over quantity or quality, and payment went out after the due date.
sat.x: Automatic means the payment office computes and pays the penalty with no request from the contractor — once the invoice was proper, the receiving report was clean, and payment left late. Interest here isn't a claim to be won; it's a consequence the file produces on its own. Paying late is self-billing.

cite.quote: The designated payment office will pay an interest penalty automatically, without request from the contractor, when all the following conditions, if applicable, have been met:

sat.q: How must contractors submit payment requests on DoD contracts?
sat.a: Electronically — and Wide Area WorkFlow (WAWF) is the only acceptable electronic form; facsimile, email, and scanned documents do not count. The exceptions are narrow: classified work where electronic submission would compromise safeguarding; performance where electronic submission is not feasible (no internet connectivity); cases where DoD cannot receive or accept electronically; cases where the contractor asked in writing and the contracting officer put an alternative method in the contract; and purchase-card payments, where only the receiving report must be electronic.
sat.x: Electronic means WAWF, specifically — fax, email, and scanned paper don't qualify. The exceptions are narrow and mostly environmental: classified safeguarding, no connectivity, DoD unable to receive, a written-request alternative in the contract, and purchase-card buys, where only the receiving report must be electronic. 'We emailed the invoice' is a nonpayment story.

cite.quote: The only acceptable electronic form for submission of payment requests and receiving reports is Wide Area WorkFlow (WAWF)

sat.q: What is the simplified acquisition threshold?
sat.x: The reflex answer is $250,000 — a stale figure from outside the RFO, and the distractor every board reaches for. Get this one exact because it is load-bearing: the SAT gates simplified procedures and dozens of clause prescriptions, so an error here propagates into every one of them. $350,000, from 2.101, no qualifiers.

cite.quote: Simplified acquisition threshold means $350,000

sat.q: What is the micro-purchase threshold?
sat.x: $10,000 is the reflex and it is wrong here — the RFO sets $15,000. Below the MPT the rules genuinely relax: awards may be made without soliciting competitive quotations when the price is reasonable, no written provisions or clauses are required, and the purchase card is a primary method. Get the ceiling wrong and you are either strangling small buys or waiving rules that still apply.

cite.quote: Micro-purchase threshold means $15,000

5m.q: Which acquisitions are exempt from the part 6 competition requirements?
5m.a: Simplified acquisitions under part 13; procedures expressly authorized by statute; in-scope modifications (including exercising priced options evaluated in the original competition); orders under requirements and definite-quantity contracts; and orders against task- and delivery-order contracts entered into under part 16. Orders under indefinite-quantity contracts are exempt only conditionally: the contract must have been awarded under 6.101 or 6.102 with all responsible sources realistically permitted to compete for the order's requirements, or under 6.103 with a J&A that adequately covers the order. The IDIQ exemption is earned by the underlying award — it is not automatic. DoD adds one exemption of its own: contracts awarded to individuals under the 10 U.S.C. 1091 personal-services authority for health care (R-DFARS 237.201-170(b)) are exempt from part 6 (R-DFARS 206.001).
5m.x: The bait is 'IDIQ orders are exempt' as a flat rule. The exemption is inherited — a clean 6.101/6.102 award where all sources could realistically compete for the order, or a J&A that covers it. An order the J&A doesn't reach has no exemption to inherit. DoD's add: 10 U.S.C. 1091 health-care personal-services awards sit outside part 6.

cite.quote: Orders placed under indefinite-quantity contracts that were entered into according to this part when— (1) The contract was awarded under 6.101 or 6.102, and all responsible sources were realistically permitted to compete for the requirements contained in the order; or (2) The contract was awarded under 6.103, and the justification and approval, if required, adequately covers the requirements contained in the order;

dod.quote: As authorized by 10 U.S.C. 1091, contracts awarded to individuals using the procedures at 237.201-1(ii) are exempt from the competition requirements of FAR Part 6.

5m.q: May other than full and open competition be justified by a lack of planning or a shortage of funds?
5m.a: No. It must not be justified on the basis of a lack of planning by the requiring activity or concerns about the amount of funds available to the agency or activity.
5m.x: This is an absolute bar, not a balancing test. Real urgency justifies 6.103-2; urgency you manufactured by starting late justifies nothing — otherwise every late requirement would mint its own sole-source authority. 'The money expires in September' fails the same way: funding pressure is the second forbidden basis, verbatim.

cite.quote: Contracting without providing for full and open competition must not be justified on the basis of— (1) A lack of planning by the requiring activity; or (2) Concerns related to the amount of funds available to the agency or activity for acquisition.

5m.q: Which competition exceptions do not require a justification and approval?
5m.a: Under 6.104(a) there are two: authorized or required by statute (6.103-5) and public interest (6.103-7). But an Air Force reader has a third — 6.103-4(c) provides that contracts awarded by DoD, NASA, and the Coast Guard under the international agreement authority do not require the written justifications and approvals described in 6.104, and R-DFARS 206.103-4(c) adds that the head of the contracting activity instead prepares a document describing the terms of the agreement, treaty, or written directions (such as a Letter of Offer and Acceptance) that require other than competitive procedures. Every other 6.103 authority requires the 6.104 justification and approval. Two carve-backs inside the statute lane: 6.103-5(e) restores the J&A requirement for sole-source 8(a) contracts over $30 million, and for DoD R-DFARS 206.104-70 moves that trigger to $100 million — no J&A up to $100 million, but above it the contracting officer must justify the sole-source award in writing under FAR 6.104-1, obtain approval, and make the justification public after award.
5m.x: 'Two — statute and public interest' is the civilian half. A DoD reader adds the international-agreement lane, where an HCA document describing the agreement or LOA replaces the J&A. And the 8(a) carve-back splits: the J&A comes back at $30 million civilian-side, $100 million for DoD. Boards ask this to see which set of numbers you reach for.

cite.quote: A justification and approval must support procedures under 6.103, except 6.103-5 and 6.103-7.

dod.quote: In accordance with section 823 of the National Defense Authorization Act for Fiscal Year 2020 (Pub. L. 116-92), no justification and approval is required for a sole- source contract under the 8(a) authority (15 U.S.C. 637(a)) for an amount not exceeding $100 million.

5m.q: Under the one-responsible-source exception, when may a follow-on for a major system be sole-sourced?
5m.a: When award to another source would result in substantial duplication of cost to the Government not expected to be recovered through competition, or unacceptable delays in fulfilling the agency's requirements. The authority covers follow-ons for the continued development or production of a major system or highly specialized equipment — and, for DoD, NASA, and the Coast Guard, for the continued provision of highly specialized services as well. For DoD, a justification citing this authority must also include the information required by PGI 206.104-71(b) (R-DFARS 206.104-71), and a non-competitive follow-on to a previous award justified under it takes the procedures at PGI 206.104-270 (R-DFARS 206.104-72(b)).
5m.x: The trap is treating 'the incumbent knows the program' as the justification. The authority demands evidence of harm from switching: duplicated cost competition won't recover, or delay the requirement can't absorb. And DoD adds teeth to exactly this scenario — the justification carries the PGI 206.104-71(b) content, and a repeat follow-on takes the PGI 206.104-270 procedures.

cite.quote: (2) When awarding a follow-on contract for the continued development or production of a major system or highly specialized equipment and, for DoD, NASA, and the Coast Guard, for the continued provision of highly specialized services, would result in— (i) Substantial duplication of cost to the Government that is not expected to be recovered through competition; or (ii) Unacceptable delays in fulfilling the agency's requirements.

dod.quote: Include the information required by PGI 206.104-71(b) in justifications citing the authority at FAR 6.103-1.

5m.q: Does the only-one-responsible-source authority ever reach more than one source?
5m.a: Yes — for DoD, NASA, and the Coast Guard, the authority extends to situations where only a limited number of responsible sources can satisfy the requirement. Civilian agencies get the one-source version only. The one-or-a-limited-number distinction tells a board whether you know which statute you operate under — 10 U.S.C. 3204(a)(1) versus 41 U.S.C. 3304(a)(1).
5m.x: Civilian agencies must show one source; DoD may show a limited number — a J&A candidly naming two or three capable sources is legitimate under 10 U.S.C. 3204(a)(1) and fatal under 41 U.S.C. 3304(a)(1). The question is really asking whether your authority citations match the department you serve.

cite.quote: Agencies may contract without providing for full and open competition when the supplies or services required by the agency are available from only one responsible source and no other type of supplies or services will satisfy agency requirements. For DoD, NASA, and the Coast Guard, this authority extends to situations where only a limited number of responsible sources can satisfy agency requirements.

5m.q: Does a brand-name purchase description restrict competition? What about brand-name or equal?
5m.a: A pure brand-name description (or attributes peculiar to one manufacturer) prevents full and open competition and must be justified and approved under 6.104. Under the RFO, brand-name-or-equal descriptions provide for full and open competition and need no justification — but DoD flips that second half: section 888(a) of the FY 2017 NDAA requires the 6.104 justification and approval to use brand-name-or-equal descriptions, and to use proprietary specifications and standards (R-DFARS 206.103-170).
5m.x: The reflex — 'or-equal preserves full and open, so no paperwork' — is right in the RFO and wrong in DoD. Section 888 makes DoD justify brand-name-or-equal and proprietary specs too. So the working DoD rule is simpler than the civilian one: any brand name in the purchase description, with or without 'or equal,' means a 6.104 J&A.

cite.quote: use of brand-name descriptions, or specification of attributes peculiar to one manufacturer, prevents full and open competition and should only be used when justified and approved according to 6.104. This does not apply to “brand name or equal” descriptions as they provide for full and open competition.

dod.quote: (c) Application for brand-name descriptions. Notwithstanding FAR 6.103-1(d), in accordance with section 888(a) of the National Defense Authorization Act for Fiscal Year 2017 (Pub. L. 114-328), the justification and approval addressed in FAR 6.104 is required in order to use brand name or equal descriptions.

5m.q: How long may a contract awarded under the urgency exception run?
5m.a: For a contract greater than the simplified acquisition threshold, no longer than needed to meet the urgent requirement and to competitively award a follow-on — and not more than one year including all options, unless the head of the agency determines that exceptional circumstances apply. That determination is separate from the J&A, goes in the contract file, and any later extension must be approved at the same level. Two traps: the cap is conditional on exceeding the SAT, not universal; and 6.103-2(d) lets the J&A and the exceptional-circumstances determination be made after award when making them before award would unreasonably delay the acquisition.
5m.x: The one-year cap forces you to run the competitive follow-on while the urgent award burns — urgency buys a bridge, not a program. Two details boards probe: the cap attaches only above the SAT, and 6.103-2(d) lets the J&A follow award when writing it first would delay the buy. That is relief for genuine emergencies, not a grace period for slow files.

cite.quote: The total period of performance of a contract greater than the simplified acquisition threshold awarded or modified using this authority— (1) May not exceed the time necessary— (i) To meet the unusual and compelling requirements of the work to be performed under the contract; and (ii) For the agency to enter into another contract for the required goods and services through competitive procedures; and (2) May not exceed one year, including all options, unless the head of the agency determines that exceptional circumstances apply.

5m.q: Recite the justification approval ladder.
5m.a: Up to $900,000 — the contracting officer (the 6.104(a)(12) certification is the approval). Over $900,000 to $20 million — advocate for competition, not delegable. Over $20 million to $90 million ($150 million for DoD, NASA, and the Coast Guard) — head of the procuring activity, who may delegate to a general or flag officer or a civilian above GS-15. Above that — senior procurement executive, not delegable except in the case of USD(A&S) acting as DoD's senior procurement executive, who may send the authority to an Assistant Secretary of Defense or, for a defense agency, an official above brigadier general or rear admiral (lower half) or a civilian at a comparable grade (R-DFARS 206.104-72(a)). Include the estimated dollar value of all options when setting the level, and note that a higher-level official may always approve a lower-dollar justification. One more DoD lane: sole-source 8(a) contracts need no justification and approval at all up to $100 million, and above $100 million the head of the procuring activity — not the senior procurement executive — approves, delegable only to that same flag-or-above level (R-DFARS 206.104-70, 206.104-72(c)).
5m.x: Set the level on the value including all options — undervaluing the action is how J&As get approved one rung too low and die in review. Keep the ceilings straight: $90 million civilian, $150 million for DoD, NASA, and the Coast Guard. Know the DoD lanes — USD(A&S) may hand the top tier to an ASD, and sole-source 8(a) skips the ladder until $100 million, where the HPA owns it.

cite.quote: $900,000 or below Contracting officer. Accomplished by certification required at 6.104(a)(12). >$900,000 - $20,000,000 Advocate for competition. Not delegable.

dod.quote: In accordance with section 823 of the National Defense Authorization Act for Fiscal Year 2020 (Pub. L. 116-92), the head of the procuring activity is the approval authority for a proposed sole-source 8(a) contract exceeding $100 million.

5m.q: When must a justification for other than full and open competition be posted publicly?
5m.a: Within 14 days after contract award — except urgency (6.103-2) justifications post within 30 days, and brand-name justifications post with the solicitation.
5m.x: Fourteen days is the default; the two outliers are principled. Urgency justifications get 30 because the mission outran the paperwork. Brand-name justifications post with the solicitation because industry needs to see the restriction while there is still time to challenge it — after award is too late to matter.

cite.quote: The justification must be made publicly available within 14 days after contract award, except— (1) Justifications under 6.103-2 must be posted within 30 days after contract award

5m.q: Does full and open competition after excluding sources (for example, a set-aside) require its own justification and approval?
5m.a: No. It still uses the competitive procedures of 6.101 among the narrowed field, and requires no separate justification and approval or determination and findings.
5m.x: A set-aside narrows who may compete, never whether you compete — inside the narrowed field, 6.101 procedures run at full strength. That is why no J&A: you are redirecting competition, not excusing it. Filing set-asides mentally under 'exceptions to competition' is the miss this card exists to prevent.

cite.quote: Acquisitions under this section do not require separate justification and approval or determination and findings.

5m.q: When may sealed bidding be used instead of competitive proposals?
5m.a: Only when all four conditions hold: time permits soliciting, submitting, and evaluating sealed bids; award will be made on price and price-related factors; discussions with bidders are unnecessary; and more than one sealed bid is reasonably expected.
5m.x: The test is conjunctive — lose any one leg and you are in competitive proposals. In practice the killer is 'discussions unnecessary': the moment you expect to negotiate technical approach or terms, sealed bidding is gone. And award on price and price-related factors means past-performance and technical-merit trade-offs have no home here.

cite.quote: (i) Time permits staff to solicit, submit, and evaluate sealed bids; (ii) The award will be made on the basis of price and other price-related factors; (iii) Discussion with bidders is unnecessary; and (iv) Contracting officers reasonably expect to receive more than one sealed bid.

5m.q: Competitive DoD solicitation, one offer received. What must the contracting officer do?
5m.a: If the solicitation allowed fewer than 30 days for proposals: consult the requiring activity on revising the requirements document to promote competition, then resolicit for at least 30 more days. If resolicitation is not required, still establish a fair and reasonable price — obtaining additional cost or pricing data where needed, certified above the certified-cost-or-pricing-data threshold unless an exception applies. The resolicit rule does not apply to acquisitions at or below the SAT, contingency/disaster support, small business set-asides, science-and-technology and architect-engineer acquisitions, commercial solutions openings, or commercial part 12 acquisitions — and the head of the contracting activity may waive it, delegable no lower than one level above the contracting officer. No exception relieves you of seeking maximum practicable competition (R-DFARS 215.202-71).
5m.x: Two duties hide in one offer. Resoliciting for 30 more days (when the window was short) cures the competition defect — never the pricing one: one offer means the market checked nothing, so you still owe a fair-and-reasonable determination on data. And the waiver belongs to the HCA, delegable no lower than one level above you.

cite.quote: (1) If only one offer is received when competitive procedures were used and the solicitation allowed fewer than 30 days for receipt of proposals, the contracting officer must— (i) Consult with the requiring activity as to whether the requirements document should be revised to promote more competition (see FAR 6.003(a) and 11.102); and (ii) Resolicit, allowing an additional period of at least 30 days for receipt of proposals

5m.q: What is the baseline ordering rule on a multiple-award contract?
5m.a: Each awardee must be given a fair opportunity to be considered for every order or BPA valued above the micro-purchase threshold, unless a sole-source order is justified and approved under 16.507-6. For DoD, ordering also carries two DFARS guardrails: the limitations on lowest-price-technically-acceptable source selection apply to orders under multiple-award contracts, and reverse auctions are prohibited for personal protective equipment and aviation critical safety items (R-DFARS 216.507-2).
5m.x: The trigger is the micro-purchase threshold, not the SAT — far lower than most people's reflex. Above the MPT every awardee gets a fair shot unless a 16.507-6 exception is justified. DoD keeps two guardrails even in this streamlined lane: the LPTA restrictions follow orders, and reverse auctions are off-limits for PPE and aviation critical safety items.

cite.quote: The contracting officer must provide each awardee a fair opportunity to be considered for each order or BPA valued above the micro-purchase threshold according to paragraph (c) and 16.507-3 through 16.507-5, unless a sole source order or BPA is justified and approved according to 16.507-6.

dod.quote: See 215.103-270 for the limitations and prohibitions on the use of the lowest price technically acceptable source selection process, which are applicable to orders placed against multiple award indefinite delivery contracts.

5m.q: Are task orders subject to part 6 competition or the subpart 15.3 source selection rules?
5m.a: No. The ordering process is not subject to part 6, subpart 15.3, or part 14 — streamlined procedures are allowed, with no required evaluation plans, scoring, or competitive range. Streamlined is not unconstrained in DoD, though — the DFARS limitations on lowest-price-technically-acceptable source selection still reach orders placed against multiple-award indefinite-delivery contracts (R-DFARS 216.507-2).
5m.x: The competition happened at contract award; orders get a lighter regime by design. The twin traps: importing part 15 machinery — competitive ranges, formal evaluation plans — into ordering, or hearing 'streamlined' as 'anything goes.' In DoD the LPTA limitations reach into the ordering process regardless.

cite.quote: The ordering process is not subject to the competition requirements in part 6 or the policies in subpart 15.3 or part 14.

dod.quote: See 215.103-270 for the limitations and prohibitions on the use of the lowest price technically acceptable source selection process, which are applicable to orders placed against multiple award indefinite delivery contracts.

5m.q: Name the exceptions that allow a sole-source order despite fair opportunity.
5m.a: Urgency causing unacceptable delays; only one awardee capable (unique or highly specialized); logical follow-on in the interest of economy and efficiency; satisfying a minimum guarantee; a statute authorizing a specified source (orders over the SAT); and, for DoD, NASA, and the Coast Guard, the 6.103 exceptions — with the caveat that the public interest exception must not be used unless Congress is notified under 10 U.S.C. 3204(a)(7). Setting an order aside under part 19 is a separate lane that is not subject to these justification, approval, and posting requirements at all (16.507-6(c)). DoD adds a tripwire: an over-SAT order that is a follow-on to an order previously justified under the only-one-capable or logical-follow-on exception requires the procedures at PGI 216.507-6(b) (R-DFARS 216.507-6).
5m.x: Map them against 6.103 but keep the lanes apart: urgency, one-capable, and minimum-guarantee have part 6 cousins; logical follow-on does not. Set-asides are missing because they are not an exception at all — 16.507-6(c) puts them outside the justification machinery. DoD's tripwire: a follow-on to an already-excepted order takes the PGI procedures.

cite.quote: (1) The agency need for the supplies or services is so urgent that providing a fair opportunity would result in unacceptable delays. (2) Only one awardee is capable of providing the supplies or services required at the level of quality required because the supplies or services ordered are unique or highly specialized. (3) The order must be issued on a sole-source basis in the interest of economy and efficiency because it is a logical follow-on to an order already issued under the contract, provided that all awardees were given a fair opportunity to be considered for the original order. (4) It is necessary to place an order to satisfy a minimum guarantee.

dod.quote: (b) Exceptions. For an order exceeding the simplified acquisition threshold, that is a follow-on to an order previously issued for the same supply or service based on a justification for an exception to fair opportunity citing the authority at FAR 16.507-6(b)(2) or (3), follow the procedures at PGI 216.507-6(b).

5m.q: What condition is built into the logical-follow-on exception?
5m.a: All awardees must have been given a fair opportunity to be considered for the original order — and the justification must describe why the relationship between the initial order and the follow-on is logical. And for DoD, serial follow-ons get extra scrutiny — an over-SAT order following one previously justified under exception (b)(2) or (3) must follow the PGI 216.507-6(b) procedures.
5m.x: The condition protects the exception from swallowing the rule: if awardees never had a fair shot at the original order, each 'logical follow-on' just extends the original foreclosure. Write the justification around why the relationship is logical — 'the incumbent is already in place' is an economy argument, and economy alone is not the test.

cite.quote: it is a logical follow-on to an order already issued under the contract, provided that all awardees were given a fair opportunity to be considered for the original order.

dod.quote: (b) Exceptions. For an order exceeding the simplified acquisition threshold, that is a follow-on to an order previously issued for the same supply or service based on a justification for an exception to fair opportunity citing the authority at FAR 16.507-6(b)(2) or (3), follow the procedures at PGI 216.507-6(b).

5m.q: Recite the approval ladder for a fair-opportunity exception justification.
5m.a: Above the SAT to $900,000 — the ordering activity contracting officer's certification serves as approval, unless agency procedures set a higher level. Above $900,000 to $20 million — the advocate for competition of the activity placing the order, not delegable. Above $20 million to $90 million ($150 million for DoD, NASA, and the Coast Guard) — the head of the procuring activity, a general or flag officer, or a civilian above GS-15. Above that — the senior procurement executive, not delegable except for DoD's USD(A&S). Below the SAT, documenting the basis for the exception suffices. This is the order-level ladder — do not confuse it with the 6.104-2 contract-level J&A ladder.
5m.x: Two details separate pass from stumble: below the SAT there is no formal justification at all — documenting the basis suffices — and the approvers belong to the activity placing the order. The dollar rungs deliberately mirror 6.104-2, which is exactly why boards ask which ladder you are climbing; 'same numbers, different regime' shows you see both.

cite.quote: (1) For proposed orders valued above the SAT, but not valued above $900,000, the ordering activity contracting officer’s certification that the justification is accurate and complete to the best of the ordering activity contracting officer’s knowledge and belief will serve as approval, unless a higher approval level is established in accordance with agency procedures. (2) For a proposed order valued above $900,000, but not above $20 million, the justification must be approved by the advocate for competition of the activity placing the order, or by an official named in paragraph (e)(3) or (4). This authority is not delegable. (3) For a proposed order valued above $20 million, but not above $90 million (or, for DoD, NASA, and the Coast Guard, not above $150 million, the justification must be approved by— (i) The head of the procuring activity placing the order; (ii) A designee who— (A) If a member of the armed forces, is a general or flag officer; (B) If a civilian, is serving in a position in a grade above GS-15 under the General Schedule (or in a comparable or higher position under another schedule); or (iii) An official named in paragraph (e)(4) of this subsection. (4) For a proposed order valued above $90 million (or, for DoD, NASA, and the Coast Guard, above $150 million), the justification must be approved by the senior procurement executive of the agency placing the order.

5m.q: Who hears a contract holder's complaint about order placement?
5m.a: The agency's task-order and delivery-order ombudsman — a senior official independent of the contracting officer who reviews complaints and ensures awardees are afforded a fair opportunity consistent with the contract's procedures.
5m.x: The ombudsman exists because most orders cannot be protested — below the 16.508 dollar floors GAO's door is closed, so a senior official independent of the contracting officer is the contract holder's forum. Desk answer: a fair-opportunity complaint routes to the ombudsman, not to GAO and not back to the ordering CO who made the call.

cite.quote: The head of the agency must designate a task-order and delivery-order ombudsman. The ombudsman must review complaints from contractors and ensure they are afforded a fair opportunity to be considered, consistent with the procedures in the contract.

5m.q: What must the fair notice include for orders above $7.5 million?
5m.a: A clear statement of the agency's requirements, a reasonable response period, and disclosure of the significant evaluation factors and subfactors — including cost or price — and their relative importance.
5m.x: Above $7.5 million, ordering starts to look like a mini source selection: stated requirement, real response time, disclosed factors and their relative importance — with cost or price always among them. What it still is not: a part 15 competition. And keep this tier's number separate from DoD's $10 million debriefing trigger — nearby figures, different rules.

cite.quote: Orders valued above $7.5 million (a) Procedures . Provide a fair notice of the intent to place an order to all contractors offering the products or services according to 16.507-4. A fair notice must— (1) Include a clear statement of the agency’s requirements; (2) Allow for a reasonable response period; and (3) Disclose the significant factors and subfactors, as applicable, including cost or price, that the agency expects to consider in evaluating quotations, offers, or other responses to notices, and their relative importance;

5m.q: Do losing contract holders get a debriefing on large task orders?
5m.a: Yes — for orders in the above-$7.5 million tier, postaward notifications and debriefings follow part 15, and a summary of the debriefing goes in the order file. DoD hardens this with its own statutory trigger: a written or oral postaward debriefing of successful and unsuccessful awardees is required for task and delivery orders valued at $10 million or more (section 818, FY 2018 NDAA; R-DFARS 216.507-5). Know both numbers — $7.5 million is the RFO procedures tier; $10 million is the DoD debriefing mandate.
5m.x: Two numbers that look like a contradiction until you see they answer different questions. $7.5 million is the RFO tier where order procedures import part 15 debriefings; $10 million is DoD's statutory mandate that successful and unsuccessful awardees be debriefed. A board wants both held at once — and the debrief summary belongs in the order file.

cite.quote: (c) Postaward notices and debriefings. Provide postaward notifications and debriefings according to part 15. A summary of the debriefing must be included in the task or delivery order file.

dod.quote: (c) Postaward notices and debriefing. In addition to the notice required by FAR part 15 and 16.507-5(c), a written or oral postaward debriefing of successful and unsuccessful awardees is required for task orders and delivery orders valued at $10 million or more (section 818 of the National Defense Authorization Act for Fiscal Year 2018 (Pub. L. 115-91)).

5m.q: When can a task or delivery order be protested?
5m.a: Only on grounds that the order increases the scope, period, or maximum value of the contract — or, at GAO only, for orders valued over $35 million (DoD, NASA, Coast Guard) or $10 million (other agencies).
5m.x: Scope, period, or maximum value is the universal lane — really a claim that the order is a new procurement wearing the contract's clothes. Everything else goes to GAO alone, above $35 million for DoD, NASA, and the Coast Guard. Quoting $10 million for a DoD order is the standard miss: that number belongs to the other agencies.

cite.quote: (1) A protest on the grounds that the order increases the scope, period, or maximum value of the contract; or (2) (i) For agencies other than DoD, NASA, and the Coast Guard, a protest of an order valued in excess of $10 million (41 U.S.C. 4106(f)); or (ii) For DoD, NASA, or the Coast Guard, a protest of an order valued in excess of $35 million (10 U.S.C. 3406(f)).

5m.q: What makes an indefinite-quantity contract binding?
5m.a: The stated minimum quantity the Government must order — it must be more than a nominal quantity, but should not exceed the amount the Government is fairly certain to order.
5m.x: The minimum is the consideration — a nominal minimum risks an illusory promise nobody can enforce. But the ceiling on the floor matters too: a minimum above what you are fairly certain to order converts a planning tool into a real liability the Government must buy its way out of. Set it meaningful, keep it modest.

cite.quote: The contract must require the Government to order and the contractor to furnish at least a stated minimum quantity of supplies or services. To ensure that the contract is binding, the minimum quantity must be more than a nominal quantity, but it should not exceed the amount that the Government is fairly certain to order.

5m.q: Single award or multiple awards on an indefinite-quantity solicitation?
5m.a: Multiple awards are preferred to the maximum extent practicable, with the decision documented — and a single-award task- or delivery-order contract estimated over $150 million (including options) requires a written head-of-agency determination. In DoD, that $150 million determination belongs to the senior procurement executive, who must find the expected orders so integrally related that only a single source can efficiently — not merely reasonably — perform the work; the congressional-notification requirement does not apply to DoD; and no determination is required at all if a 6.104 justification has been executed (R-DFARS 216.504-3).
5m.x: Multiple award is the default; single award over $150 million is an exception you earn in writing. DoD hardens every joint: the SPE decides, 'reasonably perform' becomes 'efficiently perform,' no congressional notice — and an executed 6.104 justification moots the determination. Citing the civilian head-of-agency approver on a DoD action is the giveaway miss.

cite.quote: No task or delivery order contract in an amount estimated to exceed $150 million (including all options) may be awarded to a single source unless the head of the agency determines in writing

dod.quote: (a)(4)(i) The senior procurement executive has the authority to make the determination authorized in FAR 16.504-3(a)(4)(i). (A) In accordance with 10 U.S.C. 3403(d)(3), when making the determination at FAR 16.504-3(a)(4)(i)(A), the senior procurement executive must determine that the task or delivery orders expected under the contract are so integrally related that only a single source can “efficiently perform the work,” instead of “reasonably perform the work” as required by the FAR. (a)(4)(ii) The congressional notification requirement at FAR 16.504-3(a)(4)(ii) does not apply to DoD. (a)(4)(iii) In accordance with 10 U.S.C. 3403(d)(3), the determination at FAR 16.504-3(a)(4)(iii) is not required if a justification has been executed, in accordance with FAR 6.104 and section 206.104.

5m.q: When does an advisory and assistance services IDIQ force multiple awards?
5m.a: When the indefinite-quantity contract is estimated to exceed 3 years and $20 million including all options, the solicitation must provide for multiple awards — unless a written determination finds more than one award impracticable because the services are unique or highly specialized or the tasks integrally related, the evaluation shows only one offeror capable at the required quality level, or only one offer is received. The preference does not apply when the head of the agency determines in writing during planning that A&AS is necessarily incident to, and not a significant component of, the contract.
5m.x: Both triggers must fire — over 3 years and over $20 million with options. Then multiple award is a mandate with enumerated outs (impracticability, one capable offeror after evaluation, one offer received), not the ordinary documented preference. The escape runs the other way: A&AS merely incidental to the contract takes the rule off the table.

cite.quote: if an indefinite-quantity contract for advisory and assistance services is estimated to exceed 3 years and $20 million (including all options), the solicitation must provide for multiple awards unless- (i) The contracting officer or other official designated by the head of the agency determines in writing- (A) It is not practicable to award more than one contract because the services required are unique or highly specialized or the tasks are so integrally related; or (B) After the evaluation of offers, that only one offeror is capable of providing the services required at the level of quality required; or (ii) Only one offer is received.

5m.q: Can an order under a multiple-award contract be set aside for small business?
5m.a: Yes — contracting officers may, at their discretion, set aside orders for small business concerns, and that discretionary decision is not itself a basis for protest.
5m.x: Discretionary is the operative word: 19.111-2 permits order set-asides under multiple-award contracts, never compels them, and the exercise of that discretion is not itself protestable. Pair it with the fair-opportunity rule: a set-aside order also sits outside the 16.507-6 justification machinery — it is a lane, not an exception.

cite.quote: contracting officers may, at their discretion, set aside orders placed under multiple-award contracts for any of the small business concerns identified in 19.000(a)(3).

5m.q: How long may a DoD task- or delivery-order contract run?
5m.a: Up to five years, extendable by option or modification — but the total period as extended may not exceed 10 years unless the head of the agency determines in writing that exceptional circumstances require a longer period (R-DFARS 217.201-270(a) restates the same 5/10-year rule for DoD). One carve-out a board will probe: a task-order contract for advisory and assistance services is capped at a 5-year ordering period including all extensions (16.501-2(c)(2)), unless a longer period is specifically authorized by statute or the A&AS is determined incidental and not a significant component of the contract — plus a sole-source extension of up to 6 months when a follow-on award is delayed by circumstances not reasonably foreseeable and continuity of services requires it. DoD adds one more tripwire: senior procurement executive approval is required before issuing an order expected to extend more than 1 year beyond that 10-year (or extended) limit (R-DFARS 217.201-270(c)).
5m.x: Five years by design, ten by determination — but A&AS task-order contracts stop at 5 years including extensions unless a statute says otherwise, plus a 6-month sole-source continuity bridge when the follow-on slips unforeseeably. DoD's tripwire: an order reaching more than a year past the limit needs SPE approval before it issues.

cite.quote: may provide for the contract to cover any period up to five years and may extend the contract period for one or more successive periods pursuant to an option provided in the contract or a modification of the contract. The total contract period as extended may not exceed 10 years unless such head of an agency determines in writing that exceptional circumstances necessitate a longer contract period.

dod.quote: (1) May be for any period up to 5 years; (2) May be subsequently extended for one or more successive periods in accordance with an option provided in the contract or a modification of the contract; and (3) Must not exceed 10 years unless the head of the agency determines in writing that exceptional circumstances require a longer ordering period.

5m.q: List the determinations required before exercising an option.
5m.a: Written notice within the contract's specified time; funds available; the option fulfills an existing Government requirement; it was synopsized unless exempt; no active SAM exclusion; acceptable performance on the current contract; the price is fair and reasonable under current market conditions and exercise is in the Government's best interest; and the exercise complies with part 6. DoD adds two more gates before exercise: the contractor's SAM record is active with the UEI, CAGE code, name, and physical address accurate in the contract document; and SPRS shows both a current NIST SP 800-171 DoD Assessment summary score (not more than 3 years old) for each covered contractor information system and a current CMMC certificate at the level the contract requires (R-DFARS 217.204-170).
5m.x: Recite the RFO checklist and a DoD board hears half the answer. A DoD option isn't ripe until you also verify SAM active with UEI, CAGE, name, and address matching the contract, a NIST SP 800-171 score in SPRS under 3 years old, and a current CMMC certificate at the contract's level. The cyber gates are where real option exercises stall.

cite.quote: (1) Providing written notice to the contractor of the Government’s intention to exercise the option, within the time specified in the contract; (2) Confirming that funds are available; and (3) Determining that– (i) The option fulfills an existing Government requirement; (ii) The option was synopsized as required, unless exempt (see part 5); (iii) The Contractor does not have an active exclusion record in the System for Award Management (see part 9); (iv) The contractor’s performance on the current contract has been acceptable

dod.quote: In addition to the requirements at FAR 17.204-1(b), exercise an option only after: (a) Determining that the contractor’s record in the System for Award Management database is active and the contractor’s unique entity identifier, Commercial and Government Entity (CAGE) code, name, and physical address are accurately reflected in the contract document. See PGI 217.204-170 for the requirement to perform cost or price analysis of spare parts prior to exercising any option for firm- fixed-price contracts containing spare parts. (b) Verifying in the Supplier Performance Risk System (SPRS) (https://www.sprs.csd.disa.mil/) that— (1) The summary level score of a current NIST SP 800-171 DoD Assessment (i.e., not more than 3 years old, unless a lesser time is specified in the solicitation) for each covered contractor information system that is relevant to an offer, contract, task order, or delivery order are posted. (2) The contractor has a CMMC certificate at the level required by the contract, and that it is current (i.e., not more than 3 years old).

5m.q: Why does exercising an option not require a new competition?
5m.a: Because the exercise must comply with part 6 by having been evaluated as part of the initial competition and being exercisable at an amount specified in, or reasonably determinable from, the terms of the contract.
5m.x: Both legs must hold: evaluated in the original competition, and exercisable at a price the contract fixes or makes reasonably determinable. An option that fails either — never evaluated, or priced 'to be negotiated' — no longer complies with part 6, and exercising it becomes a new noncompetitive action, not a routine unilateral right.

cite.quote: The option exercise complies with the requirements of part 6 for full and open competition, i.e., the option was evaluated as part of the initial competition and is exercisable at an amount specified in or reasonably determinable from the terms of the contract.

5m.q: When are options prohibited?
5m.a: When the price or availability of necessary material or labor is not reasonably foreseeable — introducing significant option-pricing risk — or when market prices for the supplies or services are likely to change significantly.
5m.x: Both prohibitions are about pricing honesty: an option priced today against unforeseeable material, labor, or market swings is a guess someone will regret — the Government overpaying or the contractor underwater. When markets are volatile the answer is shorter commitments, not longer priced tails bolted on for convenience.

cite.quote: The contracting officer must not use options when- (1) Price or availability of necessary material or labor is not reasonably foreseeable, introducing significant risk into option pricing; or (2) Market prices for the supplies or services are likely to change significantly.

5m.q: How far can the Option to Extend Services clause stretch a service contract?
5m.a: It may be exercised more than once, but the total extension of performance may not exceed 6 months, at the rates specified in the contract.
5m.x: Six months total, cumulative across every exercise — not six months per pull. The clause is a bridge to a delayed follow-on at the contract's existing rates, not a seventh option year. Treat -8 as free extension runway and you hit the cap mid-bridge with no clean way to keep services running.
d: It may be exercised only once, for a single extension of up to 6 months at the contract's rates.
It may be exercised more than once, up to 6 months per exercise, with no cap on the total extension.
It may be exercised more than once, but the total extension may not exceed 1 year, at rates the parties negotiate at exercise.

cite.quote: The option provision may be exercised more than once, but the total extension of performance hereunder shall not exceed 6 months.

5m.q: After market research, in what order of priority must an agency source its requirement?
5m.a: (1) A commercial product or service on an existing governmentwide contract; (2) modify the requirement so an existing governmentwide contract can be used; (3) a commercial product or service from another source; (4) a commercial product or service that could be modified; and only then (5) a nondevelopmental item.
5m.x: The sequence is a policy statement: existing governmentwide vehicles beat new contracts, commercial beats nondevelopmental. Step (2) is the tell — the regulation would rather you modify your requirement than duplicate an existing contract. A nondevelopmental item is the floor you reach only after the commercial rungs fail, not a peer option you may prefer.

cite.quote: (1) A commercial product or commercial service on an existing governmentwide contract can meet the agency's requirements; (2) The requirements could be modified so the agency could use an existing governmentwide contract; (3) A commercial product or commercial service is available from another source; (4) A commercial product or commercial service could be modified to meet the agency's requirements; or (5) The requirement can only be satisfied by a nondevelopmental item.

5m.q: How much information may you ask potential sources to submit during market research?
5m.a: No more than the minimum information necessary to make the determinations required by 10.001(f). Market research is the Government doing its homework — not a vehicle for extracting free proposals from industry.
5m.x: The rule polices a real abuse: RFIs that demand near-proposals at industry's expense. Free engineering dressed up as market research burns vendor goodwill and chills the very competition you are researching. Ask what the 10.001(f) determinations require, and stop — the homework is the Government's to do.

cite.quote: When conducting market research, agencies must not ask potential sources to submit more than the minimum information necessary to make the determinations required in paragraph (f).

5m.q: Can a requirement that is not commercial be bought as if it were?
5m.a: Yes — and for DoD there is more than one lane. The RFO lane: the head of the agency may determine that supplies or services used to facilitate defense against or recovery from cyber, nuclear, biological, chemical, or radiological attack are to be treated as commercial products or commercial services — though a sole-source award over $25 million under this treatment remains subject to Cost Accounting Standards and certified cost or pricing data requirements. R-DFARS 212.001-70 adds two statutory lanes of its own: supplies and services provided by nontraditional defense contractors may be treated as commercial (10 U.S.C. 3457), and supplies or services resulting from a commercial solutions opening are treated as commercial (10 U.S.C. 3458) — none of the three lanes requires a commercial product or commercial service determination. And remember part 12's rank: it takes precedence over other parts whenever there is an inconsistency.
5m.x: Three doors into part 12 without a commerciality determination: the attack/recovery lane, nontraditional defense contractors, and commercial solutions openings. None waives everything — the attack lane keeps CAS and certified cost or pricing data on sole-source awards over $25 million. The nontraditional lane is permission to treat, not a finding the item is commercial.

cite.quote: Agencies may treat any acquisition of supplies or services that, as determined by the head of the agency, are to be used to facilitate defense against or recovery from cyber, nuclear, biological, chemical, or radiological attack, as an acquisition of commercial products or commercial services. However, if the contract is awarded on a sole-source basis for an amount greater than $25 million, the contract is not exempt from Cost Accounting Standards (CAS) (see 48 CFR chapter 99) or certified cost or pricing data requirements (see part 15).

dod.quote: Use of FAR part 12 procedures is based on applicability of one of the following statutes that provide for treatment as a commercial product or commercial service and use of FAR part 12 procedures, even though the item may not meet the definition of “commercial product” or “commercial service” at FAR 2.101 and does not require a commercial product or commercial service determination: (1) 41 U.S.C. 1903 - Supplies or services to be used to facilitate defense against or recovery from cyber, nuclear, biological, chemical, or radiological attack pursuant to FAR 12.001(b). (2) 10 U.S.C. 3457 - Supplies or services from nontraditional defense contractors pursuant to paragraph (d) of this section. (3) 10 U.S.C. 3458 - Supplies or services resulting from a commercial solutions opening pursuant to subpart 212.70.

5m.q: How are commercial acquisitions over $9 million solicited?
5m.a: Using the subpart 12.2 procedures in conjunction with part 15 (requests for proposals) or part 14 (invitations for bids) — with the RFP preferred because it considers past performance. Know the moving line underneath the number: $9 million is the ceiling for the simplified procedures at 12.201-1, and 12.001(c) raises that ceiling to $15 million when the head of the agency determines the supplies or services support a contingency operation, facilitate defense against or recovery from a cyber, nuclear, biological, chemical, or radiological attack, support a State/USAID request for international disaster assistance, or support response to an emergency or major disaster. Do not divide requirements merely to stay under a threshold (12.001(d)).
5m.x: $9 million is where standalone simplified commercial procedures end and part 12 rides a part 15 or 14 chassis — RFP preferred because sealed bidding cannot weigh past performance. The moving piece is the ceiling: $15 million under the contingency/attack/disaster determinations. Splitting a requirement to stay under either line is its own violation.

cite.quote: For acquisitions valued at greater than $9 million, use the procedures in this subpart in conjunction with the procedures in part 15 for requests for proposals (RFPs) or part 14 for invitations for bids (IFBs), as appropriate.

5m.q: How detailed do commercial evaluation factors need to be?
5m.a: For most commercial acquisitions, no more detailed than technical (capability of the products or services to meet the need), price, and past performance — predetermined technical subfactors are not required. DoD adds one mandatory factor: supply chain risk, whenever acquiring information technology — as a service or as a supply — that is, is part of, or supports a covered system (R-DFARS 212.203).
5m.x: Technical, price, past performance is a sufficiency statement, not a floor to build on — for most commercial buys, more subfactors buy evaluation burden, not insight. A ten-subfactor commercial plan recreates the part 15 machinery part 12 exists to avoid. DoD's one mandatory add: supply chain risk whenever the IT touches a covered system.

cite.quote: For most acquisitions of commercial products or commercial services, evaluation factors need not be more detailed than technical (capability of the products or services offered to meet the agency’s needs), price, and past performance.

dod.quote: (a)(1)(i) Include an evaluation factor regarding supply chain risk (see subpart 239.70) when acquiring information technology, whether as a service or as a supply, that is a covered system, is a part of a covered system, or is in support of a covered system, as defined in 239.7001.

5m.q: Which termination machinery applies to commercial contracts?
5m.a: The termination paragraphs of clause 52.212-4 — not part 49. And before terminating for cause, send a cure notice unless the reason is late delivery.
5m.x: Part 49 is the trap answer — the commercial clause carries its own self-contained termination scheme, and 12.304 flatly says not to use part 49. The working detail is the cure notice: skip it before a termination for cause (for anything except late delivery) and you have skipped a required step the contractor's counsel will not miss.
d: Part 49, as for any other contract — commercial status changes the clauses, not the termination procedures.
The termination paragraphs of 52.212-4 for convenience, but part 49 procedures for any termination for cause.
Part 49, supplemented by 52.212-4 — and a cure notice is required in every case, including late delivery.

cite.quote: Follow the procedures in this section and the termination paragraphs of the clause at 52.212-4, when terminating contracts for commercial products or commercial services. Do not use the procedures in part 49.

5m.q: Which contract types are the default?
5m.a: Fixed-price types are the default and preferred. If a fixed-price type is not appropriate for the entire contract, consider whether a portion of it can be established on a fixed-price basis. DoD draws a hard line at development work: for programs other than major defense acquisition programs, R-DFARS 235.170(b) forbids awarding a fixed-price type contract for a development program effort unless the level of program risk permits realistic pricing, the fixed-price type allocates program risk equitably and sensibly between the Government and the contractor, and a written determination to that effect is executed — by USD(A&S) when the contract is over $25 million and covers non-major-system R&D or development of a major system or its subsystem, otherwise by the contracting officer. Major defense acquisition programs run a different track: 235.170(a) sends you to 234.7202.
5m.x: 'Fixed-price preferred' has a hard DoD boundary at development. For non-MDAP development, R-DFARS bars a fixed-price type unless risk permits realistic pricing, allocation is equitable, and a written determination says so — USD(A&S) signs above $25 million. The trap: reciting the preference and getting walked into pricing genuine development FFP.

cite.quote: Fixed-price contract types are the default and preferred contract types. If a fixed-price contract type is not appropriate for an entire contract, consider whether a portion of the contract can be established on a fixed-price basis.

dod.quote: Do not award a fixed-price type contract for a development program effort unless— (i) The level of program risk permits realistic pricing; (ii) The use of a fixed-price type contract permits an equitable and sensible allocation of program risk between the Government and the contractor; and (iii) A written determination that the criteria of paragraphs (b)(1)(i) and (ii) of this section have been met is executed—

5m.q: When must firm-fixed-price be used, and what if a reasonable basis for firm pricing does not exist?
5m.a: FFP must be used when the risk involved is minimal or predictable with an acceptable degree of certainty. Without a firm pricing basis, select a type (or combination) that appropriately ties profit to contractor performance. DoD bounds that rule for development: under R-DFARS 235.170(b), and for programs other than major defense acquisition programs, a fixed-price type contract may not be awarded for a development program effort unless program risk permits realistic pricing and the fixed-price type permits an equitable and sensible allocation of risk — backed by a written determination, executed by USD(A&S) for covered development contracts over $25 million and otherwise by the contracting officer. For major defense acquisition programs, 235.170(a) routes you to 234.7202 instead.
5m.x: The rule cuts both ways: minimal, predictable risk makes FFP mandatory, but genuine unknowns make it reckless — without a firm pricing basis the selection becomes a profit-motive question, tying fee to the performance you actually need. And in DoD development, the written risk determination stands between you and any fixed-price award.

cite.quote: A firm-fixed-price contract (see section 16.202) must be used when the risk involved is minimal or can be predicted with an acceptable degree of certainty.

dod.quote: Do not award a fixed-price type contract for a development program effort unless— (i) The level of program risk permits realistic pricing; (ii) The use of a fixed-price type contract permits an equitable and sensible allocation of program risk between the Government and the contractor; and (iii) A written determination that the criteria of paragraphs (b)(1)(i) and (ii) of this section have been met is executed—

5m.q: What gates must a cost-reimbursement contract clear before award?
5m.a: A written acquisition plan approved at least one level above the contracting officer; the agency-head justification for other than fixed-price if 16.104 requires it; a contractor accounting system that can segregate, accumulate, and allocate contract costs; and sufficient Government resources — including a designated COR — to manage it. And one absolute bar: cost-reimbursement is not allowed for the purchase of commercial products and commercial services (16.301-3(b)). DoD adds a statutory bar of its own: no cost-plus-fixed-fee, cost-plus-award-fee, or cost-plus-incentive-fee contracts in connection with military construction or military family housing — even under a declaration of war or national emergency (10 U.S.C. 3323; R-DFARS 216.301-3).
5m.x: All four gates answer one question: can both sides manage a contract where the Government holds the cost risk? Two absolutes sit on top: never cost-reimbursement for commercial buys, and in DoD never cost-plus for military construction or family housing — 'notwithstanding a declaration of war,' a phrase boards quote because it means exactly what it says.

cite.quote: (1) A written acquisition plan has been approved at least one level above the contracting officer (see 7.102(d)); (2) The agency head approves a justification if required by 16.104; (3) The contractor’s accounting system can adequately segregate, accumulate and allocate costs specifically attributed to the contract or order during contract performance; and (4) Before award of the contract or order, sufficient Government resources are available to award and manage a contract other than firm-fixed-priced (see part 7). This includes designating a contracting officer’s representative to monitor contractor performance and cost controls (see part 1). (b) The use of cost-reimbursement contracts is not allowed for the purchase of commercial products and commercial services (see part 12).

dod.quote: For contracts in connection with a military construction project or a military family housing project, contracting officers must not use cost-plus-fixed-fee, cost-plus-award- fee, or cost-plus-incentive-fee contract types (10 U.S.C 3323). This applies notwithstanding a declaration of war or the declaration by the President of a national emergency under section 201 of the National Emergencies Act (50 U.S.C. 1621) that includes the use of the Armed Forces.

5m.q: At what values does the Executive Order 14402 other-than-fixed-price justification apply?
5m.a: $100 million for DoD, $35 million for NASA, $25 million for DHS, and $10 million for all other Federal agencies — approved by the head of the agency before using a covered contract or order. Know the exceptions: multiple-award contracts are exempt — but task orders, delivery orders, and BPAs under them are not — along with contracts supporting an emergency, major disaster, or contingency operation; R&D contracts or orders; and pre-production development for a major system acquisition (16.104(e)).
5m.x: Four tiers, one rule: head-of-agency justification before going other-than-fixed-price at $100M DoD, $35M NASA, $25M DHS, $10M elsewhere. The exemption structure is the trap — the multiple-award contract is exempt but its orders and BPAs are not, so the question resurfaces at every order. R&D, emergencies, and pre-production major-system development stay out.

cite.quote: a justification is required for covered contracts and orders valued at or above— (i) $100 million, for DoD; (ii) $35 million, for NASA; (iii) $25 million, for Department of Homeland Security; or (iv) $10 million, for all other Federal agencies.

5m.q: What distinguishes a cost-plus-fixed-fee contract?
5m.a: The fixed fee does not change with actual cost — it may be adjusted only as a result of changes in the work to be performed under the contract.
5m.x: Fixed means fixed against cost — the fee moves only when the work itself changes, so CPFF pays the same fee for excellent and mediocre cost control. That is why it fits effort-based work, and why 16.101 bans its lookalike, cost-plus-a-percentage-of-cost, where fee rises as spending rises. Know which side of that line the fixed fee sits on.
d: The fee is a fixed percentage of actual allowable cost, so it rises and falls with what the contractor spends.
The fee is fixed at award but adjusted annually based on the Government's evaluation of contractor performance.
The fee never changes for any reason once the contract is awarded, even if the work itself changes.

cite.quote: A cost-plus-fixed-fee contract is a cost-reimbursement contract that includes payment of an agreed upon fixed-fee. The fixed fee does not change with actual cost but may be adjusted as a result of changes in the work to be performed under the contract.

5m.q: What elements does a fixed-price incentive (firm target) contract specify, and who absorbs cost above the price ceiling?
5m.a: A target cost, a target profit, a price ceiling (but no profit ceiling or floor), and a profit-adjustment formula. If final negotiated cost exceeds the price ceiling, the contractor absorbs the difference as a loss.
5m.x: The geometry is the answer: profit floats through the formula; price does not. Candidates flip the detail — there is no profit ceiling or floor, the ceiling is on price — and above that ceiling every dollar is the contractor's loss. That ceiling is what keeps FPIF on the fixed-price side of the line between FFP and cost-type risk.

cite.quote: A fixed-price incentive (firm target) contract specifies a target cost, a target profit, a price ceiling (but not a profit ceiling or floor), and a formula for profit adjustments. When the final cost is less than the target cost, application of the formula results in a final profit greater than the target profit; conversely, when final cost is more than target cost, application of the formula results in a final profit less than the target profit, or even a net loss.
