The trap is treating the override as routine schedule relief; it is an exception built for national-level stakes, and the finding has to read like one.

cite.quote: The head of the contracting activity, on a nondelegable basis, may authorize contract performance, upon a written finding that— (i) Contract performance will be in the best interests of the United States; or (ii) Urgent and compelling circumstances that significantly affect the interests of the United States will not permit waiting for the GAO's decision.

25m.q: Who approves a J&A above $900,000 up to $20M, and is it delegable?
25m.a: The advocate for competition. Not delegable.
25m.x: Half-credit trap: candidates name the advocate and drop 'not delegable.' Note the asymmetry — the next tier up, the head of the procuring activity, IS delegable to the general/flag-officer or above-GS-15 level, so non-delegability is specific to the advocate's tier, not a blanket rule. And officials at a higher level may always approve lower-dollar justifications; the table sets floors, not exclusive lanes.
d: The head of the procuring activity. Delegable to the flag-officer level.
The senior procurement executive. Not delegable.
The advocate for competition. Delegable in writing.

cite.quote: Advocate for competition.

unlimited.q: What two pieces make up the fee on a cost-plus-award-fee contract?
unlimited.a: A base amount fixed at inception (if used, at the contracting officer's discretion) and an award fee the contractor may earn in whole or in part to motivate excellence in cost, schedule, and technical performance — decided each evaluation period by the Fee-Determining Official on the Award-Fee Board's recommendations. DoD adds hard guardrails: base fee capped at 3 percent of the estimated cost exclusive of fee, at least 40 percent of the award fee held for the final evaluation (going lower takes nondelegable HCA approval), award-fee payments outside the end-of-period evaluation prohibited, and the FDO's rating due to the contractor within 45 calendar days of the end of the period.
unlimited.x: The FAR definition earns nothing here — the board wants the DoD guardrails a civilian-trained candidate won't have: 3 percent base-fee cap, 40 percent of award fee held for the final look (going lower is a nondelegable HCA call), no interim award-fee payments, FDO rating in 45 days. Award fee motivates future performance; pay it mid-period and the motivation is already spent.

cite.quote: A cost-plus-award-fee contract is a cost-reimbursement contract that provides a fee consisting of (1) a base amount fixed at inception of the contract, if applicable and at the discretion of the contracting officer, and (2) an award fee that the contractor may earn in whole or in part to provide motivation for excellence in the areas of cost, schedule, and technical performance.

dod.quote: The base fee must not exceed three percent of the estimated cost of the contract exclusive of the fee.

unlimited.q: By when must a UCA's definitization schedule provide for definitization?
unlimited.a: By the earlier of 180 days after the contractor submits a qualifying proposal, or the date obligated funds exceed 50 percent of the not-to-exceed price. The 180 days runs from the qualifying proposal — not from award.
unlimited.x: The clock trap: 180 days runs from the qualifying proposal, not from award — a contractor slow-rolling its proposal keeps the window from ever opening. That is exactly why the 50-percent obligation trigger exists as the second tripwire: one clock the contractor controls, one the Government does, and the earlier governs.

cite.quote: UCAs must contain definitization schedules that provide for definitization by the earlier of— (1) The date that is 180 days after the contractor submits a qualifying proposal.

unlimited.q: How much of a UCA's not-to-exceed price may be obligated before definitization?
unlimited.a: No more than 50 percent — raised to no more than 75 percent if the contractor submits a qualifying proposal before 50 percent has been obligated.
unlimited.x: 50 is the rule; 75 is a reward, not a default — it unlocks only if the qualifying proposal lands before you cross 50 percent. That is the desk leverage: the contractor who wants more obligated funding has to hand over the very proposal that starts the 180-day definitization clock.

cite.quote: The Government must not obligate more than 50 percent of the not-to-exceed price before definitization. However, if a contractor submits a qualifying proposal before 50 percent of the not-to-exceed price has been obligated by the Government, then the limitation on obligations before definitization may be increased to no more than 75 percent

unlimited.q: What definitization schedule applies to a DoD letter contract?
unlimited.a: The UCA schedule at 217.7404-3(a): definitize by the earlier of 180 days after the contractor submits a qualifying proposal (extendable up to 90 more days only by HCA-level written determination) or the point where obligations exceed 50 percent of the not-to-exceed price. R-DFARS 216.603-2(c) applies that schedule instead of the civilian baseline at 16.603-2(c) — 180 days from the letter contract or 40 percent of the work — so for a DoD contracting officer the baseline rule simply does not apply.
unlimited.x: The bait is the civilian baseline — 180 days from the letter contract, or 40 percent of the work. R-DFARS 216.603-2(c) swaps it out wholesale for the UCA schedule: 180 days from the qualifying proposal, or 50 percent of the not-to-exceed. Answering a DoD letter-contract question with the 40-percent figure is answering from the wrong book.

cite.quote: In accordance with 10 U.S.C. 3372, establish definitization schedules for letter contracts following the requirements at 217.7404-3(a) instead of the requirements at FAR 16.603-2(c).

unlimited.q: A UCA definitizes after the 180-day window from the qualifying proposal has run. What does that do to the contractor's profit?
unlimited.a: Normally the profit on a late-definitized UCA reflects the contractor's reduced cost risk for costs already incurred. But when the contracting officer definitizes after the 180-day period from the qualifying proposal, the allowed profit must accurately reflect the contractor's cost risk as it existed on the date the qualifying proposal was submitted — the Government's own delay cannot be used to ratchet profit down further. The HCA ensures it, and the risk assessment is documented in the price negotiation memorandum.
unlimited.x: The reduced-risk-reduced-profit logic normally holds — but once the Government blows the 180-day window, freezing the risk picture at the qualifying-proposal date keeps the Government from profiting off its own delay. The HCA polices it, and the risk assessment lives in the price negotiation memorandum, which is where a board will ask to see it.

cite.quote: the profit allowed on the contract must accurately reflect the cost risk of the contractor as such risk existed on the date the contractor submitted the qualifying proposal

unlimited.q: R-DFARS splits its LPTA restrictions into limitations and prohibitions. What falls on each side of the line?
unlimited.a: Limitations — avoid to the maximum extent practicable: acquisitions predominantly for information technology, cybersecurity, systems engineering and technical assistance, advanced electronic testing, or other knowledge-based professional services; personal protective equipment generally; and knowledge-based training or logistics services in contingency or other overseas operations. Prohibitions — do not use, period: PPE or aviation critical safety items where quality failure could cause combat casualties; engineering and manufacturing development for a major defense acquisition program; and auditing services. Mixing the two lists is the classic board trap — "avoid" is judgment, "do not use" is absolute.
unlimited.x: The line tracks consequence. Where LPTA merely buys bad value — IT, cyber, knowledge-based services, most PPE — it is 'avoid to the maximum extent practicable,' a judgment call you must be able to defend. Where failure costs lives or corrupts the program — combat-casualty PPE and aviation critical safety items, MDAP EMD, auditing — it is flatly banned. Know why each item sits on its side and you will never mix the lists.

cite.quote: Avoid using the lowest price technically acceptable source selection approach, to the maximum extent practicable, for acquisitions that are predominately for— (i) Information technology services, cybersecurity services, systems engineering and technical assistance services, advanced electronic testing, or other knowledge-based professional services; (ii) Items designated by the requiring activity as personal protective equipment (except see paragraph (b)(1) of this section); or (iii) Services designated by the requiring activity as knowledge-based training or logistics services in contingency operations or other operations outside the United States. (b) Prohibitions. Do not use the lowest price technically acceptable source selection approach to procure— (1) Items designated by the requiring activity as personal protective equipment or as an aviation critical safety item, for which the level of quality or failure of the equipment or item could result in combat casualties.

unlimited.q: The Government decides it will pay any fair and reasonable price for the highest quality performance, with no tradeoffs. What source selection approach is that, and how does award actually work?
unlimited.a: Highest technically rated with a fair and reasonable price. All proposals are evaluated on the non-price factors in the solicitation; the source selection authority identifies the highest technically rated proposal and only then evaluates that proposal's price for fair-and-reasonableness under subpart 15.4. If the price passes, that proposal is selected — no tradeoffs. If it does not, the SSA moves to the next highest technically rated proposal and repeats until award. The RFP must tell offerors up front that tradeoffs between price and non-price factors will not be considered.
unlimited.x: This is LPTA's mirror image: there, price wins among the technically acceptable; here, technical rank wins among the fairly priced. The discipline is in the sequencing — price is examined only after the ranking, one proposal at a time, and there is no reaching back to trade a cheaper runner-up against the leader. If the RFP never said tradeoffs were off the table, you cannot run it this way.

cite.quote: If the highest technically rated proposal’s price is fair and reasonable, the proposal is selected for award. If the price is not fair and reasonable, the source selection authority must determine the next highest technically rated proposal and evaluate whether the price is fair and reasonable in accordance with subpart 15.4. This process continues until a contract is awarded to the highest technically rated responsible offeror with a fair and reasonable price.

unlimited.q: Who is the source selection authority by default, and what must the SSA lock down before the RFP goes out?
unlimited.a: The contracting officer is the SSA unless the agency head appoints another individual for a particular acquisition or group of acquisitions. Before RFP release the SSA approves the source selection approach or acquisition plan, and establishes an evaluation team tailored to the acquisition with contracting, legal, logistics, technical, and other expertise. The SSA must ensure proposals are evaluated solely on the RFP's factors and subfactors, and may reject all proposals when that serves the Government's best interest. In DoD, high-dollar acquisitions also require SSA approval of a source selection plan before the solicitation issues.
unlimited.x: Start with the default: the contracting officer IS the SSA until the agency head names someone else — candidates who assume every source selection gets an appointed senior official miss the easy half. The senior half is timing: approach approved, tailored team stood up, and in DoD high-dollar work the source selection plan approved before the solicitation issues, not after.

cite.quote: Agency heads are responsible for source selection. A contracting officer is designated as the source selection authority (SSA), unless the agency head appoints another individual for a particular acquisition or group of acquisitions.

dod.quote: For high-dollar value and other acquisitions, as prescribed by agency procedures, the source selection authority must approve a source selection plan before the solicitation is issued.

unlimited.topic: Certified Cost or Pricing Data & Proposal Analysis
unlimited.q: How are forward pricing rate agreement rates used once established?
unlimited.a: As the bases for pricing all contracts, modifications, and other contractual actions performed during the period the agreement covers; conditions affecting the agreement's validity must be promptly reported to the administrative contracting officer. In DoD the rates are not optional: use FPRA rates whenever they are available unless the head of the contracting activity waives them on a case-by-case basis — and advise the ACO of each case waived.
unlimited.x: An FPRA's whole value is negotiating rates once and applying them everywhere — relitigating them per action spends what the agreement bought. In DoD, 'available' means mandatory: skipping FPRA rates takes a case-by-case HCA waiver, with the ACO advised each time. And validity is perishable — report anything that undercuts the agreement promptly, because stale agreed rates are worse than none.

cite.quote: Contracting officers will use FPRA rates as bases for pricing all contracts, modifications, and other contractual actions to be performed during the period covered by the agreement.

dod.quote: Use forward pricing rate agreement (FPRA) rates when such rates are available, unless waived on a case-by-case basis by the head of the contracting activity.

unlimited.q: What are DoD's customary progress payment rates — and when should progress payments not be the first choice?
unlimited.a: 80 percent for large business concerns and 90 percent for small business concerns — the same rates apply to contracts carrying foreign military sales requirements. Progress payments are not the default, though: performance-based payments are the preferred financing method when practical and the contractor agrees, and in DoD they must be conditioned on the achievement of performance outcomes, never on costs incurred.
unlimited.x: Two traps in one card: reversing the split — small business gets the higher 90 — and treating progress payments as the default. Performance-based payments come first when practical and the contractor agrees, and DoD ties them to performance outcomes, never costs incurred. The FMS mention is there because candidates guess foreign content changes the rates; it does not.

cite.quote: The customary progress payment rates for DoD contracts, including contracts that contain foreign military sales (FMS) requirements, are 80 percent for large business concerns and 90 percent for small business concerns.

unlimited.q: When does the Government get unlimited rights in technical data?
unlimited.a: When the item, component, or process was or will be developed exclusively with Government funds — plus categories like form, fit, and function data; data necessary for installation, operation, maintenance, or training purposes other than detailed manufacturing or process data (that OMIT carve-out is the most-fought-over line in DoD data rights — dropping it flips the answer); and publicly available data.
unlimited.x: OMIT data buys operation and maintenance, not a build-to-print package — the 'other than detailed manufacturing or process data' parenthetical is where reprocurement strategies go to die. Contractors read that carve-out for a living; assume maintenance data equals manufacturing data and you have promised a sustainment competition the data cannot support.

cite.quote: The Government obtains unlimited rights in technical data, computer software, or computer software documentation that are— (1) Technical data related to an item, component, or process which has been or will be developed exclusively with Government funds; (2) Studies, analyses, test data, or similar data produced in the performance of a contract when the study, analysis, test, or similar work was specified as an element of performance; (3) Created exclusively with Government funds in the performance of a contract that does not require the development, manufacture, construction, or production of items, components, or processes; (4) Form, fit, and function data; (5) Necessary for installation, operation, maintenance, or training purposes (other than detailed manufacturing or process data);

unlimited.q: Mixed Government and private funding produced the technical data. What rights arise, and for how long?
unlimited.a: Government purpose rights. The period is negotiable with a five-year period nominal, and it begins upon execution of the contract, subcontract, or similar instrument that required the development — not at delivery. When it expires the Government's rights become unlimited, including the right to authorize others to use the data or software for commercial purposes.
unlimited.x: Two probes hide here: five years is nominal, not fixed — either side may seek a different period — and the clock starts at execution of the instrument that required the development, not at delivery, so data arriving late in a long effort can reach you with the period nearly spent. The payoff is expiration: rights go unlimited, commercial licensing included, so calendar management is the whole game.

cite.quote: The period during which government purpose rights are effective is negotiable. A five year period is nominal. Either the Government or the contractor may request a different period. (3) The government purpose rights period begins upon execution of the contract, subcontract, or similar contractual instrument that required the development. Upon expiration of the Government rights period, the Government has unlimited rights in the data or software including the right to authorize others to use the data or software for commercial purposes.

unlimited.q: Development was exclusively at private expense. What rights does the Government get in the technical data versus the noncommercial software?
unlimited.a: Limited rights in the technical data; restricted rights in the noncommercial computer software. Limited rights data cannot be used, released, or disclosed outside the Government without the asserting contractor's permission — except when necessary for emergency repair and overhaul, to a covered Government support contractor, or to a foreign government (other than detailed manufacturing or process data) for evaluational or informational purposes in the interest of the United States.
unlimited.x: Hold the vocabulary under pressure: limited rights ride on technical data, restricted rights on noncommercial software — swapping the labels is the reflex miss. Then know the three doors out of the no-release rule: emergency repair and overhaul, covered Government support contractors, and foreign governments minus the detailed manufacturing or process data.

cite.quote: Do not use, release, or disclose data in which the Government has limited rights outside the Government without the permission of the contractor asserting the restriction except when it is— (i) Necessary for emergency repair and overhaul; (ii) To a covered Government support contractor; or (iii) To a foreign government, other than detailed manufacturing or process data, when use, release, or disclosure is in the interest of the United States and is required for evaluational or informational purposes.

unlimited.q: Delivered technical data arrives marked with restrictive legends the program doubts. What is the Government's recourse, and how long does it have?
unlimited.a: A contractor's assertions do not, by themselves, determine the Government's rights. Review asserted restrictions before accepting the deliverable, and the contracting officer may challenge an assertion when reasonable grounds exist to believe it is invalid — within six years after final payment or six years after delivery of the data or software, whichever is later. Commercial products and services are presumed developed exclusively at private expense whether or not the contractor submits a justification, so challenging one takes specifically stated reasonable grounds — and on that commercial presumption a failure to respond to the challenge notice cannot be the sole basis for a final decision denying the restriction.
unlimited.x: Markings are assertions, not adjudications — but the challenge power decays: six years from final payment or from delivery, whichever is later, so review restrictions at acceptance, not when the sustainment fight starts. The commercial layer is the senior probe: private-expense development is presumed, challenges need specifically stated grounds, and the contractor's silence alone cannot sink a commercial restriction.

cite.quote: Challenge assertions within six years after final payment under the contract or six years after delivery of the data or software, whichever is later.

unlimited.q: A contractor helped write the work statement for a competitive services acquisition. May it compete to perform the services?
unlimited.a: Not generally. A contractor that prepares or assists in preparing the work statement may not supply the system or services unless it is the sole source, it participated in the development and design work, or more than one contractor was involved in preparing the work statement.
unlimited.x: The reflex is 'wrote the SOW, can't bid — period.' The rule is narrower, and the exceptions explain it: the concern is a single author quietly slanting the ground rules toward itself. Sole source (no competition to slant), genuine development-and-design participation, or multiple hands on the work statement each drain that concern, and with it the bar.

cite.quote: that contractor may not supply the system, major components of the system, or the services unless— (i) It is the sole source; (ii) It has participated in the development and design work; or (iii) More than one contractor has been involved in preparing the work statement.

unlimited.q: How long does the contracting officer have to issue a final decision on a certified claim over $100,000?
unlimited.a: 60 days after receiving the certified claim — or, within those 60 days, notify the contractor of the time within which a decision will be issued. One senior-level escape hatch: if a claim over $100,000 carries a defective certification, the contracting officer has no obligation to render a final decision at all, provided the contractor is notified in writing, within 60 days of receiving the claim, of the reasons the attempted certification was found defective.
unlimited.x: Everyone knows the 60-day rule; the panel is fishing for the defective-certification branch. A bad certification on a claim over $100,000 lifts the duty to decide entirely — but only if you tell the contractor in writing, within 60 days of receipt, why the certification failed. Skip that notice and the escape hatch never opened.

cite.quote: For claims over $100,000, 60 days after receiving a certified claim; provided, however, that if a decision will not be issued within 60 days, the contracting officer must notify the contractor, within that period, of the time within which a decision will be issued.

unlimited.q: The contracting officer never issues a decision within the required time. What happens to the claim?
unlimited.a: The failure is deemed a decision denying the claim, and it authorizes the contractor to file an appeal or suit.
unlimited.x: The trap is thinking Government silence protects the Government — it does not stall the contractor, it releases them. Nothing is granted, nothing lapses; the appeal rights simply ripen. At the desk: if you cannot decide in time, use the notice option and say when you will — the rule exists so silence never becomes the record.
d: The claim is deemed granted, and the Government must pay it.
The claim lapses, and the contractor must resubmit it with a new certification.
The contractor must wait for the decision before it may appeal or file suit.

cite.quote: Any failure of the contracting officer to issue a decision within the required time periods will be deemed a decision by the contracting officer denying the claim and will authorize the contractor to file an appeal or suit on the claim.

unlimited.q: The Government terminates a contract for convenience. How does the contractor get paid, and on what clock?
unlimited.a: Through settlement with the termination contracting officer. The final settlement proposal is due within one year of the termination date unless the TCO allows more time, and it covers all cost elements including subcontract settlements and proposed profit. The TCO negotiates a fair and prompt settlement where possible, settling by determination only when agreement fails; a no-cost settlement closes it out when no costs were incurred or the contractor waives them and nothing is owed the Government. Partial payments may flow before settlement when the contract authorizes them. And if a default termination is later found improper or excusable, the parties' rights and obligations convert to those of a convenience termination.
unlimited.x: The architecture: negotiated settlement is the goal, settlement by determination the fallback, no-cost the clean exit when nothing was incurred. The one-year proposal clock belongs to the contractor; extending it belongs to the TCO. And keep the conversion rule loaded — a default termination found improper does not unwind, it becomes a convenience termination, which is precisely why you paper a default so carefully.

cite.quote: The final settlement proposal must be submitted within one year from the termination date, unless the TCO allows more time.

unlimited.q: Transfers of Government contracts are statutorily prohibited. When does recognizing a successor in interest require a novation agreement — and when is a novation unnecessary?
unlimited.a: A novation is the vehicle when it is in the Government's interest and the third party's interest arises from the transfer of all the contractor's assets, or the entire portion involved in performing the contract. It is unnecessary for a change in ownership by stock purchase with no legal change in the contracting party, where that party remains in control of the assets and keeps performing — the ownership changed, the contractor did not. A name-only change with rights and obligations unaffected takes a change-of-name agreement instead.
unlimited.x: Ask what moved: the assets or the stock. Assets to a new performing entity — novation, and only if the Government's interest supports recognizing it. Stock to new owners while the same legal entity holds the assets and performs — no novation, however total the change upstairs. The DoD follow-on probe is restructuring costs: barred on novated contracts without an audit, a reduced-cost determination, and an advance agreement with a cost ceiling.

cite.quote: A novation agreement is unnecessary when there is a change in the ownership of a contractor as a result of a stock purchase, with no legal change in the contracting party, and when that contracting party remains in control of the assets and is the party performing the contract.

dod.quote: Restructuring costs are prohibited on novated contracts unless there is an audit of the restructuring proposal; a determination by the contracting officer of overall reduced costs to DoD/NASA; and an Advance Agreement setting forth a cumulative cost ceiling for restructuring projects and the period to which such costs shall be assigned

unlimited.q: Suspension of work versus a stop-work order — which contracts, and what happens to profit?
unlimited.a: A suspension of work applies to construction and architect-engineer contracts; if unreasonable, the contractor may claim increased costs of performance excluding profit. Stop-work orders are for negotiated fixed-price or cost-reimbursement supply, R&D, and service contracts, require approval above the contracting officer, and are never a substitute for a termination notice.
unlimited.x: Sort by contract family first — suspension is a construction and architect-engineer creature; stop-work belongs to negotiated supply, R&D, and services. Then the two probes: an unreasonable suspension pays increased costs but never profit, and a stop-work order needs approval above the contracting officer because it is a pause, not a soft termination — using it to dodge a termination notice is the named abuse.

cite.quote: A suspension of work under a construction or architect-engineer contract may be ordered by the contracting officer for a reasonable period of time. If the suspension is unreasonable, the contractor may submit a written claim for increases in the cost of performance, excluding profit.

unlimited.q: A final determination disapproves one of a contractor's business systems. Which systems are covered, and what happens to the contractor's payments?
unlimited.a: Six systems: accounting, earned value management, estimating, material management and accounting, property management, and purchasing. On a final determination with a notice to withhold, the contracting officer withholds 5 percent from progress payments and performance-based payments and directs a 5 percent withhold on interim cost vouchers until all material weaknesses are corrected. An acceptable corrective action plan submitted within 45 days and effectively implemented drops the withhold to 2 percent. Ceilings: 5 percent for material weaknesses in any single system, 10 percent across multiple systems.
unlimited.x: There is no civilian analogue — candidates raised on the FAR alone do not know this lever exists. Hold the numbers: 5 percent on a final determination, 2 once an acceptable corrective action plan lands within 45 days, ceilings of 5 for a single system and 10 across systems. The withhold is leverage, not punishment — it makes material weaknesses expensive until they are fixed, and it releases when they are.

cite.quote: the Contracting Officer will withhold 5 percent of amounts due from progress payments and performance-based payments, and direct the Contractor, in writing, to withhold 5 percent from its billings on interim cost vouchers on cost-reimbursement, labor-hour, and time-and-materials contracts

unlimited.q: Are liquidated damages a penalty for late delivery?
unlimited.a: No. They are not punitive and not negative performance incentives — the rate must be a reasonable forecast of just compensation for the harm caused by late delivery or untimely performance, used when timely performance is critical and actual damage would be hard to prove. For DoD construction the liquidated-damages clause (52.211-12) is mandatory in every contract exceeding $900,000 — except cost-plus-fixed-fee contracts or where the contractor cannot control the pace of the work — and optional at or below that figure.
unlimited.x: 'Penalty' is the disqualifying word. A rate untethered from a reasonable forecast of actual harm is legally a penalty and will not survive, which is why the forecast discipline matters more than the arithmetic. The DoD layer: construction over $900,000 makes the clause mandatory — unless it is CPFF or the contractor cannot control the pace, the two cases where damages-for-delay logic has nothing to grip.

cite.quote: Liquidated damages are not punitive and are not negative performance incentives (see 16.403-2). Liquidated damages are used to compensate the Government for probable damages. Therefore, the liquidated damages rate must be a reasonable forecast of just compensation for the harm that is caused by late delivery or untimely performance of the particular contract.

dod.quote: Insert the clause at FAR 52.211-12, Liquidated Damages—Construction, in all construction contracts exceeding $900,000, except cost-plus-fixed-fee contracts or contracts where the contractor cannot control the pace of the work. Use of the clause in contracts of $900,000 or less is optional.

unlimited.q: Under which contract types is the contractor generally not held liable for loss of Government property?
unlimited.a: Cost-reimbursement, time-and-material, labor-hour, and fixed-price contracts awarded on the basis of certified cost or pricing data. DoD extends the shield to negotiated fixed-price contracts awarded on a basis other than certified cost or pricing data — so in DoD practice the carve-out reaches essentially every negotiated fixed-price award, leaving sealed-bid fixed-price as the main place full liability survives.
unlimited.x: The civilian list reads like an exception; the DoD extension makes it the rule — negotiated fixed-price awards without certified data get the same shield, which is nearly every negotiated award there is. So invert the working assumption: in DoD practice, full contractor liability for Government property is the rarity, surviving mainly in sealed bidding. The Government self-insures rather than paying every contractor to price the risk.

cite.quote: Generally, contractors are not held liable for loss of Government property under the following types of contracts: (1) Cost-reimbursement contracts. (2) Time-and-material contracts. (3) Labor-hour contracts. (4) Fixed-price contracts awarded on the basis of submission of certified cost or pricing data.

dod.quote: In addition to the contract types listed at FAR 45.104, contractors are not held liable for loss of Government property under negotiated fixed-price contracts awarded on a basis other than submission of certified cost or pricing data.

unlimited.q: On a small business set-aside for services, how much may the prime pay to subcontractors that are not similarly situated?
unlimited.a: No more than 50 percent of the amount the Government pays for contract performance. The limit is also 50 percent for supplies, 85 percent for general construction, and 75 percent for special trade construction — and on all three of those the cost of materials is excluded from the base. Only services carries no materials exclusion.
unlimited.x: The hinge is ‘similarly situated’ — payments to subcontractors holding the same program status do not count against the cap at all, which is what makes small-business teaming on set-asides work. Then keep the four figures straight: 50 services, 50 supplies, 85 general construction, 75 special trade. Watch the materials exclusion: 52.219-14(e) attaches “excluding the cost of materials” to supplies, general construction AND special trade — not to services. Boards swap the construction numbers to see who has memorized versus who is guessing.

cite.quote: Services (except construction), it will not pay more than 50 percent of the amount paid by the Government for contract performance to subcontractors that are not similarly situated entities.

unlimited.q: What two-part test makes a manufactured end product "domestic" under the Buy American statute?
unlimited.a: The article must be manufactured in the United States, and the cost of domestic components must exceed the applicable content threshold — 60 percent, rising to 65 percent for 2024-2028 deliveries and 75 percent from 2029 (with a separate less-than-5-percent foreign iron and steel rule for predominantly iron or steel products). Per 41 U.S.C. 1907 the domestic content test is waived for COTS items — though not for the iron/steel test, except COTS fasteners. For DoD, the content test counts U.S. and qualifying country components toward the threshold.
unlimited.x: The escalator — 60, 65 through 2028, 75 from 2029 — is the memory test; the carve-outs are the judgment test. The COTS waiver kills the content test but not the iron-and-steel test (fasteners excepted), and DoD counts qualifying-country components toward content. Manufacture in the United States is the first gate regardless — no content math rescues an article manufactured abroad.

cite.quote: The article must be manufactured in the United States; and (2) (i) Except for an end product that consists wholly or predominantly of iron or steel or a combination of both, the cost of domestic components must exceed 60 percent of the cost of all the components, except that the percentage is 65 percent for items delivered in calendar years 2024 through 2028 and 75 percent for items delivered starting in calendar year 2029. But see paragraph (d) of this section. In accordance with 41 U.S.C. 1907, this domestic content test of the Buy American statute has been waived for acquisitions of COTS items (but see paragraph (a)(2)(ii) of this section).

dod.quote: the cost of its U.S. and qualifying country components exceeds 60 percent of the cost of all its components, except that the percentage will be 65 percent for items delivered in calendar years 2024 through 2028 and 75 percent for items delivered starting in calendar year 2029

unlimited.q: What does the Berry Amendment restrict DoD from buying unless it is domestic?
unlimited.a: Items such as food, clothing, tents, cotton and other natural fiber products, wool, canvas products, and hand or measuring tools — they must have been grown, reprocessed, reused, or produced in the United States unless an exception applies.
unlimited.x: Do not blur Berry into Buy American. Buy American runs on content percentages and waivers; Berry names categories — food, clothing, tents, natural fibers, hand tools — and prohibits outright unless a listed exception applies. It is DoD-only and it reaches components, not just end products: foreign fiber in a domestically sewn garment still fails. When a Berry item is in the buy, the analysis is exception-hunting, not math.

cite.quote: do not acquire— (1) Any of the following items, either as end products or components, unless the items have been grown, reprocessed, reused, or produced in the United States: (i) Food.

unlimited.q: In an acquisition covered by the WTO Government Procurement Agreement, what end products may be acquired?
unlimited.a: Only U.S.-made or designated country end products (or U.S. or designated country services), unless offers for them are not received or are insufficient to fulfill the requirements. DoD narrows the field twice: trade agreements apply only to end products in the product service groups enumerated at 225.401-70 — if the end product is not in a listed group, the trade agreements do not apply — and in covered acquisitions DoD buys only U.S.-made, qualifying country, or designated country end products unless such offers are not received or are insufficient, or a national interest waiver is granted.
unlimited.x: The senior answer starts one step earlier than the civilian one: check the 225.401-70 list first — if the end product's group is not on it, trade agreements simply do not apply in DoD and you are back to standard foreign-acquisition analysis. On the list, the field narrows to U.S.-made, qualifying country, or designated country, and the outs are exactly two: insufficient offers, or a national interest waiver.

cite.quote: in acquisitions covered by the WTO GPA, acquire only U.S.-made or designated country end products or U.S. or designated country services, unless offers for such end products or services are either not received or are insufficient to fulfill the requirements.

dod.quote: If an end product is not in one of the listed groups, the trade agreements do not apply.

unlimited.q: What contract types must be used for awards resulting from a commercial solutions opening?
unlimited.a: Fixed-price type contracts, including fixed-price incentive. A CSO is a general solicitation for innovative commercial products or services under 10 U.S.C. 3458, and what it buys is treated as commercial.
unlimited.x: The instinct for unproven work is cost-type; the CSO breaks it deliberately. What a CSO buys is treated as commercial, so fixed-price — FPI included — is mandatory notwithstanding FAR 12.104. That is the discipline in the vehicle: the Government is buying an innovative commercial solution, not underwriting its development. If the risk genuinely demands cost-type, the CSO was the wrong instrument.

cite.quote: Notwithstanding FAR 12.104, contracting officers must use fixed-price type contracts, including fixed-price incentive contracts, for awards resulting from a CSO.

unlimited.q: How can a follow-on production contract from an other-transaction prototype project skip a new competition?
unlimited.a: It is excepted from the competition requirements when the OT agreement for the prototype, awarded under 10 U.S.C. 4022, included provisions for a follow-on production contract and the statutory conditions are documented.
unlimited.x: The exception is not claimed at production — it was earned at prototype award. The 10 U.S.C. 4022 agreement must have carried the follow-on production provisions, and the statutory conditions must be documented. An OT that is silent on follow-on production buys no pass from part 6 later. The competition decision was really made at prototype solicitation; senior review of an OT should read it that way.

cite.quote: Also excepted from this part are follow-on production contracts for products developed pursuant to the “other transactions” authority of 10 U.S.C. 4022 for prototype projects

unlimited.q: When is an Earned Value Management System required?
unlimited.a: The civilian baseline is major acquisitions for development, per OMB Circular A-11. DoD replaces that wholesale with thresholds: on cost or incentive contracts, EIA-748 compliance is required at $50 million or more, and at $100 million or more the contractor must have a system the cognizant Federal agency has validated against EIA-748. Below $50 million, applying EVM is optional and a risk-based decision; on firm-fixed-price contracts of any value it is discouraged (waiver procedures apply); and the subpart does not apply to contracts primarily for software.
unlimited.x: The civilian answer — major acquisitions for development, per A-11 — earns nothing at a DoD board, because DoD replaced it with hard numbers: EIA-748 compliance at $50 million, an agency-validated system at $100 million, risk-based and optional below $50 million. The judgment tails matter as much: EVM on firm-fixed-price is discouraged at any value, and software-primary contracts sit outside the subpart entirely.

cite.quote: In accordance with OMB Circular A-11, agencies must require an Earned Value Management System (EVMS) in major acquisitions for development.

dod.quote: For cost or incentive contracts and subcontracts valued at $50 million or more, the clause at 252.234-7999, Earned Value Management System, requires the contractor’s earned value management system to comply with the guidelines in Electronic Industries Alliance Standard 748, Earned Value Management Systems

sat.scenario: The comm squadron sends you a $180K purchase request for noncommercial network test sets. Stapled to it is a quote from TechServe, and the requirements owner is direct about it: "Award to TechServe — they did the site survey, they know our racks, and we already told them it's coming." The PR narrative was written around TechServe's product sheet.
sat.ask: The customer says the vendor is already picked and the quote is attached. Walk me through what you do with this purchase request.
sat.script: This is a competition question wearing a customer-service disguise. RFO 13.101 requires me to promote competition to the maximum extent practicable at this tier — a quote the customer solicited isn't competition, and "we already told them" isn't a determination. My move is a candid conversation: incumbent knowledge can earn TechServe the award through evaluation, not before it. Then I run the normal play — set-aside check under RFO 13.102, scrub the requirement so it isn't written around one product sheet, and solicit quotes from at least three sources per RFO 12.201-1. If the customer truly believes only TechServe can perform, that's a determination and findings under RFO 13.101(b), and I own that decision, not the requiring activity.

follow_ups.q: The customer says three quotes is just paperwork — TechServe wins anyway. Can you sole-source it?
follow_ups.h: There is a door for single-source at this tier. What has to be true to walk through it?
follow_ups.d: RFO 13.101(b): the contracting officer may solicit from a single source based on a D&F that only one source is reasonably available — the examples are urgency, exclusive licensing agreements, brand-name, industrial mobilization. "They know our setup" and "we promised them" are on nobody's list. The trap is letting the requiring activity's pre-selection masquerade as a one-source market. The D&F is the CO's determination, supported by findings, and a weak one invites protest and audit findings.

follow_ups.q: What would change if this requirement were over the SAT?
follow_ups.h: The streamlined justification has a heavier cousin.
follow_ups.d: Above the SAT you leave Part 13 entirely — full competition rules apply, and restricting competition takes a written justification and approval under RFO 6.104, with technical and requirements personnel certifying their supporting data as accurate and complete. A good answer contrasts the tiers: below the SAT a D&F under 13.101(b); above it a J&A. The trap is the candidate who thinks below-SAT means no justification at all — the D&F is still a written, supportable decision.

follow_ups.q: Where does small business fit in your plan for this buy?
follow_ups.h: At this dollar value the answer is not discretionary.
follow_ups.d: RFO 13.102: noncommercial acquisitions above the MPT and at or below the SAT must be set aside for small business concerns. So before anyone debates TechServe, the real first question is whether TechServe is even eligible to compete. If they're a large business, the customer's hand-picked awardee may be out of the lane altogether — which is exactly why the CO runs the process front-to-back instead of papering a done deal.

cites.quote: Agencies must promote competition to the maximum extent practicable when procuring noncommercial products and services valued at or below the SAT.
Acquisitions of supplies or services that have an anticipated dollar value above the MPT, but at or below the SAT, must be set aside for small business concerns (see part 19).
Solicit quotations from at least three sources

sat.scenario: Your RFQ for $95K of noncommercial shop equipment closed Friday at 1400. Monday morning you find a quote that hit the org box at 1427 Friday — 27 minutes late — and it's $8K below the next lowest. Your buyer wants to toss it: "Late is late. That's the rule."
sat.ask: Your buyer says the low quote is late, so it's out. Is she right? What do you do?
sat.script: She's applying the wrong rulebook. Under simplified procedures, RFO 13.202 tells me to exercise good business judgment in deciding whether to accept a quotation received after the due date — there is no automatic late-is-late rule here. The legal footing matters: under RFO 12.201-1, neither a quotation nor the purchase order forms a binding contract, so a quote is market information, not an offer I'm barred from touching. My judgment factors: has award already been decided, would accepting prejudice the quoters who met the deadline, is the process still fair, and what's the value to the Government — $8K on $95K is real money. Whatever I decide, RFO 13.203(b) says the file gets a written description of the procedures I used, so the reasoning is on paper either way.

follow_ups.q: Why doesn't the strict late-offer discipline from negotiated procurement apply here?
follow_ups.h: Start with what a quotation legally is.
follow_ups.d: RFO 12.201-1(b): a quotation is not an offer — the purchase order the Government issues is the offer, and no contract exists until the supplier accepts it. Because quotes carry no contract-law formality, RFO 12.203(c) gives the CO broad discretion: quotation evaluation is expressly not subject to Part 15 or 14 procedures. The trap is the candidate who recites late-proposal doctrine from negotiated acquisitions — importing that rigidity into SAP is exactly the burden simplified procedures exist to shed.

follow_ups.q: What facts would push you to refuse the late quote?
follow_ups.h: Think about fairness to the vendors who made the deadline.
follow_ups.d: A strong answer names real limits on the discretion: award decision already made or announced, evidence the late quoter gained information the others lacked, a vendor who habitually quotes late to see the field, or a delay long enough that acceptance starts looking like a reopened competition. Good business judgment cuts both ways — RFO 13.202 licenses acceptance, it doesn't compel it. The trap is treating discretion as "always take the low number."

follow_ups.q: How do you paper this file?
follow_ups.h: Part 13 tells you exactly what the award file contains.
follow_ups.d: RFO 13.203(b): include in the contract file a written description of the procedures used in awarding the purchase order and the number of quotations received. For a judgment call like a late quote, the description should say what arrived when, what I decided, and why the process stayed fair. Thin files are where reasonable judgment calls go to die in an audit.

cites.quote: Exercise good business judgment in deciding whether or not to accept a quotation received after the due date or time.
Neither a quotation nor the purchase order issued by the Government in response to a quotation form a binding contract.
Include in the contract file a written description of the procedures used in awarding the purchase order and the number of quotations received.

sat.scenario: Two months ago the vehicle maintenance shop chief signed a vendor "service agreement" for hydraulic lift repairs — $38K. The lifts are fixed, the vendor is invoicing, finance bounced the invoice for lack of a contract, and the package landed on your desk with a sticky note: "Please fix."
sat.ask: The work is done, the price looks fine, and the unit needs this vendor paid. How do you fix it?
sat.script: This is an unauthorized commitment, and I say that out loud before anything else — RFO 1.402-1: only contracting officers may sign contracts on behalf of the Government, and a shop chief's signature bound nothing. My phone-a-friend is Legal, immediately. Then I work RFO 1.405: the shop chief writes the facts down, and I test the ratification criteria — the Government accepted the work and benefited, the action would have been proper if a CO had done it, I can determine the price fair and reasonable, funds were available when the commitment was made and still are, Legal concurs, and the ratifying official actually holds contractual authority. Package goes to the right approval level. Then the part that actually fixes anything: training that unit on who can obligate the Government, because ratification is a cleanup, not a process.

follow_ups.q: Who can ratify this, exactly?
follow_ups.h: There's a floor below which the authority cannot go.
follow_ups.d: RFO 1.405(b): the head of the contracting activity may ratify, and agencies may delegate — but cannot delegate below the level of the chief of the contracting office. A strong candidate knows the floor cold and adds the design logic: ratification is deliberately elevated and independent, so the person who created the mess, or their chain, never blesses it themselves. The trap is answering "the CO ratifies" — a line contracting officer processing the package is not the ratifying official.

follow_ups.q: What if the price turns out high, or funds weren't actually available back in the spring?
follow_ups.h: The criteria are conjunctive. What happens when one fails?
follow_ups.d: Then it isn't ratifiable — every RFO 1.405(c) criterion must hold, including a fair and reasonable price and funds available both at the time of the commitment and now. RFO 1.405(d) is the exit: nonratifiable actions may be resolved under 31 U.S.C. 3702 or subpart 50.1. The trap is treating ratification as an automatic payment fix; the vendor's path to money isn't guaranteed, which is a point worth making loudly to the unit that caused it.

follow_ups.q: The shop chief says the vendor should have known he wasn't a contracting officer. Does that matter?
follow_ups.h: Look at the definition — whose lack of authority makes it a UC?
follow_ups.d: RFO 1.405(a) defines the unauthorized commitment: an agreement that is not binding solely because the Government representative lacked authority to make it. The vendor's diligence doesn't change the classification — contractors deal with the Government at their peril when the signer holds no warrant, which is precisely why the Government isn't bound. But the Government took the benefit, so ratification is the equitable route. The mature answer adds RFO 1.405(b)(1): agencies should act to avoid ratifications — prevention is the CO's real deliverable here.

cites.quote: Only contracting officers may sign, administer, or terminate contracts on behalf of the Government.
Unauthorized commitment means an agreement that is not binding solely because the Government representative who made it lacked the authority to enter into that agreement on behalf of the Government.
Agencies cannot delegate this authority below the level of the chief of the contracting office.

sat.scenario: The civil engineer flight sends a $140K noncommercial purchase request for lift-station pumps specifying "Brand X only — no substitutes." The stated reason: "Everything else in the plant is Brand X." No salient characteristics, no engineering analysis. Your market research turns up two other manufacturers whose pumps claim full compatibility.
sat.ask: Your customer insists it's Brand X or nothing. How do you proceed?
sat.script: Brand-name is a restriction on competition, so the customer's preference is the start of my analysis, not the end of it. First I test the premise: RFO 13.101 makes maximum-practicable competition the rule at this tier, and my market research already shows two claimed equals — so I push the engineers to give me salient characteristics for a brand-name-or-equal description, which usually dissolves the problem. If the technical case for Brand X-only survives — real interface, sustainment, or standardization facts — then RFO 13.101(b) is the vehicle: a determination and findings that only one source is reasonably available, with brand-name expressly among the examples. Either way the decision is documented and it's mine. What I won't do is launder a preference into a specification.

follow_ups.q: The engineer signs a memo saying only Brand X works. Is that enough?
follow_ups.h: Whose determination is a D&F?
follow_ups.d: No — it's an input. RFO 1.501: a D&F is a special form of written approval, a determination supported by findings covering each requirement of the regulation. The engineer supplies facts I can test — interface constraints, failure history, the cost of mixed fleets — and I make the determination. A strong candidate says plainly: technical advice feeds the decision; it doesn't replace the contracting officer's ownership of it. The trap is the CO as stenographer, filing the memo and calling it findings.

follow_ups.q: Same pumps, but they're commercial products under Part 12. What changes?
follow_ups.h: Part 12 has its own documentation line for this exact move.
follow_ups.d: RFO 12.102: for commercial acquisitions at or below the SAT, document the decision that only one source is available and the basis for it; over the SAT it escalates to a written justification per 6.104. So the discipline survives the commercial determination — only the paperwork's shape changes. Good answers also catch that brand-name-without-equal is called out by name in 12.102 as a restriction that must be documented.

follow_ups.q: You're in DoD. Anything extra ride along with a brand-name description?
follow_ups.h: There's a statute DoD implements on exactly this.
follow_ups.d: R-DFARS 212.102-70(b), implementing section 888(a) of the FY17 NDAA: the documentation addressed in 12.102 is required to use brand name or equal descriptions or proprietary specifications. That's the pattern worth naming for the board — where the streamlined baseline relaxes, DoD statute frequently keeps the documentation duty alive. The weak answer stops at the baseline rule and never checks the supplement.

cites.quote: Contracting officers may solicit from a single source based on a determination and findings (see subpart 1.5) that only one source is reasonably available (e.g., urgency, exclusive licensing agreements, brand-name or industrial mobilization).
For acquisitions valued at or below the simplified acquisition threshold (SAT), document the decision that only one source is available and the basis for the decision.
the documentation addressed in FAR 12.102 is required to use brand name or equal descriptions or proprietary specifications and standards.

sat.scenario: A program manager hands you a $200K purchase request for ruggedized tablets and a fleet-management application — the same package sold to trucking companies, lightly configured for the unit. He's already labeled it: "Part 13 simplified buy, it's under $350K."
sat.ask: He's under the SAT, so he says Part 13 it is. Is he right? Walk me through your gate checks.
sat.script: He's confused the dollar gate with the commerciality gate. RFO 13.001(a) says Part 13 may be used only if no commercial products or services can satisfy the need — and tablets plus a fleet app sold to the trucking industry are about as commercial as it gets. RFO 10.001(f) points the same direction: procure commercial to the maximum extent practicable, and my market research documents that determination. So this rides Part 12, whose own simplified procedures under RFO 12.201-1 run up to $9 million — well past this buy. Second gate before I move: required sources under Part 8, per 13.001(a)(2) — inventories, excess, AbilityOne. The dollar value picks thresholds and clauses; market research picks the part.

follow_ups.q: Why does it matter which part you use if the procedures feel similar?
follow_ups.h: Think about what changes in the resulting order.
follow_ups.d: The parts carry different clause architectures and different postaward machinery — RFO 13.204(c) flatly prohibits using the Part 12 clauses (52.212-1, -2, -4) in noncommercial acquisitions, and the reverse mismatch buries a commercial vendor under noncommercial terms it never agreed to price. Wrong-part awards create clause conflicts on inspection, termination, and payment that surface exactly when something goes wrong. The strong candidate frames part selection as a legal-effect decision, not a filing preference.

follow_ups.q: What's the other applicability gate in 13.001 besides commerciality?
follow_ups.h: Someone may already be required to supply this.
follow_ups.d: RFO 13.001(a)(2): the supplies or services must not be available from a required source under Part 8 — agency inventories, excess from other agencies, Federal Prison Industries, AbilityOne Procurement List. A good answer runs the gates in order: required sources, then commerciality, then method. The trap is jumping straight to "how do I buy" before "may I buy it on the open market at all."

follow_ups.q: Where does the $9 million figure come from, and what's the classic mistake around it?
follow_ups.h: Simplified is bigger than the SAT — in one lane.
follow_ups.d: RFO 12.201-1(a): for commercial acquisitions valued up to $9 million, issue an RFQ followed by a purchase order — that's the commercial simplified lane. The classic mistake is treating $350K as the ceiling on all simplified buying. The SAT bounds Part 13's noncommercial procedures; commercial simplified runs far higher. A board loves the candidate who can keep the two ceilings straight and say which one governs the buy on the table.

cites.quote: There are no commercial products or commercial services that can satisfy the agency’s needs
For acquisitions valued up to $9 million, issue a request for quotations (RFQ) followed by a purchase order.
Agencies must procure commercial products and commercial services to the maximum extent practicable.

sat.scenario: A customer with a $520K noncommercial ramp-lighting retrofit across two adjacent buildings offers you a helpful idea: "Cut two purchase orders, $260K each, one per building. Keeps everything under your simplified threshold and we move faster."
sat.ask: Two purchase orders, each under the SAT. What's wrong with that picture, and what do you tell the customer?
sat.script: That's a split, and the rule is written for exactly this conversation. RFO 13.001(c): do not divide requirements whose aggregate value exceeds the SAT merely to permit use of Part 13 procedures. The test is the requirement, not the paperwork — this is one $520K need that happens to touch two buildings, and the SAT is $350,000 under RFO 2.101. So I tell the customer no, and I tell him why it isn't just bureaucracy: the thresholds are where competition, publicizing, and justification rules attach, and splitting is engineering around all of them at once. Then I give him the real path — the buy runs under above-SAT procedures, and my job is to make that as fast as the rules allow, which is usually faster than he fears.

follow_ups.q: When are two buys legitimately two requirements instead of a split?
follow_ups.h: The rule's own verb is "divide" — and its test is intent plus aggregation.
follow_ups.d: The line is whether one known requirement was carved up "merely to permit" simplified procedures. Needs that arise independently — different times, different funded requirements, genuinely severable work — can stand alone. One project, one funding action, one designer, two POs on the same day fails the smell test every time. A strong candidate says they'd document the independence if they split, because the file has to defend the aggregate-value call.

follow_ups.q: Give me the SAT's exception tiers and when you'd see them.
follow_ups.h: The definition itself carries the exceptions.
follow_ups.d: RFO 2.101: the SAT is $350,000, except for acquisitions supporting contingency operations or defense/recovery from cyber, nuclear, biological, chemical, or radiological attack, or disaster response — then $1 million inside the United States and $2 million outside. Boards probe this because it's where deployed COs live. The trap is quoting the higher tiers without the qualifying purpose — the head of the agency's determination that the acquisition supports the covered operation is what unlocks them.

follow_ups.q: Same trick at the bottom of the scale — a buyer splits a $25K buy into two purchase-card transactions. Different answer?
follow_ups.h: Same principle, different threshold.
follow_ups.d: Same violation, smaller numbers: the MPT is $15,000 under RFO 2.101, and splitting to stay under it dodges the competition and set-aside duties that attach above it — remember RFO 13.102's set-aside obligation starts right above the MPT. Know the carve-downs too: $2,000 for construction under wage-rate requirements, $2,500 for services under labor standards. And the DoD wrinkle: class-deviation special acquisition authorities can raise micro-purchase thresholds for purchases directly supporting covered combatant-commander operations — deviation-driven, not a blanket raise.

cites.quote: Do not divide requirements, the aggregate value of which exceeds the SAT, merely to permit use of the procedures in this part.
Simplified acquisition threshold means $350,000, except for—
Micro-purchase threshold means $15,000

sat.scenario: Your buyer is drafting an RFQ for $120K in noncommercial calibration services and plans to post it unrestricted "to get the widest field." She notes, almost in passing, that the two incumbents everyone knows are both large businesses.
sat.ask: The buyer wants to run this unrestricted. What's your call, and how do you get there?
sat.script: My call is that unrestricted isn't the default she thinks it is. RFO 13.102 is categorical for this lane: noncommercial buys above the MPT and at or below the SAT must be set aside for small business. So the posture starts set-aside, and my market research question flips — not "who are the incumbents" but "are there small businesses that can do calibration to this standard." Part 19 supplies the working test: RFO 19.104-1(a), a reasonable expectation of offers from two or more responsible small businesses, competitive on price, quality, and delivery. If honest research says the small-business field genuinely can't cover it, RFO 19.104-1(b) makes me document the reason the buy isn't set aside. The incumbents being large is a fact about the past, not a market-research conclusion.

follow_ups.q: Your research finds exactly one capable small business. Now what?
follow_ups.h: The rule-of-two is an expectation about offers — count them.
follow_ups.d: One capable small business defeats the RFO 19.104-1(a) expectation of two or more, so a total set-aside isn't supportable on that ground — and the decision not to set aside gets documented under 19.104-1(b). The strong answer doesn't stop there: it asks whether one of the socioeconomic-program paths in Part 19 fits before defaulting to unrestricted, and whether the requirement's scope is what's shrinking the small-business field. The trap is treating one good small business as "close enough" to set aside — or as a license to sole-source.

follow_ups.q: Does the set-aside obligation reach micro-purchases or your AbilityOne buys?
follow_ups.h: The rule has an explicit floor and an explicit carve-out.
follow_ups.d: No — RFO 19.104-1(c): the set-aside requirement does not apply at or below the micro-purchase threshold or to purchases from required sources under Part 8, the AbilityOne Procurement List being the canonical example. Boards ask this to see if the candidate knows where the obligation starts and stops rather than reciting "always set aside." Required sources outrank set-asides in the order of operations.

follow_ups.q: Any DoD-specific boundaries on the set-aside rule you'd flag?
follow_ups.h: The supplement draws dollar lines the baseline doesn't.
follow_ups.d: R-DFARS 219.104-1 scopes the FAR 19.104-1(a) and (b) requirements for certain work: construction including maintenance and repair under $3.5 million, dredging under $2 million, A-E services for military construction or family housing under $1 million — and carves out supplies developed under the U.S.-Canadian Defense Development Sharing Program. The point for a board: the set-aside machinery is baseline-plus-supplement, and a DoD CO who has never opened the 219 pages is guessing.

cites.quote: must be set aside for small business concerns
For contracts above the micro-purchase threshold, the contracting officer must set the contract aside for small business if there is a reasonable expectation of obtaining offers—
The requirements at FAR 19.104-1(a) and (b) apply to acquisitions for—

sat.scenario: On your $290K noncommercial grounds-maintenance purchase order, the COR emails the contractor: "Add the two new buildings to your route starting Monday — we'll square up the paperwork later." The contractor complies. Three weeks on, an invoice arrives 12 percent over the order value, and the COR tells you he was "just keeping the mission moving."
sat.ask: The COR says he was keeping the mission moving. Untangle this for me — what happened, and what do you do about it?
sat.script: What happened is an unauthorized commitment issued by the one person the contractor had every reason to trust. RFO 1.404(d) is unambiguous: a COR has no authority to make commitments or changes affecting price, quantity, delivery, or any other term — and RFO 1.402-1 reserves binding the Government to contracting officers. So the Government isn't bound to the extra work, but it took the benefit, which puts me in RFO 1.405 ratification territory: facts in writing, criteria tested, Legal in the loop, package to the proper level. In parallel I level with the contractor about where their invoice actually stands. Then the fix that outlives this order: re-brief the COR against his designation letter, remind him it warns of personal liability for unauthorized acts, and reset the who-can-direct line with the contractor in writing.

follow_ups.q: The COR's designation letter never mentions directing changes. Does that silence help him?
follow_ups.h: What must the designation specify — and which way does silence cut?
follow_ups.d: It cuts against him. RFO 1.404(a): the designation must specify the extent of the COR's authority, its period, that it cannot be redelegated, and that the COR may be personally liable for unauthorized acts. Authority in this system is affirmative — it exists where granted in writing, and silence grants nothing. The trap is the instinct that an ambiguous letter creates wiggle room; the baseline is zero authority to change the contract, and the letter can only add within the CO's own limits.

follow_ups.q: The contractor says the COR is the Government's own representative — why isn't the Government simply bound?
follow_ups.h: Whose signature can create a contract obligation?
follow_ups.d: Because binding the Government takes actual authority, and RFO 1.402-1(a) places that with contracting officers acting within their delegated limits. A COR's direction is apparent authority at best, and contractors rely on it at their peril — which is precisely why RFO 1.405 exists as the equitable cleanup when the Government has accepted the benefit. The strong answer holds both truths: the contractor doesn't get automatic payment, and the Government doesn't get free work — ratification or another 1.405(d) path resolves it.

follow_ups.q: How do you keep this from happening again on your contracts?
follow_ups.h: The regulation states the goal in one line — prevention.
follow_ups.d: RFO 1.405(b)(1): agencies should take actions to avoid the need for ratifications. In practice: postaward kickoff where the CO — not the COR — explains who can direct what; a who-can-direct letter in the contractor's hands; COR files reviewed periodically against the designation; and fast, visible processing of this UC so the unit learns the cost. A board wants to hear that the candidate treats every ratification as a training failure with a name on it.

cites.quote: A COR has no authority to make any commitments or changes that affect price, quality, quantity, delivery, or other terms and conditions of the contract.
Only contracting officers may sign, administer, or terminate contracts on behalf of the Government.
Agencies should take actions to avoid the need for ratifications.

sat.scenario: The vendor on your $85K purchase order emails an invoice missing the contract number and the defective-invoice notice contact. It sits in an org inbox for 12 days before anyone forwards it to the billing office. Now the vendor is on the phone demanding late-payment interest and threatening to stop work on the follow-on.
sat.ask: The vendor wants interest. Do they have a case? Walk me through how invoices are supposed to move on this order.
sat.script: Both sides fumbled, and prompt-payment rules score each fumble separately. RFO 32.905(a): payment rides on a proper invoice plus satisfactory performance. This invoice isn't proper — 32.905(b) lists the required content, and the contract number is on it. But the Government has a clock too: the designated billing office must return a defective invoice within 7 days with the reasons, and if it doesn't, the due date adjusts for interest-penalty purposes. Twelve days in an org inbox means we own part of this. So: get the invoice back to the vendor today with the specific defects, fix my routing so invoices land at the designated billing office, confirm the receiving report is in place per 32.905(c), and walk the vendor through what a proper invoice looks like so round two pays clean.

follow_ups.q: Name the load-bearing elements of a proper invoice.
follow_ups.h: Think about what the payment office needs to match money to performance.
follow_ups.d: From RFO 32.905(b): contractor name and address, invoice date and number, the contract number or other authorization, description-quantity-unit price-extended price of what was delivered, shipping and payment terms, remit-to official, a contact for defective-invoice notices, plus TIN and EFT data where agency procedures require them, and anything else the contract itself demands. The candidate who can name even five signals they've actually cleared a payment problem rather than memorized a slide.

follow_ups.q: The billing office sat on it 12 days. Why does that matter if the invoice was defective anyway?
follow_ups.h: A defective invoice doesn't stop the Government's own clock.
follow_ups.d: RFO 32.905(b)(3): the billing office must return an improper invoice within 7 days after receipt with the reasons; if the notice isn't timely, the due date adjusts for determining any interest penalty. So "it was defective" is not absolution — the Government's delay converts into interest exposure. The trap is the one-sided answer that lectures the vendor about proper invoices while ignoring that the file shows the Government failed its own return deadline.

follow_ups.q: The vendor is a small business and you're in DoD. Does that change your payment posture?
follow_ups.h: DoD has a statutory acceleration goal.
follow_ups.d: Yes — R-DFARS 232.009-1: 10 U.S.C. 3801(b) requires DoD to provide accelerated payments to small business contractors and subcontractors to the fullest extent permitted by law, with a goal of 15 days. The board is listening for whether the candidate treats small-business cash flow as a compliance afterthought or as a policy DoD is statutorily leaning into — and whether they know acceleration is a goal that still presupposes a proper invoice.

cites.quote: Payment will be based on receipt of a proper invoice and satisfactory contract performance.
the designated billing office must return it within 7 days after receipt
10 U.S.C. 3801(b) requires DoD to provide accelerated payments to small business contractors and subcontractors, to the fullest extent permitted by law, with a goal of 15 days.

sat.scenario: Your $145K noncommercial fabrication purchase order carries the 52.213-4 terms. The day after the delivery date passes, the vendor calls: a flood shut their plant for two weeks, they're requesting a no-cost extension. Your customer, already burned by this timeline, wants them terminated for cause today.
sat.ask: The customer says terminate for cause today. What's your analysis?
sat.script: Not today — analysis first, and the clause supplies the framework. Under 52.213-4(b), the contractor is liable for default unless nonperformance was caused by an occurrence beyond its reasonable control and without its fault or negligence — and floods are on the clause's own list of examples. So I verify: did the flood actually cause this miss, or was the vendor already behind? Did they meet the clause's duties — written notice as soon as possible, remedy the delay quickly, notify when it's over? If the delay is excusable, there's no default to terminate for, and the businesslike answer is an extension sized to the flood. If the facts fall apart, then the cause path opens — but I explain to the customer that terminating over an excusable delay hands the vendor an improper-termination argument, converts my leverage into liability, and still doesn't get parts delivered.

follow_ups.q: The vendor never sent written notice during the flood — game over for their excuse?
follow_ups.h: Separate the notice duty from the causation test.
follow_ups.d: Not automatically. The clause obligates the contractor to notify in writing as soon as possible, remedy the delay, and report when it ends — but the substantive test in 52.213-4(b) is causation beyond reasonable control without fault or negligence. Blown notice hurts their credibility and my ability to mitigate, and I document it; it doesn't manufacture a default where the flood genuinely caused the miss. The trap is the gotcha answer that terminates on a procedural foot-fault and loses on the merits.

follow_ups.q: Say the delay isn't excusable. Walk me through what your termination has to get right.
follow_ups.h: There's a notice you usually owe first — with one exception.
follow_ups.d: Under 52.213-4(d), the Government sends a cure notice before terminating for cause unless the reason is late delivery — which is this fact pattern, so I could move without one. The termination itself must be defensible: documented default, remedies stated, and the knowledge that an improper cause termination is deemed a termination for convenience, with the Government paying for the privilege. Strong candidates also mention checking with Legal and reporting the termination per policy rather than firing off a letter solo.

follow_ups.q: Why is this clause in your purchase order at all?
follow_ups.h: Part 13 built one clause to do four jobs.
follow_ups.d: RFO 13.204(b): contracting officers may use 52.213-4 to provide a streamlined set of terms for inspection/acceptance, excusable delays, terminations, and warranties — in lieu of the separate clauses, or tailored. The design point a board rewards: simplified acquisition trades the heavyweight clause architecture for one integrated set of terms, so the CO must actually know what's inside it — because on this order, that clause is the whole postaward rulebook.

cites.quote: The Contractor shall be liable for default unless nonperformance is caused by an occurrence beyond the reasonable control of the Contractor and without its fault or negligence.

Contracting officers may use the clause at 52.213-4, Terms and Conditions—Simplified Acquisitions (Noncommercial), to provide a streamlined set of terms and conditions for inspection/acceptance, excusable delays, terminations, and warranties.

sat.scenario: The day after you issue a $190K purchase order for bleacher systems, the requirement dies — mission change, event cancelled. The vendor never returned a written acceptance, but when you call about cancelling, they push back hard: "We already ordered the steel. You can't just cancel."
sat.ask: Can you just cancel this order, or does the vendor have you? Walk me through it.
sat.script: This turns on contract formation, and simplified procedures are unusual here. Under RFO 12.201-1(b), my purchase order was the Government's offer — a binding contract forms only when the supplier accepts, by written acceptance or by substantial performance. RFO 13.302(a) lets me withdraw or cancel by written notice any time before acceptance occurs. No written acceptance exists, so the live question is whether ordering steel is substantial performance — placing an upstream material order usually isn't performance of my order, but I get the facts before I get confident. If acceptance hasn't occurred: written cancellation today, and per 13.302(b) I ask the vendor to acknowledge it in writing. If they claim real costs from beginning performance, 13.302(c) routes me to a termination under Part 49 or the 52.213-4 clause rather than a shouting match — the vendor gets process, not a veto.

follow_ups.q: What exactly turns your purchase order into a binding contract?
