follow_ups.h: The offer is yours. What are the two ways they take it?
follow_ups.d: RFO 12.201-1(b): written acceptance of the purchase order, or substantial performance of it. Until one happens, there's no contract — which is why 13.302(a) cancellation-by-notice works at all. The discriminating question is what counts as substantial performance: mobilizing, fabricating, delivering against the order points one way; internal preparations like ordering raw stock generally don't. Weak candidates either treat every PO as instantly binding or assume the Government can walk away at any point — both wrong.

follow_ups.q: The vendor proves they cut steel to your drawings before your notice arrived. Now what?
follow_ups.h: The regulation names your off-ramp when cancellation is contested.
follow_ups.d: RFO 13.302(c): if the contractor doesn't accept the cancellation or claims costs from beginning performance, follow Part 49 or the 52.213-4 clause to terminate. Under the clause's convenience terms, the contractor is paid the percentage of the contract price reflecting work performed plus reasonable demonstrable charges resulting from the termination — no cost-accounting-standards apparatus, and nothing for costs that could reasonably have been avoided. The trap is digging in on "it never became a contract" when the facts have moved; termination for convenience is the clean, defensible exit.

follow_ups.q: Why doesn't the full Part 49 termination machinery automatically govern here?
follow_ups.h: Check what Part 49 says about orders carrying the simplified clause.
follow_ups.d: RFO 49.501 states the subpart on termination clauses does not apply to contracts using the 52.213-4 terms — the streamlined clause carries its own self-contained termination scheme, deliberately lighter: percentage-of-price settlement, standard record keeping, no audit right. The board point: simplified acquisition simplifies the exit too, and a CO who reflexively fires up full Part 49 settlement machinery on a purchase order is burning exactly the effort Part 13 exists to save.

cites.quote: The Government may withdraw, amend, or cancel purchase orders by written notice to the supplier at any time before acceptance of the order occurs
A binding contract is formed when the supplier accepts the Government’s offer, either by written acceptance of the purchase order or substantial performance of the purchase order.
the Contractor shall be paid a percentage of the contract price reflecting the percentage of the work performed prior to the notice of termination

sat.scenario: For a $60K buy of industrial shelving and racks, your customer wants inspection at the vendor's plant plus a battery of acceptance tests — "we got burned on the last delivery and I'm not signing for junk again." The items are catalog-standard, nothing safety-critical.
sat.ask: How much inspection does this buy actually need — and how do you handle the customer?
sat.script: The default answer is in the rulebook: RFO 13.103 — inspection and acceptance should generally be at destination, with source inspection specified only where 46.404 requires it. And 46.404's calculus for at-or-below-SAT work weighs criticality of application, the size of possible losses, and how likely the vendor is to replace defective items without a fight. Catalog shelving fails every trigger for the heavyweight treatment: at destination we check type and kind, quantity, damage, operability if readily determinable, and packaging — that's the prescribed scope. For the customer, I don't dismiss the scar tissue; I redirect it. Getting burned once argues for a crisp receiving process and knowing our post-acceptance remedies, not for buying plant-visit inspection the item's risk profile can't justify — inspection rigor is priced into every quote we'll get.

follow_ups.q: When would source inspection be the right call at this dollar level?
follow_ups.h: The section names the situations that escalate.
follow_ups.d: RFO 46.404(b)(2): special situations may require more detailed quality assurance, including standard or higher-level quality requirements — the flags are items with critical applications, real potential for harm to personnel or property, or losses the Government can't absorb. Dollar value alone is not the trigger; consequence is. The strong answer shows the candidate scaling QA to risk in both directions rather than owning one default they apply everywhere.

follow_ups.q: The shelving arrives dented and acceptance is already signed. What are your options?
follow_ups.h: The simplified clause keeps rights alive after signature — with time limits.
follow_ups.d: Under 52.213-4(a), the Government may require repair or replacement of nonconforming supplies at no increase in price, and if that won't cure it, seek an equitable price reduction or consideration. The conditions matter: post-acceptance rights must be exercised within a reasonable time after the defect was or should have been discovered, and before any substantial change in the item's condition. So acceptance isn't absolution for the vendor — but a receiving official who sits on obvious damage can burn those rights. That's the answer to give the once-burned customer.

follow_ups.q: Same vendor has now delivered clean nine straight times. Do you adjust anything?
follow_ups.h: The regulation rewards a defect-free history.
follow_ups.d: RFO 46.404(b)(3): for repetitive purchases of the same item from the same manufacturer with a history of defect-free work, Government inspection may be reduced to periodic checks of occasional purchases. Inspection intensity is a dial, not a switch — history earns relief, incidents crank it back up. Boards like this probe because it separates the CO who manages quality risk from the one who just performs the same ritual on every delivery.

cites.quote: Generally, inspection and acceptance should be at destination.

the Government must inspect contracts at or below the simplified acquisition threshold at destination and only for type and kind; quantity; damage; operability (if readily determinable); and preservation, packaging, packing, and marking, if applicable.
The Government may require repair or replacement of nonconforming supplies or reperformance of nonconforming services at no increase in contract price.

sat.scenario: Your buyer has a $150K noncommercial repair-parts requirement and a plan: email the RFQ to three vendors she already knows and skip any posting. "It's a simplified buy," she says. "SAP means I don't have to advertise."
sat.ask: Is she right that nothing gets posted? Walk me through the publicizing rules for this buy.
sat.script: Half right, which in publicizing is wrong. Simplified buys have two lanes under RFO 12.201-1(c), which Part 13 borrows: post the RFQ to the Governmentwide point of entry — the normal route — or solicit directly from suppliers. Direct solicitation isn't a free pass; it comes with conditions: a presolicitation notice per subpart 5.1 unless an exemption applies, quotes from at least three sources, and whenever practicable two sources not included in the last solicitation. The backbone rule is RFO 5.101(a): actions expected to exceed $20,000 get a presolicitation notice to the GPE unless exempted — and the exemption she's probably thinking of, 5.101(b)(1)(i), applies precisely because the solicitation itself gets posted with electronic response. So something touches the GPE either way. Her three-friendly-vendors plan, unposted and unrotated, fails on both lanes.

follow_ups.q: Which exemption lets you skip the separate presolicitation notice here, and what's its logic?
follow_ups.h: One posting can do the work of two.
follow_ups.d: RFO 5.101(b)(1)(i): no presolicitation notice is required when the action is at or below the SAT and the solicitation itself will be posted to the GPE and allow electronic response. The logic is substitution, not waiver — industry still gets visibility and a way in, just via the solicitation instead of an advance notice. The trap is reading the exemption as "below SAT means no posting": it trades one posting for another, and if the buyer refuses to post the RFQ, the notice obligation comes right back.

follow_ups.q: She emailed these same three vendors last quarter too. Any problem beyond optics?
follow_ups.h: The direct-solicitation rules address repeat fields directly.
follow_ups.d: Yes — RFO 12.201-1(c)(2): when soliciting directly, quote at least three sources and, whenever practicable, include two sources not in the previous solicitation. A standing trio of favorite vendors quarter after quarter defeats the rotation the rule builds in, and over time it quietly rebuilds the closed market that maximum-practicable competition exists to prevent. The strong candidate also notes the rotation is a fresh-pricing mechanism, not just a fairness gesture.

follow_ups.q: Award's made and an unsuccessful quoter calls. What do they get?
follow_ups.h: Part 13's postaward section is short — and this is in it.
follow_ups.d: RFO 13.301: comply with the award-notice posting requirements, and upon request give a brief explanation of the award decision — why that quoter wasn't selected. Not a formal debriefing with slides and Q&A; a brief, honest explanation. Boards use this to test tier discipline: the candidate who promises full negotiated-procurement debriefings on a purchase order is gold-plating, and the one who says "they get nothing, it's SAP" is violating the section outright.

cites.quote: For proposed contract actions expected to be greater than $20,000, post a presolicitation notice to the GPE unless an exemption in paragraph (b) applies.
For acquisitions at or below the SAT, the contracting officer may choose to solicit quotations directly from suppliers.
Upon request, provide a brief explanation of the award decision that explains why the unsuccessful quoter was not selected.

sat.scenario: Your competitive RFQ for $310K of noncommercial paint-booth filtration units was posted properly — and drew exactly one quote, priced 9 percent above your independent government estimate. The customer needs award in two weeks to hold the depot schedule.
sat.ask: One quote, above your estimate, clock running. How do you get to award — or do you?
sat.script: One quote doesn't kill the buy; it kills my easiest price story. RFO 13.203(a) requires me to determine the price fair and reasonable, based whenever possible on competitive quotations — I don't have those, so I work the other tools: prior purchase prices for the same units, published catalog and market pricing, a hard look at whether my IGE's assumptions are current, and, because quotes aren't sealed offers, direct negotiation with the quoter — 9 percent above an estimate is a conversation, not a verdict. I also diagnose the silence: was the requirement written too tight, the response window too short, the posting easy to miss? If the tools close the gap, I award and document the whole path — RFO 13.203(b) puts my procedures and the number of quotes in the file. If I can't get to fair and reasonable, the schedule loses to the determination, and I resolicit with the defect fixed.

follow_ups.q: Name your price-analysis moves when there's no second quote to compare.
follow_ups.h: Competitive quotes are the preferred basis, not the only one.
follow_ups.d: A solid list: historical prices paid for the same or similar items adjusted for quantity and time; published catalog or market prices; the IGE itself, decomposed and defended rather than waved at; value analysis against the next-best alternative; and negotiation with the quoter — under RFO 12.201-1 a quotation isn't a binding offer, so dialogue and revised pricing are natural, not exceptional. The weak answer knows only "compare the quotes" and stalls the moment competition thins.

follow_ups.q: You're in DoD. Does one response to a competitive solicitation trigger anything special?
follow_ups.h: There's a one-offer policy — and an exception aimed at exactly this tier.
follow_ups.d: R-DFARS 215.202-71 sets DoD's only-one-offer drill — consult the requiring activity and resolicit for at least 30 more days when the window was short — but its exceptions say the resolicitation requirements do not apply to acquisitions at or below the simplified acquisition threshold. Fair-and-reasonable still must be established; the mandatory resolicit machinery doesn't attach here. This probe separates candidates cleanly: one group doesn't know the DoD policy exists, another applies it below the SAT where it doesn't belong. And for commercial SAP, R-DFARS 212.102-71 points to the same procedures.

follow_ups.q: What does your file look like at award?
follow_ups.h: Part 13's documentation standard is one sentence — know it.
follow_ups.d: RFO 13.203(b): a written description of the procedures used in awarding the purchase order and the number of quotations received. On this buy that means the posting history, the one-quote result and my read on why, each price-analysis technique and what it showed, the negotiation outcome, and the fair-and-reasonable determination it all supports. Simplified documentation scales with the story's difficulty — a one-quote, above-IGE award needs a paragraph that would survive a skeptical reviewer, not a checkbox.

cites.quote: The contracting officer must determine the price to be fair and reasonable. Whenever possible, base price reasonableness on competitive quotations.
The requirements at 215.202-71(b) do not apply to— (i) Acquisitions at or below the simplified acquisition threshold

5m.scenario: A program office brings you a follow-on requirement for engineering support on a fielded sensor system — about $12 million over three years. The incumbent has held the work for six years. The package contains one paragraph of justification: "Contractor X is the only vendor with the necessary experience — request sole source." The last market research in the file is four years old.
5m.ask: The program manager wants the sole-source paperwork started today. Walk the panel through how you handle this request.
5m.script: The default is full and open competition, and the burden of escaping it sits on the file, not on incumbency. The only plausible authority is only-one-responsible-source, and for a follow-on that means demonstrating substantial duplication of cost not recoverable through competition, or unacceptable delay — demonstrated, not asserted. My first move is market research, because four-year-old research supports nothing. If the facts hold, the J&A carries the full 6.104-1 content: the unique-qualifications demonstration, efforts to solicit as many sources as practicable, a fair-and-reasonable price determination, the market research results, and the statement of actions to remove barriers before the next buy. "They have the experience" is a starting allegation, never the demonstration.

follow_ups.q: Say the facts support the J&A. At $12 million, who approves it?
follow_ups.h: Above $900,000 but not above $20 million.
follow_ups.d: The advocate for competition, and that authority is not delegable (6.104-2). The contracting officer's certification carries approval only at $900K or below. A good answer also knows a higher official may approve a lower-dollar justification — the trap is treating the bands as exclusive lanes, or 'delegating' the advocate's approval to make routing easier.

follow_ups.q: The base is $12 million, but two option years could take it to $24 million. Does that change anything?
follow_ups.h: What dollar value sets the approval level?
follow_ups.d: 6.104-2(c): the justification must include the estimated value of all options to determine the approval level — at $24M this climbs out of the advocate band into the head-of-the-procuring-activity band. The trap is pricing only the base to keep the approval low; that is threshold engineering and boards hunt for it.

follow_ups.q: What does DoD change about the only-one-source authority itself?
follow_ups.h: Read the DoD sentence in 6.103-1(b) and the follow-on prong in (c)(2).
follow_ups.d: For DoD, NASA, and the Coast Guard the authority extends to a limited number of responsible sources, and the follow-on prong extends beyond major systems and highly specialized equipment to continued provision of highly specialized services. A strong candidate volunteers the deviation; a weak one recites the civilian rule and stops.

follow_ups.q: The PM adds: "We're out of runway to compete this — the money expires."
follow_ups.h: What can never be the basis for other than full and open competition?
follow_ups.d: 6.103(b): lack of planning by the requiring activity and funding concerns are expressly barred as justification. The answer isn't 'no' — it's that urgency of the calendar has to trace to a legitimate authority and the Government's need, and the file must never lean on the schedule the office burned.

cites.quote: Substantial duplication of cost to the Government that is not expected to be recovered through competition
A justification must include the estimated dollar value of all options to determine the approval level.
A lack of planning by the requiring activity

5m.scenario: A repair requirement sat in the program office for eight months. Now a fielded system has failed a safety inspection, operations wants it fixed within weeks, and an engineer has already obtained a quote from the vendor he likes. The PM hands you a draft urgency J&A with that vendor's name in it.
5m.ask: Is this an urgency action at all — and what do you do with the J&A already on your desk?
5m.script: Two separate questions. First, is the urgency real: the test is that the Government would be seriously injured, financially or otherwise, unless sources are limited. A safety failure can genuinely qualify even when the office also slept on the requirement — but the injury must be the Government's, now, not the schedule they burned, because lack of planning can never be the basis. Second, the process: urgency limits competition, it doesn't eliminate it — I still solicit as many sources as practicable under the circumstances. The pre-selected vendor is the red flag I run down: the file has to show why sources were limited, not that somebody's favorite got ratified. Then I scope the period of performance to the urgency and get the competitive successor moving in parallel.

follow_ups.q: How long can an urgency contract run?
follow_ups.h: There are two ceilings — one tied to the need, one in months.
follow_ups.d: No longer than necessary to meet the urgent need and to award a competitive successor, and not more than one year including all options unless the head of the agency determines exceptional circumstances apply — a determination separate from the J&A and documented in the file. The trap: writing a three-year PoP 'for stability' under an urgency authority.

follow_ups.q: Ops says there's no time for approvals. Can the J&A come after award?
follow_ups.h: Urgency has a documented timing exception.
follow_ups.d: Yes — 6.103-2(d) allows the justification and approval after award when doing it before would unreasonably delay the acquisition. A good answer treats that as a documented exception with the full content requirement intact, not a license to paper the file at leisure.

follow_ups.q: The PM argues the eight months of delay is itself the urgency. Answer him.
follow_ups.h: What does 6.103(b) prohibit?
follow_ups.d: Other than full and open competition must not be justified on lack of planning or funding concerns. The urgency must stand on present harm to the Government — the safety failure — and the J&A should be written on that harm, with the delay acknowledged honestly. Hiding the history is how justifications die at the advocate's desk.

cites.quote: the Government would be seriously injured, financially or otherwise, unless the agency is permitted to limit the number of sources
May not exceed one year, including all options, unless the head of the agency determines that exceptional circumstances apply
Contracting without providing for full and open competition must not be justified on the basis of

5m.scenario: A requiring office sends you a purchase description for commercial network hardware, about $2.1 million: "Brand X Model 4400 or equal." Reading the salient characteristics, you realize they were lifted from Brand X's own spec sheet — down to a proprietary management protocol no other manufacturer implements.
5m.ask: What do you do with this purchase description before anything goes on the street?
5m.script: An "or equal" whose salient characteristics only one product can meet is a brand-name spec wearing a costume — no equal can ever qualify, so it restricts competition exactly like pure brand name. True brand-name descriptions prevent full and open competition and ride on a justification; a genuine or-equal preserves it. So my first move is back to the requiring activity: strip the salient characteristics to actual minimum needs, stated in performance terms — a proprietary protocol is only salient if the mission truly requires it. If brand name survives that scrub, this commercial buy over the SAT takes a written justification approved per 6.104. And for DoD there's no documentation escape by adding "or equal" — the 12.102 documentation is required for brand-name-or-equal and proprietary specs too.

follow_ups.q: Same item, but the buy is at or below the SAT. What changes?
follow_ups.h: 12.102 splits the documentation duty at the SAT.
follow_ups.d: Below the SAT you document the decision that only one source is available and the basis; above it you prepare a written justification and get it approved per 6.104. Lighter paper, same discipline. The trap is treating below-SAT as no-documentation territory.

follow_ups.q: Now it's an order under a multiple-award IDIQ instead of a new contract. Does the brand-name discipline follow it?
follow_ups.h: Items peculiar to one manufacturer have their own ordering rule.
follow_ups.d: Yes — 16.507-7: a brand-name item, even if available on more than one contract, is an item peculiar to one manufacturer. The restriction is justified in the 16.507-6(d)-(e) format, and above $40,000 the justification gets posted or sent with the solicitation to all awardees. Weak candidates think fair-opportunity-land has no brand-name rules.

follow_ups.q: Who owns the claim that the proprietary protocol is a real minimum need?
follow_ups.h: The J&A's supporting data has certifiers besides the contracting officer.
follow_ups.d: Technical and requirements personnel are responsible for providing — and certifying as accurate and complete — the data supporting other than full and open competition (6.104(b)). The CO signs the justification, but the requirement owner signs for the requirement. A good answer assigns that accountability out loud.

cites.quote: use of brand-name descriptions, or specification of attributes peculiar to one manufacturer, prevents full and open competition
the documentation addressed in FAR 12.102 is required to use brand name or equal descriptions or proprietary specifications and standards
A brand-name item, even if available on more than one contract, is an item peculiar to one manufacturer.

5m.scenario: An Air Force base-operations-support requirement, roughly $40 million, is headed to the 8(a) program, and SBA has identified a participant for a sole-source award. A sharp new specialist objects: "Anything sole source over $900K needs a J&A through the competition advocate" — and drafts one for your signature.
5m.ask: Is your specialist right? What actually governs this award, and what do you do with the draft?
5m.script: The instinct is right and the answer is still no — this is the classic DoD deviation. Under 206.104-70, implementing section 823 of the FY20 NDAA, no justification and approval is required for a sole-source 8(a) award up to $100 million. The 8(a) authority is its own statutory lane, not a 6.103 exception riding the approval ladder. What I do owe the file: the acquisition sits far above the 8(a) competitive thresholds — $8.5M manufacturing, $5.5M for everything else — so the real question is why this isn't a competitive 8(a) among eligible participants, and that conversation happens with SBA before acceptance, not in a J&A. I thank the specialist for the reflex, park the draft, and document the offering-and-acceptance trail instead.

follow_ups.q: Same requirement at $120 million. Now what?
follow_ups.h: The $100 million line flips the whole posture.
follow_ups.d: Above $100M DoD requires the works: a justification with the FAR 6.104-1 content, approval by the head of the procuring activity — delegable only to an official above brigadier general or rear admiral (lower half), or the civilian equivalent — and public posting after award. A strong candidate states the approval level and the delegation floor; a weak one says 'SPE, probably.'

follow_ups.q: Why isn't this simply competed among 8(a) firms?
follow_ups.h: What do the competitive thresholds command when two participants exist?
follow_ups.d: Above the thresholds, the acquisition must be awarded competitively among eligible 8(a) participants when there's a reasonable expectation of two responsible participants and award at fair market price. Sole source above the threshold is the exception that has to be walked through SBA acceptance — that's the pressure point the board wants you to feel.

follow_ups.q: The PM offers a fix: split it into two $20 million packages and place both sole source.
follow_ups.h: There's an express prohibition on exactly this.
follow_ups.d: 19.108-7(c): a requirement exceeding the competitive threshold shall not be divided into lesser amounts to use 8(a) sole-source procedures for a single firm. That's not creativity, it's splitting — and the answer the panel wants is the flat no, followed by the legitimate alternatives: competitive 8(a), or a defensible sole-source case at full value.

cites.quote: no justification and approval is required for a sole- source contract under the 8(a) authority (15 U.S.C. 637(a)) for an amount not exceeding $100 million
the head of the procuring activity is the approval authority for a proposed sole-source 8(a) contract exceeding $100 million
shall not be divided into several requirements for lesser amounts in order to use 8(a) sole source procedures for award to a single firm

5m.scenario: On a five-awardee services MAC, one vendor won the original engineering-support order in open competition two years ago. Since then the program has issued two "logical follow-on" orders to the same vendor without notifying the field, and a third — $4.8 million — just arrived with a one-line justification: "continuation of ongoing work."
5m.ask: The third order is on your desk. Take the panel through your review.
5m.script: Fair opportunity is the default for every order above the micro-purchase threshold; the logical follow-on exception exists for economy and efficiency, but it's earned order by order, never inherited as a habit. Three checks. Anchor: the exception is available only if all awardees had a fair opportunity at the original order — and if these chained follow-ons have drifted in scope, the chain back to that competed order may already be broken. Content: above the SAT the justification carries the full 16.507-6(d)(2) package, and the rationale must say why the relationship is logical in terms of scope, period of performance, or value — "continuation of ongoing work" is a wish, not a rationale. Approval and posting: at $4.8M this goes to the advocate for competition, not delegable, and the justification gets posted. If the package can't clear those, the order competes.

follow_ups.q: What does a defensible logical-follow-on rationale actually contain?
follow_ups.h: The regulation names the three axes of the relationship.
follow_ups.d: It describes why the follow-on relationship is logical in terms of scope, period of performance, or value — concretely: same technical baseline, continuity of a defined effort, transition costs that make re-competition uneconomical for this order. The trap is circularity: 'it's a follow-on because it follows on.'

follow_ups.q: What does DoD add for exactly this situation?
follow_ups.h: DoD saw the chaining problem coming.
follow_ups.d: R-DFARS 216.507-6: for an order above the SAT that is a follow-on to an order previously issued for the same supply or service under the (b)(2) or (b)(3) exceptions, follow the PGI procedures — extra scrutiny aimed precisely at serial follow-ons. Volunteering the deviation is what separates the Air Force answer from the textbook answer.

follow_ups.q: One of the other four awardees says they never see these orders. Where does that complaint go?
follow_ups.h: There's a designated official independent of you.
follow_ups.d: The task-order ombudsman — a senior agency official, independent of the contracting officer, who reviews complaints and ensures awardees are afforded fair opportunity consistent with the contract's procedures (16.507-2(b)). Knowing the ombudsman exists, and that this pattern is exactly what draws one in, shows ordering-vehicle maturity.

cites.quote: it is a logical follow-on to an order already issued under the contract, provided that all awardees were given a fair opportunity to be considered for the original order
the justification must be approved by the advocate for competition of the activity placing the order
that is a follow-on to an order previously issued for the same supply or service based on a justification for an exception to fair opportunity citing the authority at FAR 16.507-6(b)(2) or (3)

5m.scenario: A delivery order on a single-award IDIQ for aircraft ground-equipment maintenance has grown by modification: first a software-sustainment task was added, and now the PM wants to fold in facility repairs at a second base. "There's plenty of ceiling left on the contract," he says.
5m.ask: Ceiling is available. What's your analysis before you sign the next modification?
5m.script: Ceiling isn't authority — scope is. Orders escape part 6 only conditionally: the exemption holds when the underlying contract was competed and all responsible sources were realistically permitted to compete for the requirements contained in the order. Work outside the scope of what was competed inherits no exemption; it's a new procurement wearing a mod number, and it must be competed or justified under 6.103 with its own approval. So I test the mod against what offerors reasonably anticipated when the IDIQ was competed. Software sustainment on a GSE-maintenance contract was already a stretch; facility repair at another base fails on arrival. In scope, I sign. Out of scope, the honest answer is a new action — compete it, or write the J&A and take the approval that comes with it.

follow_ups.q: The PM says a modification can't be protested, so where's the risk?
follow_ups.h: What kind of modification does 6.001 actually except from part 6?
follow_ups.d: Only modifications within the scope of the contract are excepted. An out-of-scope mod is functionally a new sole-source award made without authority — and that is a protestable, sustainable ground. The shield is scope, not the instrument. A strong candidate says the risk isn't the mod form, it's the unauthorized award hiding inside it.

follow_ups.q: What if the IDIQ itself had been awarded under a J&A rather than competed?
follow_ups.h: The conditional exemption has a second prong.
follow_ups.d: Then orders are exempt only where the justification and approval adequately covers the requirements contained in the order (6.001(e)(2)). An order the J&A never contemplated has no exemption to inherit — the J&A's own scope becomes the fence line. That's the subtlety most candidates miss.

follow_ups.q: Funds on the order expire in three weeks. Does that tip the call?
follow_ups.h: What can never justify skipping competition?
follow_ups.d: No — funding concerns are expressly barred as a basis for other than full and open competition (6.103(b)(2)). Expiring money makes the conversation urgent; it doesn't make the mod in scope. The disciplined answer is to size a bridge inside scope if one honestly exists, and start the new action for the rest.

cites.quote: The contract was awarded under 6.101 or 6.102, and all responsible sources were realistically permitted to compete for the requirements contained in the order
Concerns related to the amount of funds available to the agency or activity for acquisition

5m.scenario: You're placing an $8.5 million task order for logistics IT support on a seven-awardee MAC. Last cycle, the program office solicited two favorites by email and a losing awardee went to the ombudsman. Your chief wants this one clean.
5m.ask: Design the order competition for me. What does an order above $7.5 million require that a smaller one doesn't?
5m.script: Above $7.5 million the procedures stiffen: a fair notice of intent to all awardees offering the service — not two favorites — with a clear statement of the requirement, a reasonable response period, and disclosure of the significant evaluation factors and subfactors, including cost or price, and their relative importance. Then I document that every response was fairly considered, and on a best-value selection, the relative importance of quality against price. Postaward, notices and debriefings run per part 15 and a summary of the debriefing goes in the order file. What I don't need is part 15 machinery: no formal evaluation plan, no scoring, no competitive range — the ordering process is exempt from part 6 and subpart 15.3. Streamlined is legal; selective solicitation is not. That distinction is the whole game.

follow_ups.q: With options the order lands at $10.2 million. What changes about debriefings?
follow_ups.h: DoD drew its own line above the RFO's.
follow_ups.d: R-DFARS 216.507-5: at $10 million or more a written or oral postaward debriefing is required — for successful and unsuccessful awardees — following the 215.301 procedures. Below that, part 15 debriefing practice applies via 16.507-5(c). Missing the DoD $10M line is the most common miss on this question.

follow_ups.q: Your fair notice goes to all seven and exactly one offer comes back. Now what?
follow_ups.h: DoD has a one-offer rule for competitive orders.
follow_ups.d: R-DFARS 216.507-70: one offer on a competitive order above the SAT sends you to the 215.271-6 procedures before award. [Note: 215.271-6 is a stale cross-reference in the regulation’s own text — no 215.27x section exists. The operative DoD one-offer rule is 215.202-71.] One response to a genuinely fair notice can be a fine outcome — but DoD makes you verify the price stands without competitive pressure, not just shrug and award.

follow_ups.q: The program office asks for scoring sheets and a competitive range 'to be safe.' Is safer better here?
follow_ups.h: What is the ordering process expressly not subject to?
follow_ups.d: Not subject to part 6, subpart 15.3, or part 14 — no evaluation plans, scoring, or competitive range required. Importing part 15 wholesale isn't safety, it's self-inflicted schedule and protest surface. The mature answer: tailor procedures to the order's risk and complexity, and put the discipline where the rule puts it — fair notice, fair consideration, documentation.

cites.quote: A summary of the debriefing must be included in the task or delivery order file.
a written or oral postaward debriefing of successful and unsuccessful awardees is required for task orders and delivery orders valued at $10 million or more
If only one offer is received in response to an order exceeding the simplified acquisition threshold that is placed on a competitive basis

5m.scenario: Closing out the ordering period on a multiple-award IDIQ, your specialist discovers one awardee never received a single order — and its contract minimum guarantee was never satisfied. The PM sees an opening: "Perfect. Give them the new $3 million requirement sole source and we solve both problems."
5m.ask: Does the minimum guarantee get you there? What do you actually do?
5m.script: There is a real exception here — an order may be placed sole source when necessary to satisfy a minimum guarantee — but it's sized to the problem it solves. The guarantee is whatever the contract promised that awardee, and the exception covers satisfying it, not decorating it with a $3 million requirement that happens to be convenient. If the minimum is, say, $50K, I place an order sized to the minimum, with the justification the exception requires above the micro-purchase threshold, and the new requirement gets fair opportunity like any other order. I'd also say the quiet part: an unmet minimum at closeout means our ordering discipline failed this awardee for years — the ombudsman conversation we never had. The fix going forward is honest minimums and consideration at award, not a rescue order at twilight.

follow_ups.q: So how large should the sole-source order be?
follow_ups.h: The exception reaches only as far as its purpose.
follow_ups.d: Large enough to satisfy the minimum guarantee — that's the necessity the exception names. Anything beyond rides on a different exception or on fair opportunity. Bundling the pet requirement in is using a $50K key to open a $3M door, and the justification you'd have to write would say so out loud.

follow_ups.q: What paper does even the right-sized order need?
follow_ups.h: Sole source above the MPT is never paper-free on a MAC.
follow_ups.d: A written justification per 16.507-6(d) — the exception cited with supporting rationale, a fair-and-reasonable price determination, and above the SAT the full content, approval at the level the value commands, and posting. The minimum-guarantee exception changes the rationale, not the ritual.

follow_ups.q: A different awardee sees the order and objects. Exposure?
follow_ups.h: Think about what the justification does and doesn't shield.
follow_ups.d: A properly justified minimum-guarantee order is defensible — the exception exists for exactly this. What's not defensible is the oversized version: to the other awardees it's a sole-source award of new work they never got to chase. Complaints route to the ombudsman, and an order untethered from its exception is protest bait. Size and paper are the whole defense.

cites.quote: It is necessary to place an order to satisfy a minimum guarantee.
A determination by the contracting officer that the anticipated cost to the Government will be fair and reasonable.

5m.scenario: Market research for a $3.4 million grounds-maintenance recompete: the incumbent is a large business. One capable small business answered the sources sought with directly relevant past performance; a second small firm sent a capability statement that's thin but plausible. The PM wants full and open "so we can keep the incumbent."
5m.ask: Set-aside or not — and whose decision is it?
5m.script: Above the micro-purchase threshold the rule is mandatory, not a preference: the contract must be set aside when there's a reasonable expectation of offers from two or more responsible small businesses, competitive on fair market price, quality, and delivery. Reasonable expectation — not certainty. A strong first responder plus a thin-but-plausible second can carry it, so my next move is to pressure-test the second firm: targeted questions, their contract history, capacity. If the expectation holds, the set-aside isn't optional, and keeping the incumbent is not a factor the regulation recognizes. If it doesn't hold, I document why — the rule requires documenting the reason a contract is not set aside. Either way the determination is the contracting officer's, informed by the small business specialist and SBA, not the PM's.

follow_ups.q: What if the honest answer is only one responsible small business?
follow_ups.h: The rule of two failing doesn't end the small business analysis.
follow_ups.d: No mandatory total set-aside — but 19.104-1 expressly doesn't preclude award under the HUBZone, SDVOSB, WOSB, or 8(a) programs, several of which have sole-source lanes. The disciplined sequence is socioeconomic programs before defaulting to full and open. Weak answers stop at 'rule of two fails, compete it.'

follow_ups.q: Move the same requirement onto a multiple-award contract as an order. Does the mandatory rule follow?
follow_ups.h: Order set-asides run on different statutory footing.
follow_ups.d: No — order set-asides under MACs are discretionary: contracting officers may, at their discretion, set aside orders, and that decision is an exercise of discretion that is not a basis for protest. Knowing the mandatory contract-level rule from the discretionary order-level authority is exactly the kind of distinction boards probe.

follow_ups.q: SBA formally recommends the set-aside and you still disagree. Can you just proceed?
follow_ups.h: Rejecting an SBA recommendation has its own path.
follow_ups.d: Not quietly — rejecting the SBA recommendation triggers the 19.102(f) process rather than a unilateral shrug, and the file carries the documented reason the contract is not set aside. The point the panel is testing: the decision is yours, but it is reviewable, documented, and made against a mandatory standard.

cites.quote: there is a reasonable expectation of obtaining offers— (1) From two or more responsible small business concerns; and (2) That are competitive in terms of fair market prices, quality, and delivery
contracting officers may, at their discretion, set aside orders placed under multiple-award contracts

5m.scenario: A $15 million sustainment-engineering requirement arrives with the acquisition plan already marked CPFF. The entire rationale reads: "Requirements uncertainty — consistent with prior contract." The prior contract was also CPFF. So was the one before it.
5m.ask: How do you make the contract-type call here, and what has to be in the file to defend it?
5m.script: Type follows risk, and the file has to prove the risk, not recite it. For anything other than fixed-price, 16.103 demands the full package: an analysis of why non-fixed-price is appropriate, specific facts and circumstances — not "uncertainty" as an incantation — an assessment that the Government has the resources to manage it, and planned actions to transition toward fixed-price on the next buy. Three CPFF generations with no transition story is the tell that nobody has done the analysis. Then the cost-reimbursement gates: an acquisition plan approved a level above me, a contractor accounting system that can segregate, accumulate, and allocate costs to this contract, and a designated COR before award. My move is to decompose the requirement — after years of performance, the stable core prices firm-fixed; keep cost-type only for the genuinely uncertain slice.

follow_ups.q: The contractor's accounting system hasn't been looked at in years. Proceed?
follow_ups.h: It's a condition of use, not a nice-to-have.
follow_ups.d: No — an adequate accounting system that can segregate, accumulate, and allocate costs during performance is a precondition for cost-reimbursement (16.301-3(a)(3)). Award first and verify later is exactly backwards; the verification gates the type. A strong candidate also names who they'd ask — DCAA/DCMA — without being prompted.

follow_ups.q: Your specialist proposes T&M instead, 'for flexibility.' React.
follow_ups.h: T&M has the harshest determination in part 16.
follow_ups.d: T&M requires a D&F that no other contract type is suitable — signed before the base period, approved by the HCA when base plus options exceed three years — and a ceiling price the contractor exceeds at its own risk. It's the type of last resort with the least cost discipline, not the flexible middle ground. 'Flexibility' is precisely the argument the D&F standard exists to kill.

follow_ups.q: What's the transition story the file owes, and why does anyone care?
follow_ups.h: The (a)(5) package looks forward, not just backward.
follow_ups.d: Planned actions to minimize non-fixed-price use on future acquisitions of the same requirement and transition to fixed-price to the maximum extent practicable. It matters because it converts this award into the setup for the next one — defined workload data, stabilized requirements. Its absence across three CPFF cycles is how a board knows the office is coasting.

cites.quote: transition to fixed-price contracts to the maximum extent practicable
The contractor’s accounting system can adequately segregate, accumulate and allocate costs specifically attributed to the contract or order during contract performance
no other contract type is suitable

5m.scenario: The requiring office delivers a government-unique performance spec for vehicle-fleet telematics units — "our operating environment is unique." Your market research turns up three commercial products doing this work for utility fleets today, one of them available on an existing governmentwide contract.
5m.ask: The PM is standing firm on the unique spec. What does the regulation require of you here, and in what order?
5m.script: The preference isn't advisory: agencies must acquire commercial products and services when they're available to meet the need, and 10.001(f) hands me the priority ladder — first, a commercial solution on an existing governmentwide contract; second, whether the requirement can be modified so an existing contract works; then commercial from another source; then modified commercial; and only when nothing satisfies, a nondevelopmental item. My research already found rung one. So the burden runs against the unique spec: I take "unique environment" back to the requiring office and make it testable — temperature range, shock, security interface — because most uniqueness collapses into ruggedization the market already sells. If a genuine gap survives, the honest path is modifying the requirement or a modified commercial product, documented at the level the buy deserves — not a clean-sheet development.

follow_ups.q: Fine — it's commercial. Now the PM wants cost-reimbursement 'until we understand the usage patterns.'
follow_ups.h: Part 12 has a flat answer.
follow_ups.d: Prohibited, full stop — no cost-reimbursement contract type for commercial products or services (12.104(d)), and 16.301-3(b) says the same from the part 16 side. Usage uncertainty is handled with structure — quantity bands, EPA, T&M under its conditions — not by importing cost-type into part 12.

follow_ups.q: What about T&M for the commercial installation services piece?
follow_ups.h: T&M for commercial services has three conditions.
follow_ups.d: Available if the services are acquired competitively and are commonly sold to the public on a T&M basis, with a D&F that firm-fixed-price or FPEPA is not suitable and a ceiling price the contractor exceeds at its own risk (12.104(b)). The trap is treating T&M as the default for services — the D&F burden runs the other way.

follow_ups.q: The PM asks what the commercial determination actually buys anyone.
follow_ups.h: Think about what part 12 changes downstream.
follow_ups.d: It moves the buy into part 12's streamlined solicitation, evaluation, and clause structure, opens the market that actually makes the product, and preserves fixed-price discipline — 12.104(a) drives FFP or FPEPA to the maximum extent practicable. The determination isn't paperwork; it's the gate between buying what industry sells and paying to reinvent it.

cites.quote: Agencies must acquire commercial products or commercial services when the agency determines that they are available to meet the agency’s needs
A commercial product or commercial service on an existing governmentwide contract can meet the agency's requirements
Do not use any cost-reimbursement contract type to procure commercial products or commercial services.

5m.scenario: A sources-sought for depot-level repair of a legacy radar ran ten days over the winter holidays and drew zero responses. The PM declares victory: "Market research complete — nobody else can do it. Write the sole-source J&A to the OEM."
5m.ask: Does this market research carry a sole-source justification? What do you do next?
5m.script: Zero responses to a badly aimed notice proves the notice, not the market. The standard is research appropriate to the circumstances — and for a repair market where third-party shops are known to exist, ten days over the holidays isn't it. Before any J&A, I rerun the research like I mean it: a properly timed notice, direct outreach to known repair houses, and real exchanges with industry, which the regulation encourages within the procurement-integrity rails. The J&A itself will force the issue anyway — it must contain the market research conducted and the results, the efforts to solicit as many sources as possible, any sources that expressed interest in writing, and the actions we'll take to remove barriers next time. A justification built on a dead notice hands the advocate every reason to bounce it. And if honest research still says one source, the J&A then writes itself — honestly.

follow_ups.q: What if market research genuinely wasn't conducted at all?
follow_ups.h: The J&A content rule anticipates that case — read it closely.
follow_ups.d: The J&A must state the reason market research was not conducted. But that's a confession with a signature line, not an escape hatch — for a multi-million-dollar repair requirement there is no reason the approving official should accept. The clause exists for edge cases, and this isn't one.

follow_ups.q: The PM worries that calling repair vendors directly is a procurement-integrity problem.
follow_ups.h: The regulation takes a side on talking to industry.
follow_ups.d: It says the opposite: agencies should engage in responsible and constructive exchanges with industry, so long as no firm gains an unfair advantage and 3.104 is respected. Silence isn't compliance — it's how offices end up sole-sourcing by ignorance. The discipline is evenhandedness and documentation, not avoidance.

follow_ups.q: Three weeks after the sole-source award, a repair shop emails a capability statement. Does it matter?
follow_ups.h: The J&A has two forward-looking content items.
follow_ups.d: It matters for the next acquisition. The J&A must list sources that expressed interest in writing and state the actions the agency may take to remove barriers to competition before the next buy — late interest is exactly the evidence those provisions exist to capture. Filing it as noise repeats this year's mistake on next year's requirement.

cites.quote: Agencies must conduct market research appropriate to the circumstances
The market research conducted (see part 10) and the results or a statement of the reason market research was not conducted.

5m.scenario: A firm-fixed-price services option must be exercised by 30 September; it's the 12th. Performance has been acceptable with one recent dip. Then the checks come back: the contractor's NIST SP 800-171 assessment in SPRS is three and a half years old, and market rates for this labor mix have fallen roughly fifteen percent since award.
5m.ask: Walk the panel through your option-exercise decision.
5m.script: An option exercise is a determination, not a reflex. The base checklist: written notice within the contract's window, funds confirmed, then the determinations — a continuing requirement, synopsis posture settled, no active SAM exclusion, acceptable performance, and the one with teeth here: the option price is fair and reasonable based on current market conditions and exercise is in the Government's best interest. A fifteen-percent market drop puts that determination genuinely in question — I need current pricing evidence, and if the option price can't be defended today, the best-interest answer may be to let it lapse and compete. And for DoD the gate gets longer before I ever reach price: SAM record active and accurate, and SPRS verification that the NIST assessment is current — not more than three years old — and the CMMC certificate at the required level. A 3.5-year-old assessment fails that check on its face; the contractor refreshes it or the option doesn't get exercised.

follow_ups.q: The contract requires 30 days' preliminary notice and you have 18. What are your options now?
follow_ups.h: The unilateral right lives and dies by the contract's terms.
follow_ups.d: Exercise per the contract's terms or not at all — 17.204-1(b)(1) conditions exercise on notice within the time specified. Miss the window and the unilateral right is gone; what's left is a bilateral agreement, which is new sole-source work needing its own part 6 authority, or a new competition. The trap is 'the contractor won't mind' — consent doesn't resurrect authority.

follow_ups.q: Why does an option exercise escape a J&A in the first place?
follow_ups.h: The exemption was earned at the original award.
follow_ups.d: Because part 6 was satisfied up front: the option was evaluated as part of the initial competition and is exercisable at an amount specified in or reasonably determinable from the contract — and 6.001(c) excepts in-scope mods including priced, evaluated options. An option that was never evaluated, or whose price isn't determinable from the contract, has no exemption to stand on.

follow_ups.q: Performance is rated marginal in one area on the last CPARS. Does that kill the exercise?
follow_ups.h: The standard is a determination, not a spotless record.
follow_ups.d: Not automatically — the determination is that performance has been acceptable, for example satisfactory or better ratings. One marginal area is weighed by the CO: is it material, trending, corrected? What the board wants is the documented judgment — and the recognition that exercising an option is endorsing the contractor for another year with the Government's money.

cites.quote: the option price is fair and reasonable based on current market conditions and exercise of the option is in the Government's best interest
The contractor has a CMMC certificate at the level required by the contract, and that it is current (i.e., not more than 3 years old).
exercising priced options that were evaluated as part of the original competition

5m.scenario: Mid-source-selection, behind schedule, the PM proposes a shortcut: "Drop the option-year evaluation — we'll just exercise them later if we like the contractor." The solicitation includes four one-year options worth more than the base.
5m.ask: What do you tell the PM — and what does her shortcut cost the Government downstream?
5m.script: The rule runs the other way: offers for option quantities and periods are evaluated before award of the basic contract. Skipping is possible but deliberately hard — reserved for rare instances where evaluation would not benefit the Government, in writing, approved a level above me, in the file. Here the options are most of the contract's value, so unevaluated options mean the true price of the deal was never competed. The downstream bill is the real answer: an option exercise complies with part 6 only because the option was evaluated in the initial competition at a price determinable from the contract. Skip the evaluation and each later exercise is naked new sole-source work — J&A, approval level set by the option's value, protest surface — arriving at exactly the moment the program has no time. Two weeks saved now, bought back at retail four times.

follow_ups.q: When is skipping the option evaluation actually defensible?
follow_ups.h: The exception has three procedural locks and one adjective.
follow_ups.d: When evaluation would not benefit the Government — 'rare instances' is the regulation's own phrase — and even then only in writing, approved above the contracting officer, and filed. Think options overwhelmingly unlikely to be exercised. It is a documented exception, never a schedule-recovery tool.

follow_ups.q: Step back — when are options the wrong structure entirely?
follow_ups.h: 17.201-1 lists both the not-beneficial and the must-not cases.
follow_ups.d: Options are normally not beneficial with minimum economic quantities and delivery needs far enough out for a new competition — and must not be used when price or availability isn't reasonably foreseeable or market prices are likely to change significantly. Volatile-market options lock tomorrow's price with today's ignorance; a requirements or indefinite-quantity vehicle may fit better.

follow_ups.q: The PM's fallback: 'Then we'll just extend the contract when the time comes.'
follow_ups.h: An extension the contract doesn't provide for is not an option.
follow_ups.d: A bilateral extension outside the contract's terms is new work awarded without competition — part 6 applies with no evaluated-option exemption to lean on, which means a J&A the office will hate writing. The honest choices are evaluated options now or a planned recompete later; 'we'll extend' is the unplanned J&A on layaway.

cites.quote: The contracting officer may skip the evaluation of option quantities when such evaluation would not benefit the Government. This exception should be reserved for rare instances.
the option was evaluated as part of the initial competition and is exercisable at an amount specified in or reasonably determinable from the terms of the contract
Market prices for the supplies or services are likely to change significantly.

25m.topic: Certified Cost or Pricing Data & Proposal Analysis
25m.scenario: You are negotiating a sole-source follow-on with an incumbent for aircraft ground support equipment. The estimated price is $6.2 million and the prime contract would be awarded next month. Your contract specialist has drafted a request for certified cost or pricing data, citing the $2.5 million threshold, and the contractor's counsel has already pushed back in writing.
25m.ask: Your specialist wants to require certified cost or pricing data on this action. Talk me through whether that is right.
25m.script: The instinct is right and the number is wrong for us. $2.5 million is the government-wide floor; for DoD, R-DFARS 215.403-3 applies in lieu of the FAR rule and the threshold is $10 million for primes awarded after 30 June 2026. At $6.2 million I am below it, so I cannot require certified data on my own authority. The route that remains is RFO 15.403-3(e): unless an exception at 15.403-2 applies, the HCA — without power of delegation — may authorize me to obtain certified data below the threshold, provided the action exceeds the SAT. That does not leave me empty-handed — I still need a fair and reasonable price, so I go to data other than certified, and I document what I got and what it supported. The failure mode I am avoiding is demanding a certificate I have no authority to demand and handing the contractor a legitimate grievance.

follow_ups.q: The contractor offers to certify voluntarily to make the negotiation move faster. Do you take it?
follow_ups.h: Think about what a certificate buys the Government, and what it obligates you to do with it.
follow_ups.d: A certificate is not a convenience — it carries defective pricing exposure and a whole documentation regime. Accepting one below the threshold to speed a negotiation invites the question of why you needed it, and a strong candidate says they would obtain data other than certified and reserve certification for actions where the rule requires it.

follow_ups.q: Same buy, same dollars, but you are a civilian agency contracting officer. Does your answer change?
follow_ups.h: Which title of the U.S. Code did the FY26 NDAA actually amend?
follow_ups.d: Yes — and this is the trap. Section 1804(c) amended 10 U.S.C. 3702, which is DoD. Title 41 was never touched, so civilian agencies remain at $2.5 million and the specialist's original answer would have been correct there. A candidate who states one figure without naming the agency has answered half the question.

follow_ups.q: What if the estimated price were $11 million?
follow_ups.h: Walk the exceptions before you walk the threshold.
follow_ups.d: Over the DoD threshold you still check the exceptions at RFO 15.403-2 first — adequate price competition, prices set by law or regulation, a commercial product or service, or an HCA waiver. The threshold tells you when to look; the exceptions tell you whether to require.

cites.quote: In lieu of the requirements of FAR 15.403-3(a), obtain certified cost or pricing data when a prime contract is expected to exceed $10 million and is awarded after June 30, 2026
Certified cost or pricing data must not be obtained for acquisitions at or below the simplified acquisition threshold.

Unless prohibited because an exception at 15.403-2 applies, the HCA without power of delegation, may authorize the contracting officer to obtain certified cost or pricing data for pricing actions below the pertinent threshold in paragraph (a) of this subsection, provided the action exceeds the simplified acquisition threshold.

25m.scenario: In a competitive source selection for base operating support, the evaluation team flags that one offeror's technical proposal assumes a staffing level well below every other proposal and below the independent estimate. The offeror's price is the lowest received by a wide margin. The team wants to leave the price alone and simply rate the technical approach as a weakness.
25m.ask: The team says the price is the price and the market will sort it out. How do you advise them?
25m.script: That is where cost realism belongs. Under RFO 15.404-3 I independently review each offeror's proposed cost elements to see whether they are realistic for the work, reflect a clear understanding of the requirement, and are consistent with the offeror's own technical proposal — which is exactly what is failing here, because the staffing in the technical volume does not support the price in the cost volume. On a cost-reimbursement action that produces a probable cost I must use for evaluation. The team's instinct to note it as a technical weakness is not wrong, but it is not sufficient on its own.

follow_ups.q: This is a fixed-price competition, not cost-reimbursement. May you adjust the offered price?
follow_ups.h: Separate what realism informs from what it changes.
follow_ups.d: No. On competitive fixed-price proposals realism results may inform performance-risk and responsibility assessments, but proposals are evaluated on the RFP criteria and the offered prices are not adjusted. A candidate who says 'I would adjust their price up to realistic' has just described a protest.

follow_ups.q: Where does this show up in your source selection decision?
follow_ups.h: What does the SSA actually have to document?
follow_ups.d: RFO 15.205 requires the decision to represent the SSA's independent judgement on a comparative assessment against all the RFP criteria, documented with the rationale for business judgments and tradeoffs. If realism drove the award away from the lowest price, the rationale for that is the document.

cites.quote: Cost realism analysis is the process of independently reviewing and evaluating specific elements of each offeror's proposed cost estimate to determine whether the estimated proposed cost elements are realistic for the work to be performed
The source selection decision must represent the SSA’s independent judgement and be based on a comparative assessment of proposals against all source selection criteria in the RFP.

25m.scenario: Proposals are in for a $30 million services competition. One offeror's price volume has an obvious transposition — a labor rate entered as $8,400 where every other page says $84.00. Your specialist wants to email the offeror to confirm the intended number and calls it a clarification. Nobody has established a competitive range.
25m.ask: Is that exchange a clarification, and may you have it?
25m.script: Clarifications are limited exchanges that let offerors clarify certain aspects of a proposal or resolve minor clerical errors, and a transposed rate contradicted everywhere else in the proposal is close to the paradigm case. What I will not do is let it drift — the moment the exchange lets the offeror revise its proposal, I am in negotiations, and negotiations require a competitive range. So I bound the exchange tightly, document what I asked and what came back, and treat any answer that changes price or approach as the trigger to stop and restructure the acquisition.

follow_ups.q: The offeror answers and volunteers a lower price on two other line items. Now what?
follow_ups.h: What did they just turn your clarification into?
follow_ups.d: That is a proposal revision, and accepting it converts the exchange into negotiations conducted with one offeror outside a competitive range. The candidate should say they would not accept the revision, would document the unsolicited material, and would consider whether the acquisition now requires a competitive range and negotiations with everyone in it.

follow_ups.q: If you do decide to hold negotiations, what has to happen first?
follow_ups.h: Who gets in the room?
follow_ups.d: A competitive range — the group of evaluated proposals the contracting officer determines are best suited for further negotiation, which RFO 15.204-1 requires whenever negotiations will occur after evaluating competitive proposals. Negotiating with one offeror and calling it efficiency is the fastest route to a sustained protest.

cites.quote: Agencies must evaluate each competitive proposal based solely on the factors and subfactors in the RFP.

A competitive range is the group of evaluated proposals that the contracting officer determines are best suited for further negotiation. Contracting officers must establish a competitive range if negotiations will occur after evaluating competitive proposals.

25m.scenario: A program office wants to run a $22 million recapitalization of test equipment as lowest price technically acceptable. Their reasoning is that the specification is tight, the items are commercial, and tradeoff evaluations take months they do not have. The technical lead privately tells you that vendor reliability has varied enormously on past buys.
25m.ask: They want LPTA. Do you agree, and how do you make that call?
25m.script: LPTA is appropriate when it is in the Government's best interest to award to the technically acceptable proposal with the lowest evaluated price, and it does not permit tradeoffs — technical merit above acceptable buys nothing. So the real question is whether I can write acceptability criteria that capture what the technical lead just told me. If reliability differences are material and I cannot reduce them to a pass/fail bar, LPTA is the wrong instrument and I should say so before the RFP goes out, not after the award.

follow_ups.q: Does DoD have anything to say about using LPTA here?
follow_ups.h: The RFO's limitations open with two words that matter to you.
follow_ups.d: Yes — and this is where a civilian-trained answer fails. RFO 15.103-2's limitations open 'Except for DoD,' and DoD's own limitations and outright prohibitions live at R-DFARS 215.103-270, which separates what you must avoid to the maximum extent practicable from what you must not do at all. Knowing that split is the answer.

follow_ups.q: If you go LPTA, what must the RFP say?
follow_ups.h: What does an offeror need to know to compete?
follow_ups.d: The approach does not permit tradeoffs and the solicitation has to state the minimum requirements that establish technical acceptability. Vague acceptability criteria are how LPTA competitions get protested and how you end up defending an award you did not want to make.

cites.quote: The lowest price technically acceptable (LPTA) approach to source selection is appropriate when it is in the Government’s best interest to award to the offeror that submits a technically acceptable proposal with the lowest evaluated price.

25m.scenario: You are about to release the RFP on a $40 million competition. The program manager has assembled an evaluation team of engineers and a cost analyst, and has told you who the source selection authority will be — a senior program office official, appointed by nobody in particular. Your name is on the contract.
25m.ask: Who is the source selection authority on this acquisition, and how do you handle that conversation?
25m.script: By default it is me. Under RFO 15.201 the contracting officer is designated as the SSA unless the agency head appoints another individual for that acquisition or group of acquisitions — the program office cannot simply name one. So the conversation is not adversarial: either the agency head makes that appointment properly, or the authority sits with me. Either way the SSA has to establish an evaluation team tailored to the acquisition, and I want that team documented before the RFP goes out, not reconstructed afterward.

follow_ups.q: The agency head does appoint the program official. What is left for you?
follow_ups.h: Authority moved. Did responsibility?
follow_ups.d: Plenty — the contract is still signed by a contracting officer, and the evaluation still has to run against the stated criteria with a documented decision. A candidate who treats an SSA appointment as handing off their own responsibilities has missed that the two roles coexist.

follow_ups.q: For DoD, is there anything else the SSA owes before the solicitation issues?
follow_ups.h: Think about what has to be approved, and when.
follow_ups.d: For high-dollar-value acquisitions DoD expects the SSA to approve a source selection plan before the solicitation is issued. Waiting until after release to formalize the plan is a common finding and an easy one for a panel to probe.

cites.quote: A contracting officer is designated as the source selection authority (SSA), unless the agency head appoints another individual for a particular acquisition or group of acquisitions.

25m.topic: Certified Cost or Pricing Data & Proposal Analysis
25m.scenario: A sole-source proposal for $18 million arrives with no comparable commercial sales and no recent competitive award to price against. Your specialist proposes to justify price reasonableness by pointing to what the Government paid the same contractor for a similar effort four years ago, escalated for inflation.
25m.ask: Is prior price paid a sufficient basis here?
25m.script: It is a technique, not a conclusion. Price analysis under RFO 15.404-1 examines a proposed price without evaluating separate cost elements, and comparison to previous prices is one of the recognized techniques — but only if the prior price was itself established as fair and reasonable and the conditions are genuinely comparable. A four-year-old sole-source price escalated forward proves that we paid it, not that it was right. On an $18 million action I want cost analysis behind it.

follow_ups.q: For DoD, does the preferred method change when there is no adequate price competition?
follow_ups.h: There is a DoD-specific instruction on which technique to reach for first.
follow_ups.d: Yes. R-DFARS 215.404-170 makes market-price-based pricing the preferred method absent adequate price competition, and cautions that reasonableness must not rest solely on historical prices paid by the Government — which is precisely what the specialist proposed.

follow_ups.q: The contractor says the price is fair because it is the same rate on their GSA schedule. Does that settle it?
follow_ups.h: A schedule price is a ceiling, not a determination.
follow_ups.d: A schedule price has been determined fair and reasonable for the schedule, not for this quantity, this delivery, or this scope. The candidate should treat it as one input, and should say what else they would look at before signing.

cites.quote: Price analysis is the process of examining and evaluating a proposed price without evaluating its separate cost elements and proposed profit.

25m.scenario: You awarded a $28 million contract on Tuesday. An unsuccessful offeror requested a debriefing on Thursday, you offered Friday, and they declined the offered date and asked for the following week. On the Monday after award you receive notice from GAO that a protest has been filed.
25m.ask: Walk me through your obligation on performance right now.
25m.script: I need to work the clock before I do anything else, and for a DoD action I do not work it from FAR 33.105-3 alone. R-DFARS 233.105-370 replaces the trigger dates with a latest-of test: ten days after award, ten days after a task or delivery order over $25 million is issued, five days after a debriefing date offered — expressly whether or not the protester accepted it — and five days after a required postaward debriefing is concluded. I take the latest of those that applies, and if the protest landed inside it, performance suspends or the award is terminated.

follow_ups.q: They declined the debriefing date we offered. Does that help us?
follow_ups.h: Read the trigger literally.
follow_ups.d: No, and this is the trap. The five-day clock runs from the debriefing date offered regardless of whether the protester rejected it. A candidate who reasons 'they declined, so the clock never started' has just let a contractor perform through a live stay.

follow_ups.q: When is a required postaward debriefing actually 'concluded' for DoD?
follow_ups.h: It is not when everyone leaves the room.
follow_ups.d: Under the DoD enhanced-debriefing procedures the offeror gets two business days to submit additional written questions and the agency responds within five business days, and the debriefing is not concluded until that written response is delivered. Conclusion is what starts the clock, so treating the meeting as the end date understates your exposure.

cites.quote: contracting officers must immediately suspend performance or terminate the award using the time periods in paragraphs (a) through (d) of this section, whichever is later, in lieu of the time periods in FAR 33.105-3(b)(1) if the agency receives notice of a protest from the GAO.

25m.scenario: Award went out three weeks ago on a $26 million competition. An unsuccessful offeror's counsel sends a detailed request asking for the winner's technical scores, the source selection decision document, and the evaluators' individual worksheets.
25m.ask: What do you give them, and what do you refuse?
25m.script: A postaward debriefing is a defined thing, not a discovery request. RFO 15.301-1 sets who may request one and when, and fixes the minimum content — the evaluation of their own proposal, the overall evaluated cost and technical rating of the awardee, the rationale for award, and reasonable responses to relevant questions. What I do not hand over is another offeror's proprietary and confidential information or a point-by-point comparison of proposals. Individual evaluator worksheets are not on the list and I would not release them.

follow_ups.q: They ask for the source selection decision document itself. Is that ever released?
follow_ups.h: There is a dollar-value answer, and DoD has its own numbers.
follow_ups.d: It can be. The RFO provides for redacted SSDD disclosure at defined DoD contract values, and R-DFARS 215.301-170(b) restates those tiers at DoD-specific figures. The honest board answer names both authorities and says which one governs the action in front of you rather than picking a number.

follow_ups.q: Does holding the debriefing affect anything other than good relations?
follow_ups.h: Think about what starts running.
follow_ups.d: Yes — debriefing dates and conclusion drive protest timeliness and the CICA stay window. Treating a debriefing as a courtesy rather than a scheduled legal event is how agencies lose the ability to control their own timeline.

cites.quote: The awardee and offerors that received the award notice at 15.207-2 may request a postaward debriefing after receiving a notice of contract award.

25m.topic: Certified Cost or Pricing Data & Proposal Analysis
25m.scenario: You issued a solicitation expecting three capable offerors on a $14 million requirement. One proposal arrives. Your specialist says that is still adequate price competition because you had a reasonable expectation of competition when you issued it, and proposes to skip certified cost or pricing data on that basis.
25m.ask: Can you rely on the expectation of competition here?
25m.script: Not as an Air Force buyer. That route exists — but read the heading it sits under. In RFO 15.403-2 the expectation-of-competition basis is nested under a paragraph that applies to agencies other than DoD, NASA and the Coast Guard. It is not available to me. What I have instead is one offer that I must price on its own merits, and DoD has its own resolicit-or-certify machinery for exactly this situation.

follow_ups.q: So what does DoD require when only one offer comes in?
follow_ups.h: There is a specific DoD rule about what you do next.
follow_ups.d: R-DFARS 215.202-71 governs — the general expectation is to resolicit for an additional period, with a path involving price reasonableness determination or certified data, a defined set of exceptions, and an HCA waiver. A candidate who says 'one offer, so I just do a price analysis' has skipped the rule that applies to them.

follow_ups.q: Which exceptions to certified cost or pricing data are still open to you?
follow_ups.h: Go back to the list and take out the one that is closed.
follow_ups.d: The rest of RFO 15.403-2 still applies — prices set by law or regulation, a commercial product or service including commercial modifications, and an HCA waiver. Knowing which single route is closed to DoD, and that the others remain, is the sophisticated answer.

cites.quote: (ii) For agencies other than DoD, NASA, and the Coast Guard, a price is also based on adequate price competition when (A) There was a reasonable expectation, based on market research or other assessment, that two or more responsible offerors, competing independently, would submit priced offers in response to the request for proposal’s (RFP) expressed requirement, even though only one offer is received from a responsible offeror

25m.scenario: A multiple-award solicitation for engineering support services will result in several awards for the same or similar services, and the acquisition strategy is to award to every qualifying offeror. The program office asks whether they can skip price evaluation at the master contract level and compete price only at the order level.
25m.ask: Must price or cost be evaluated in this source selection?
25m.script: For most agencies, yes — but this is one of the places DoD is treated differently and the strategy they described is the exact fact pattern. Under RFO 15.104 contracting officers for DoD, NASA and the Coast Guard may choose not to include price or cost as an evaluation factor when the solicitation is above the simplified acquisition threshold, will result in multiple-award contracts for the same or similar services, and states that the Government intends to award to each and all qualifying offerors. All three conditions hold here, so the answer is that they can — and price consideration moves to the order level.

follow_ups.q: Does that exception have a limit?
follow_ups.h: Think about what kind of orders might ride the contract.
follow_ups.d: It does not reach multiple-award solicitations that provide for sole-source 8(a) orders. A candidate who states the exception without its carve-out has given an answer that is right until the program adds an 8(a) lane.

follow_ups.q: If one of those three conditions failed, what changes?
follow_ups.h: The exception is conjunctive.
